steps.text: Heat the oil and fry the chopped onion for 5 minutes. Add the garlic, chilli powder and cumin and cook for a minute.
Add the beef and brown it, breaking it up with a spoon.
Stir in the tomatoes and kidney beans, then simmer gently for 25 minutes, stirring now and then.
Season to taste and serve with rice.
Beat the eggs with a pinch of salt and pepper until no streaks of white remain.
Melt the butter in a non-stick pan over medium heat until it foams.
Pour in the eggs. As they set, push the edges to the middle with a spatula and tilt the pan so raw egg runs underneath.
When the top is still slightly soft, scatter the cheese over one half.
Fold the omelette in half, slide it onto a plate and serve straight away.
Mix the soy sauce and honey in a small bowl.
Heat the oil in a wok over high heat and stir-fry the chicken for 5 to 6 minutes until cooked through. Lift it out.
Add the broccoli, sliced pepper, garlic and grated ginger and stir-fry for 3 minutes, adding a splash of water if it catches.
Return the chicken, pour in the sauce and toss for a minute until glossy.
Serve over rice.
Heat the oil and fry the chopped onion for 5 minutes until soft.
Add the garlic and curry powder and stir for a minute until fragrant.
Pour in the coconut milk and chickpeas and simmer for 10 minutes.
Stir in the spinach until it wilts, season, and serve with rice.
Heat the oil in a wok or large frying pan over high heat.
Add the peas and stir-fry for 2 minutes.
Push everything to one side, crack in the eggs and scramble them until just set.
Add the rice and stir-fry for 3 to 4 minutes, breaking up any clumps, until piping hot.
Stir in the soy sauce and sliced spring onions, then serve.
Whisk the flour, eggs and milk into a smooth, thin batter and rest it for 10 minutes.
Heat a little butter in a frying pan over medium heat.
Pour in just enough batter to coat the base, swirling the pan. Cook for a minute until golden underneath, then flip and cook for 30 seconds more.
Serve with a squeeze of lemon and a sprinkle of sugar.
Melt the butter in a large pan and soften the sliced leeks over low heat for 8 minutes.
Add the peeled, diced potatoes and the stock. Bring to the boil, then simmer for 15 to 20 minutes until the potatoes are soft.
Blend until smooth, stir in the milk and warm through.
Season with salt and pepper and serve.
Bring a large pot of salted water to the boil and cook the pasta until just tender.
Meanwhile, warm the olive oil in a pan and gently fry the sliced garlic for a minute without letting it brown.
Add the tomatoes and a pinch of salt and simmer for 10 minutes until thickened.
Drain the pasta, keeping a splash of the cooking water, and toss it through the sauce, loosening with the water if needed.
Serve with torn basil and grated parmesan.
Boil the soaked cod for twenty minutes, drain, cool it and flake it, discarding skin and bones.
Fry the onion and pepper in the oil for eight minutes, add the thyme and the whole scotch bonnet: uncut, it gives aroma without heat.
Add the cod and tomatoes and cook through for five minutes.
Tip in the ackee, add black pepper and warm it two minutes, swirling the pan only. No spatula.
Lift out the chilli and serve with fried plantain, bread or boiled ground provisions.
Marinate the chicken in the soy with the crushed garlic and peppercorns for thirty minutes.
Lift the chicken out, dry it and brown it skin down. Keep the marinade.
Pour in the marinade, water and vinegar, add the bay and sugar. Bring it to the boil and neither stir nor cover for ten minutes.
Cover and simmer for twenty-five minutes, turning the chicken once.
Uncover and reduce the sauce for five to ten minutes, spooning it over the chicken. Serve with rice.
Beat the softened butter with the sugar until pale, about four minutes.
Sift the flour with the cocoa and salt and fold it in with a spatula to an even dough.
Add the cornflakes and fold them through in one movement, trying not to break them.
Drop the dough onto a tray by the spoonful and press each one down lightly.
Bake at 180 °C for eighteen minutes; the biscuits stay soft to the touch and firm up as they cool.
Cool them completely on the tray, without trying to lift them hot.
Whisk the icing sugar with the cocoa and hot water into a thick icing, coat the biscuits and press a walnut half into each.
Poach the chicken breast in salted water for twenty minutes and pull it into fine threads by hand.
Soak the crustless bread in the milk for ten minutes.
Fry the onion and garlic until soft, add the ají paste and turmeric and cook five minutes.
Blend the soaked bread with its milk, the walnuts and the fried onion until smooth.
Return the mixture to the pan and cook it ten minutes on a low heat, stirring.
Stir in the chicken and parmesan, season and warm it five minutes to the thickness of soured cream.
Serve over boiled potato and rice, garnished with egg and olives.
Poach the chicken in two and a half litres of water with the spring onion and coriander for forty minutes. Lift it out and shred it; strain the broth.
Return the broth to the pot, add the small yellow potatoes and cook twenty minutes, until they collapse entirely and thicken the soup.
Add the other two potato varieties and the corn and cook twenty minutes more.
Add the guascas five minutes before the end: boiled long, they turn bitter.
Return the chicken, season, and serve with bowls of cream, capers and sliced avocado on the table.
Roast the peppers and aubergines at 220 °C or over a flame until blistered black all over.
Pile them hot into a covered pot for twenty minutes: the steam lifts the skin by itself.
Peel and seed them and leave the flesh in a colander for two or three hours. Do not press: the water should drain on its own.
Put it through a mincer or chop it by hand — not a blender: what is wanted is a coarse texture rather than a purée.
Reduce it in a pot with half the oil over a low flame for an hour, stirring every ten minutes.
Add the garlic, vinegar, salt and the rest of the oil and cook another half hour, until the oil starts separating. Pack it hot into sterilised jars.
Beat the softened butter with the icing sugar until pale, about four minutes.
Add the yolks one at a time, then the vanilla, zest and brandy.
Sift the cornflour with the flour, baking powder and salt and fold it in without long working.
Wrap the dough in film and refrigerate it an hour.
Roll it half a centimetre thick and cut four-centimetre rounds.
Bake at 170 °C for twelve minutes; the biscuits should stay pale, with only the underside going golden.
Cool them completely, sandwich them in pairs with dulce de leche and roll the sides in coconut.
Mix the oats, flour, coconut, sugar and salt in a large bowl.
Melt the butter with the golden syrup over a low heat, without letting it boil.
Dissolve the bicarbonate in the boiling water and pour it straight into the butter mixture; it foams up.
Pour the foaming mixture into the dry ingredients and stir until even.
Roll walnut-sized balls and set them on a tray with generous gaps between them.
Flatten each ball with your palm to a centimetre thick; they spread further in the oven.
Bake at 160 °C for twelve to eighteen minutes and cool them on the tray rather than a rack.
Knead a dough from the flour, warm water, oil and a pinch of salt for ten minutes, until smooth and very elastic. Oil it, cover it and leave it an hour.
Fry the breadcrumbs in half the butter until golden. Mix the apples with the sugar, cinnamon, raisins, lemon juice and zest.
Spread a cloth on the table, dust it with flour and stretch the dough with the backs of your hands from the centre outwards, until it is transparent. Trim the thick edges.
Brush the dough with melted butter, scatter the crumbs over a third of it and pile the apples onto them, leaving a border.
Roll it up by lifting the cloth — by hand the dough tears. Tuck the ends under, move it seam down onto a tray and brush with butter.
Bake at 190 °C for forty minutes, brushing with butter twice along the way. Serve warm, dusted with icing sugar.
Soak the purple corn in cold water overnight, keeping that water in the morning.
Grind the corn with its water in a blender to an even purple liquid.
Strain it through a fine sieve, pressing the pulp, and strain it a second time.
Add the remaining water, the cinnamon, cloves and orange peel.
Cook over medium heat for forty minutes, stirring with a wooden spoon, until it thickens.
Add the sugar and lemon juice and cook five minutes more.
Remove the spices and serve it hot in mugs, with a fried cheese pastry.
Peel the apples, cut them into thick wedges and spread them in a buttered dish.
Scatter half the sugar and the cinnamon over the apples and toss them lightly in the dish.
Rub the cold butter into the flour with the remaining sugar and salt, using your fingertips, to a coarse crumb.
Mix in the oats and scatter the crumble over the apples without pressing it down.
Bake at 190 °C for forty minutes, until the top is golden and juice bubbles at the edges.
Warm the milk and cream with the split vanilla pod, without letting it boil.
Whisk the yolks with the cornflour, pour in the hot milk in a thin stream and cook the sauce to thickness, stirring.
Dissolve the salt in the warm water and stir in the flour by hand. Add the butter and cheese.
Knead for three minutes and let it stand five. The dough should stop sticking and roll into a ball easily.
Shape cakes ten centimetres across and a centimetre and a half thick. Smooth the edges with wet fingers; cracks widen in the pan.
Griddle them with a drop of oil for four minutes a side, to a firm crust.
Finish them at 180 °C for ten minutes. A done arepa sounds hollow when tapped.
Split them hot lengthways, not all the way through, and stuff them: cheese, avocado, stewed meat or egg.
Boil the beans, chickpeas and lentils separately until soft; each takes its own time.
Parboil the cracked wheat and the rice and drain them.
Fry the chopped onion in oil until golden and add the tomato paste and paprika.
Combine all the grains and pulses with the onion, season, and stir in the coriander.
Rinse the cabbage leaves of excess brine and pare down the thick ribs.
Roll the filling in the leaves into tight parcels, packing them in layers in a pot.
Add water to the level of the top layer, cover with a weighted plate and cook an hour on a low heat. Cool it completely.
Pour the coconut milk into a heavy pot and cook it over medium heat, stirring.
Keep cooking until the milk separates into oil and brown solids.
The moment the solids turn deep brown, add the water at once to stop the caramelisation.
Add the sugar, salt and raisins and bring it to the boil.
Rinse the rice until the water runs clear and add it to the pot in an even layer.
Cook uncovered over medium heat until the liquid falls to the level of the rice.
Cover it, drop the heat to its lowest and hold it twenty minutes without opening it once.
Rub the chicken with salt, pepper, cumin, oregano, garlic and lime juice and leave it half an hour.
Brown the chicken in olive oil on all sides and lift it out.
Sweat the onion, pepper and garlic in the same oil for twenty minutes, until completely soft; that is the sofrito.
Add the tomato sauce and the saffron steeped in a spoon of warm water and cook five minutes.
Return the chicken, add the beer and stock, bring it up and season.
Add the rice in an even layer, cover and cook twenty minutes on a low heat without stirring.
Scatter the peas and olives over the top, cover and let it stand ten minutes before serving.
Light the firewood to one side of the grate and let it burn down to embers, about forty minutes.
Mix the parsley, garlic, oregano, vinegar, oil and chilli flakes; the chimichurri needs an hour to stand.
Rake a thin layer of embers under part of the grate and lay on the sausages; they go first.
Salt the ribs coarsely all over and lay them bone side down over a moderate heat.
Cook the ribs bone down for two hours, adjusting the embers so a palm can stay above the grate for seven seconds.
Turn the ribs and give them forty minutes meat side down, for a crust.
Add the flank for the last twenty minutes, rest the meat ten and serve it with the chimichurri.
Pierce the meat in several places with a knife, rub it with salt, pepper and garlic and leave it an hour.
Melt the panela in oil in a heavy pot until nearly black, without stirring it with a spoon.
Lower the beef into the caramel and sear it on all sides to a black crust, about fifteen minutes.
Lift out the meat and fry the onion, pepper, carrot and leek in the same fat until soft.
Return the meat, add the tomatoes, wine, Worcestershire sauce and bay, and add water to half its height.
Braise covered for four hours on the lowest heat, turning the joint every hour.
Lift out the meat, strain the sauce, reduce it by half and slice the beef across the grain.
Knead a dough from the flour, water and salt and rest it forty minutes under film.
Chop the spring onion very fine, salt it and wring it out in a cloth.
Fry the onion with the mince, add the tomato paste and stew it twenty minutes.
Whisk the yoghurt with crushed garlic and salt and leave it at room temperature.
Roll the dough thin and cut eight-centimetre rounds.
Add the leek filling, fold each into a half-moon and crimp the edge tight.
Boil the dumplings five minutes, lay them on the yoghurt, spoon the sauce over and dust with mint and chilli.
Brown the meat with the onion and garlic, then add the tomato paste and coriander.
Add water, season and stew forty minutes, until the meat is tender.
Stir in the peanut butter and rain in the ground okra in a thin stream, stirring constantly.
Cook the sauce ten minutes; it turns thick and stringy.
Bring a litre of salted water to the boil, set a cup aside and rain in the flour, working it with a stick.
Work it fifteen minutes, adding the reserved water, until the mass is dense and smooth.
Turn the asida onto a platter with a wet spoon, make a hollow and pour the mulah into it.
Grind the garlic, ginger, chilli, stock cube, salt and oil into a paste.
Slash the fish at the sides and rub the paste inside the cuts and over the skin. Leave it twenty minutes.
Break up the attiéké with your hands, sprinkle it with hot water and salt it.
Cover it and let it steam ten minutes, in a steamer or simply covered somewhere warm.
Slice the onion, tomatoes and chilli and mix them with lemon juice, salt and a spoon of oil.
Grill the fish over coals or in a griddle pan, seven minutes a side.
Serve the attiéké, fish and salad on one plate, with a wedge of lemon.
Cover the chicken with two and a half litres of cold water, bring it up and skim.
Add the onion, carrot and celery and simmer forty-five minutes.
Lift out the chicken, strain the broth and return it to the heat. Cook the rice in it for fifteen minutes.
Pull the meat into threads, discarding skin and bones.
Whisk the eggs with the lemon juice to an even froth in a separate bowl.
Ladle hot broth into the egg and lemon mixture, whisking without stopping, until the bowl warms up.
Pour the mixture back into the pot off the heat, return the meat and warm it through without boiling.
Poach the soaked cod for five minutes, cool it and pull it into flakes by hand, discarding skin and bones. By hand rather than with a fork: that is how small bones are found.
Deep-fry the potato matchsticks at 180 °C to a crisp gold, in batches. Drain on a rack and salt them.
In a wide pan sweat the onion in the olive oil for ten minutes until soft and sweet, adding the garlic for the last minute.
Add the cod and warm it through for three minutes, then tip in the potato and toss.
Take the pan off the heat, pour in the beaten eggs and stir without stopping for half a minute, until they turn creamy. Scatter over the parsley and olives.
Make the syrup: bring the sugar and water to the boil, cook fifteen minutes, add the lemon juice and cool it completely.
Melt the butter and let it settle — use only the clear upper layer and discard the sediment.
Lay twenty sheets into a greased tin, brushing each with butter. Scatter the pistachios in an even layer.
Cover with twenty more sheets, brushing each in the same way. Butter the top sheet especially generously.
Cut it into diamonds with a sharp knife, right down to the base of the tin.
Bake at 170 °C for an hour, to a deep gold. Take it out and pour the cold syrup into the cuts at once.
Leave it six hours, better overnight. Cutting and serving earlier is pointless: the syrup has not reached the lower layers.
Rub the flour with the fat and salt to a crumb, add the hot water and knead a soft dough.
Divide it into eight balls, oil them and rest them twenty minutes under a cloth.
Fry the onion in oil, add the cooked beans with some of their liquid and mash them smooth.
Fry the purée over medium heat for ten minutes, until it holds its shape on a spoon.
Roll the balls into thin twenty-centimetre rounds.
Cook them on a hot dry pan a minute a side, to spotted but not dried out.
Spread beans over half the tortilla, add cream and cheese, fold it over and serve hot.
Beat the softened butter with the sugar with a wooden spoon for twenty minutes, to a pale fluffy mass.
Add the yolks one at a time, still beating in the same direction.
Add the vanilla, salt and soda and beat five minutes more.
Work in the cornmeal a little at a time, to a firm but pliable dough.
Rest the dough fifteen minutes so the meal takes up the moisture.
Shape walnut-sized balls and set them well apart on parchment.
Bake at 170 °C for twenty minutes, to a pale gold edge, and cool them on the tray.
Boil the beans with the chopped green plantain for an hour and a half, until soft and thick.
Simmer the pork belly in salted water for forty minutes and dry it thoroughly.
Fry the belly skin down in deep oil until the skin blisters and crisps.
Make the hogao: fry the onion with the tomato and cumin, add the mince and cook it through.
Fry the chorizo, cook the rice and fry slices of ripe plantain to a caramel colour.
Cook the arepas on a dry pan and fry the eggs with runny yolks.
Build the tray: beans, rice, mince, chicharrón, chorizo, egg, arepa, plantain and avocado side by side.
Stir the vinegar, sugar and a pinch of salt into 100 ml of warm water until dissolved. Pour it over the carrot and daikon and leave for an hour at room temperature.
Marinate the pork in fish sauce with a spoon of sugar for twenty minutes, then sear it over a high flame for three minutes a side, until the edges caramelise.
Warm the baguettes at 200 °C for five minutes so the crust crisps again. Split them lengthways, not all the way through.
Spread pâté on one half and mayonnaise on the other. Layer in the pork, the drained pickles, cucumber, coriander and chilli. Press it shut with your palm and serve at once.
Crush the cheese with a fork and work in four of the eggs: the filling should stay crumbly rather than becoming a paste.
Mix the melted butter with the sunflower oil: that lets the sheets crisp without burning.
Lay two overlapping filo sheets, brush with the fat, scatter the filling in a crumbly line along the long edge and roll it loosely.
Coil the roll into a round tin from the centre outwards, leaving a couple of millimetres between the turns.
Whisk the yoghurt with the last egg and the bicarbonate and pour it over, aiming into the gaps between the coils.
Bake at 180 °C for forty-five minutes, to a deep gold. Cover with a cloth for ten minutes out of the oven.
Mix the maize and cassava doughs with a litre of water and salt to a smooth, lump-free batter.
Set it over medium heat and work it with a wooden paddle without stopping. It starts to thicken after five minutes.
Keep working it for twenty minutes, pressing it against the sides, until it turns dense and glossy.
Shape balls with wet hands and wrap each in film or a banana leaf.
Rub the fish with salt, ginger and garlic and grill or pan-fry it eight minutes a side.
Grind the tomatoes, habaneros, onion, salt and a spoon of oil in a mortar to a coarse sauce.
Serve a ball of banku, the fish and a bowl of sauce. It is eaten by hand, pinching off dough and dipping it.
Cut three slashes on each side of the fish and pat it completely dry.
Work the garlic with the butter, lemon myrtle, lime zest, salt and pepper.
Rub the mixture into the slashes and the cavity and tuck slices of lime and fennel inside.
Wrap the fish in foil with the seams on top so the juices do not run out.
Light the coals and rake them to the sides; the heat under the fish has to be indirect.
Cook it in the foil for twenty minutes, turning the parcel once halfway.
Unwrap it, move the fish onto an oiled grate over the coals and give it a minute a side for the crust.
Dissolve the yeast and sugar in the warm milk and leave it ten minutes, until it foams.
Work in the eggs, melted butter, salt and flour to a soft dough. It should stay slightly tacky.
Cover and leave somewhere warm for an hour, until the dough has doubled.
Knock it back, roll it out a centimetre and a half thick and cut it into three-centimetre squares or diamonds.
Let the pieces stand under a cloth for twenty minutes; this second rise is the reason for the hollow.
Heat the oil to 170 °C and fry in batches for two to three minutes, turning, to an even gold.
Drain on paper and serve warm, with tea, soured cream or honey.
Cover the meat with cold water, bring it up, boil two minutes and drain; this removes the scum.
Fry the ginger, garlic and doubanjiang in oil for five minutes, until the oil turns red.
Add the tomatoes, wine and soy sauce, cook three minutes and return the meat to the pot.
Add water two fingers above the meat, drop in the star anise, cinnamon and sugar and simmer two hours.
Lift out the meat, cut it into thick slices and return it to the broth for ten minutes.
Cook the noodles in a separate pot of clean water and blanch the bok choy.
Divide the noodles between bowls, add the meat and greens, ladle over the broth and top with pickled mustard greens and spring onion.
Cut the beef across the grain into centimetre strips, pat them dry and pepper them.
Heat a pan hard and sear the beef in batches for ninety seconds, without turning it often.
Lift out the meat and fry the mushrooms over a high flame until their water has gone.
Add the butter and onion and fry until soft and golden.
Stir in the flour, cook it a minute and add the stock, stirring until smooth.
Take the pan off the heat, stir in the soured cream and mustard, and season.
Return the meat with its juices, warm it a minute without boiling and scatter with parsley.
Simmer the chicken and veal with the onion, carrot and celeriac for an hour, skimming.
Lift out the meat, strain the broth and pull the chicken into fine threads.
Rinse the okra under cold water and pat it dry without trimming the caps.
Melt the butter, stir in the flour and cook it two minutes without letting it colour.
Pour the broth into the roux, add the okra and cook fifteen minutes.
Whisk the yolks with the soured cream and ladle in hot broth, stirring without stopping.
Take the pot off the heat, pour in the mixture, return the meat and warm it through without boiling. Add lemon and parsley.
Dissolve the yeast in the warm milk and leave it ten minutes, until it foams.
Knead a dough from the flour, yeast mixture, eggs, brown sugar, vanilla, cinnamon and salt.
Work in the softened butter in stages, kneading until the dough is smooth and elastic.
Let it rise somewhere warm for an hour and a half, until doubled.
Work the pearl sugar in by hand, distributing it evenly but without long kneading.
Divide the dough into ten lumps and rest them fifteen minutes.
Bake them in the iron three minutes each, to a deep gold with a caramel crust.
Cover the meat with cold water, bring it up, skim, and simmer on the lowest heat for two and a half hours with the peppercorns and bay.
Knead a stiff dough from the flour, eggs, water and salt and rest it under film for forty minutes.
Roll the dough a millimetre thick and cut it into squares of about eight centimetres.
Slice the onion into rings, pour a ladle of hot broth over it and leave it ten minutes; this is the sorpa that dresses the dish.
Lift out the meat, skim the fat into a separate bowl and boil the dough squares in that broth in batches, three to four minutes each.
Pull the meat apart into thin sheets across the grain. Lay the dough on a large platter, the meat on top, the onions and their broth over that.
Serve the remaining broth hot in bowls with herbs; it is drunk before the dish or alongside it.
Cover the meat with cold water, bring it up, skim and simmer two and a half hours with the peppercorns and bay.
Knead a stiff dough from the flour, eggs, water and salt and rest it forty minutes.
Roll it a millimetre thick and cut it into diamonds six centimetres across.
Render the mutton fat and cook the sliced onion in it until soft.
Add two ladles of broth to the onion and stew ten minutes into a thick gravy; that is the chyk.
Boil the dough diamonds in the strained broth in batches, four minutes each, and plate them straight away.
Pull the meat into sheets, lay it over the dough, spoon the chyk over and scatter with coriander. Serve the broth in bowls.
Dry-roast the moong dal for five minutes, to a nutty smell, and rinse it.
Rinse the rice and dry it. Wet rice will not toast; it steams in its own water.
Heat the ghee, brown the potatoes and lift them out.
In the same ghee fry the bay, cinnamon and cardamom, then the onion and ginger until golden.
Add the rice and dal with the turmeric and cumin and toast them five minutes, stirring.
Add boiling water at twice the volume of the grain, return the potatoes, season and add the whole chillies.
Cover and cook twenty minutes on a low heat, then let it stand ten minutes without opening it.
Marinate the beef in soy, garlic and a spoon of sesame oil for twenty minutes.
Blanch the spinach for thirty seconds, squeeze it dry and dress with sesame oil and a pinch of salt. Boil the sprouts three minutes and dress them the same way, with garlic.
Fry the carrot and the mushrooms separately, a couple of minutes each, seasoning each on its own. No need to wash the pan in between.
Sear the beef over a high flame for two minutes. Fry the eggs separately, leaving the yolks runny.
Divide the hot rice between bowls, arrange the vegetables and beef in sections, and top with an egg and a spoon of gochujang. Each person does the mixing.
Soak the dried mushrooms in a cup of warm water for half an hour and slice them, straining and keeping the water.
Squeeze the sauerkraut, shred the fresh cabbage and stew each in its own pot for thirty minutes.
Render the bacon to crackling, brown the pork and beef in its fat, then the onion.
Combine both cabbages, the meats, sausage, mushrooms with their water, prunes, tomato paste and spices in a large pot.
Add the wine, bring it up and stew two hours on the lowest heat, stirring occasionally.
Cool it completely and leave it a day in the cold, then bring it back to the boil and stew an hour.
Repeat the cycle once more on the third day. Serve with rye bread and a glass of vodka.
Dissolve the yeast and sugar in the warm milk and leave it ten minutes.
Knead a soft dough from the flour, eggs, yeast mixture, salt and two spoons of ghee, and work it fifteen minutes.
Let it rise somewhere warm for an hour, until doubled.
Divide it into ten balls, oil them and rest them twenty minutes under film.
Stretch the first ball by hand to the size of the tin, lay it in and brush it generously with ghee.
Repeat with the rest, buttering every layer. Brush the top one too and scatter it with nigella.
Bake at 190 °C for thirty-five minutes and pour the honey over immediately, while the bread is hot.
Cover the oats with water or apple juice and leave them overnight in the fridge.
In the morning stir in the yoghurt, cream and condensed milk until even.
Grate the apples, skins and all, on a coarse grater straight into the bowl.
Squeeze lemon juice over the grated apple at once and stir it through so it does not brown.
Toast the hazelnuts in a dry pan for five minutes and chop them coarsely.
Stir in the honey, divide it between bowls and top with the nuts and berries.
Simmer the beef in the stock for ninety minutes, until completely tender, and shred it fine.
Fry the onion in butter, stir in the flour and cook it three minutes without letting it colour.
Pour in the hot stock in a thin stream and cook it to a very thick paste, about ten minutes.
Stir in the meat, parsley, nutmeg, salt and pepper, spread it in a dish and chill it four hours.
Roll the set mixture into walnut-sized balls with damp hands.
Coat them in flour, egg and crumbs, chill them twenty minutes, then repeat the egg and crumbs.
Fry at 180 °C for three minutes, to a deep gold, and serve with mustard.
Soak the bread in half the milk for ten minutes and squeeze it out, keeping the milk.
Fry the onion in oil until soft, add the curry powder and turmeric and warm them a minute, until fragrant.
Add the mince and cook, breaking up lumps, until it loses its pink, about ten minutes.
Stir in the bread, apricots, raisins, chutney, vinegar, salt and pepper and take it off the heat.
Press it into a dish, level it and bake at 180 °C for forty minutes.
Beat the eggs with the remaining milk, pour it over, stand the bay leaves in the custard and scatter the almonds.
Return it to the oven for twenty minutes, until the custard sets and turns golden.
Knead a soft dough from the flour, warm water, a spoon of oil and salt.
Cover the dough and rest it thirty minutes.
Boil the potatoes soft, drain them and mash them without milk.
Work the spring onion, coriander, chilli, salt and pepper into the mash.
Divide the dough into six and roll each into a thin round.
Spread the filling thinly over half the round and fold the other half over, pressing the edge.
Cook them on a brush-oiled pan, four minutes a side, until spotted.
Dissolve the yeast with the sugar in the warm milk and leave it fifteen minutes, until it foams.
Knead a soft dough from the flour, sponge, egg, melted butter and salt.
Let it rise somewhere warm for an hour, until doubled.
Knock the dough back and roll it out to exactly a centimetre thick.
Cut it into four-centimetre diamonds and let them rest twenty minutes.
Heat the oil to 180 °C and lower the diamonds in in small batches.
Fry them a minute and a half a side, turning with a slotted spoon, to golden puffs.
Cover the meat with cold water, bring it to the boil and skim. Simmer for an hour and a half at a bare tremble — a rolling boil turns the stock cloudy.
Braise the beetroot in a pan with a spoon of oil, the tomato paste and the vinegar, covered, for about twenty minutes. The vinegar is what keeps the colour.
Separately fry the onion and carrot until soft and golden.
Lift the meat out, pull it into pieces and return it to the stock. Add the potatoes and give them ten minutes — before any acid reaches the pot.
Add the cabbage, then after five minutes the beetroot and the fried vegetables. Give it five minutes more, add the bay and garlic and take it straight off the heat.
Let it stand covered for at least twenty minutes. Serve with sour cream, which softens the acid and pulls the flavours together.
Make a stock from the ribs: an hour and a half at a bare simmer, skimmed. Lift the meat out and pull it apart.
Braise the beetroot separately with a spoon of oil, the tomato paste and the vinegar, covered, for twenty minutes. The vinegar is what holds the colour.
Fry the onion and carrot until soft. Put the potatoes into the stock and give them ten minutes, before any acid reaches the pot.
Add the cabbage, then after five minutes the beetroot, the fried vegetables and the beans. Give it five minutes.
Pound the salo with the garlic and herbs to a paste and stir it into the pot. Take it straight off the heat and let it stand covered for twenty minutes.
Cut all the vegetables into large pieces; they have to survive four hours without collapsing.
Line the bottom of the pot with the diced pork fat, put the meat on it and season.
Layer on the onion, carrot, parsley root, potato, peppers, cabbage and tomato.
Tuck in the whole head of garlic and the bay leaves, pour in the wine and add water to half the height of the pot.
Cover and put it in a 150 °C oven for four hours. Do not open it and do not stir.
Serve straight from the pot, digging to the bottom so every layer reaches the plate.
Soften the onion, leek and fennel in olive oil for ten minutes.
Add the small fish whole, the tomatoes, garlic, zest and saffron and cook five minutes.
Add two litres of water, bring it up and cook forty minutes, uncovered.
Press everything through a sieve, working the flesh through, and return the broth to the pot.
Cook the potatoes in the broth for fifteen minutes, then add the larger fish in order, firmest first.
Make the rouille: egg yolk, garlic, saffron, a pinch of cayenne and olive oil in a thin stream.
Serve the broth in bowls with croûtes and rouille, and the fish with the potatoes on a separate platter.
Mix the mashed potato with the tuna, chopped onion, capers, parsley, harissa, salt and pepper.
Heat the oil to 180 °C. Test with a scrap of pastry: it should surface at once and sizzle.
Lay a sheet on a plate, put two spoons of filling on one half and make a hollow in it.
Break an egg into the hollow, season it and fold the sheet over immediately, pressing the edges.
Slide the brik into the oil and fry forty seconds a side, steadying it with a slotted spoon.
Drain on paper and serve immediately with a wedge of lemon.
Grate the potatoes finely and squeeze them lightly; only a little water should go, as a dry mass will not bind.
Mix in the flour, egg and salt. The mass should slide off a spoon slowly rather than pour.
Fry the bacon in a dry pan until crisp and lift it out, keeping the fat.
Push the dough into boiling salted water through a colander with large holes. The dumplings are done when they float, after about three minutes.
Drain the dumplings, return them to the warm pan and stir in the brynza with a spoon of the cooking water. Keep the heat off.
Serve into bowls, spoon over the hot fat and scatter the crackling on top.
Put the guanciale into a cold dry pan and turn on a medium flame. A slow start renders the fat completely; a hot pan burns the outside and leaves it tough within.
When the pieces turn glassy and gold at the edges, lift half of them out for the top. Pour in the wine and let it cook away.
Crush the tomatoes by hand, add them with the chilli and simmer for ten minutes. The sauce should thicken without losing its red.
Boil the bucatini a minute short, move it into the sauce with a ladle of its water and finish it over the flame for half a minute.
Off the heat, stir in the pecorino and serve. The reserved guanciale goes on top with a little more cheese.
Dry the wings with kitchen paper, salt them and leave them uncovered on a rack in the fridge for at least four hours, better overnight.
Dust with the baking powder and toss so the coating is thin and even. Too much leaves a soapy taste.
Spread them on a rack over a tray and bake at 120 °C for twenty minutes: the fat renders out.
Raise the oven to 220 °C and bake another twenty-five minutes, to a deep gold and a crisp.
Melt the butter, take it off the heat and whisk in the pepper sauce, vinegar and garlic powder to an even emulsion.
Toss the hot wings with the sauce in a bowl and serve immediately with celery and blue cheese dip.
Marinate the belly slices and the mince separately in fish sauce, sugar, shallot, garlic and pepper for an hour.
Shape the mince into flat patties a centimetre thick; they cook fast and evenly.
Slice the papaya and carrot thin and pickle them in vinegar with sugar for twenty minutes.
Mix the fish sauce, sugar, lime juice, water, garlic and chilli and warm it through; that is the nước chấm.
Boil the vermicelli two minutes, rinse it in cold water and divide it between plates.
Grill the belly and the patties over coals, three minutes a side, to caramelised edges.
Drop the hot meat straight into the warm sauce with the pickles and serve with the noodles, lettuce and herbs.
Fry the onion in oil until deep gold and add the cinnamon, cardamom and curry leaves.
Stir in the ginger garlic paste and the curry powder and cook them two minutes.
Add the lamb and brown it, turning it through the spices.
Add the chopped tomatoes, season and stew covered for an hour on a low heat.
Add the potato in large pieces and stew twenty-five minutes more.
Uncover and reduce the sauce until a spoon leaves a trail in it.
Halve the loaves, pull out the crumb, fill them with the curry and set the crumb on top.
Knead a dough from the flour, warm water, a spoon of oil, the vinegar and salt, and work it fifteen minutes until elastic.
Divide it into four balls, oil them, cover and leave them forty minutes.
Mix the raw mince with the onion, salt, pepper and two spoons of water; the water keeps the filling from drying out.
Stretch a ball by hand on a cloth-covered table into a translucent sheet, working from the centre outwards.
Sprinkle the sheet with oil, lay the filling in a line along one edge and roll it into a long thin cylinder.
Coil the cylinders into a round tin from the centre outwards, brush with oil and bake at 200 °C for forty minutes.
Sprinkle the hot burek with water and cover it with a cloth for five minutes to soften the crust. Serve with yoghurt.
Rinse the tripe several times, rub it with salt and rinse it again until completely clean.
Boil the tripe in water with half the vinegar for ten minutes and throw away that first water.
Cover it with fresh water and the bay and simmer three hours, until completely tender.
Boil the beans separately until soft, an hour and a quarter, and set them aside with their liquid.
Fry the pancetta and the sliced chorizo, add the onion, carrot and celery and sweat them ten minutes.
Stir in the paprika and tomatoes, add the sliced tripe with some of its broth and the potato.
Cook twenty-five minutes, stir in the beans with their liquid, season and warm it ten more.
Rub the flour into the cold butter to a coarse crumb and bring the dough together with iced water.
Wrap it in film and chill it half an hour, without long kneading.
Roll the pastry and line muffin tins with it, taking the sides right to the top.
Melt the butter and stir in the sugar, maple syrup, vinegar, vanilla and salt.
Cool the mixture to lukewarm and only then whisk in the eggs; in a hot one they scramble.
Divide the raisins between the cases and fill them two-thirds with the mixture, no higher.
Bake at 200 °C for eighteen minutes for a runny filling, or twenty-two for a set one.
Knead a stiff dough from the flour, water and salt and rest it under film for forty minutes.
Chop the mutton and fat by hand into pieces the size of a pea.
Mix the meat with the finely chopped onion, garlic, salt, pepper and a quarter cup of water.
Roll ten-centimetre rounds, leaving the middle thicker than the edges.
Put a spoon of filling in and pleat the edges around, leaving an opening at the top.
Grease the steamer rack with fat and set the buuz on it, not touching one another.
Steam eighteen minutes. The dough turns translucent and broth collects inside.
Scald the spinach with boiling water, drain it and wring it out dry by hand.
Chop the spinach and mix it with the crumbled cheese, spring onion, dill and pepper. Salt cautiously; the cheese is salty.
Oil a tin and lay in three sheets of filo, brushing each one.
Spread a third of the filling, cover with two oiled sheets and repeat twice more.
Finish with three sheets on top, tuck the edges in and brush generously with oil.
Score it into squares down to the base with a sharp knife; cutting it after baking will not work.
Bake at 190 °C for forty-five minutes, to a deep golden crisp crust.
Cut the kernels from the cobs and blend them with the milk, sugar and salt to a coarse but pourable purée.
Let the batter stand ten minutes. The starch swells and the pancakes hold together.
Heat a pan to medium, butter it and pour in a ladle of batter, spreading it into a circle a centimetre thick.
Cook four minutes, until the edges dry and the underside is mottled, flip and give it three more.
Lay butter and cheese on the hot cachapa, fold it over and press it with a spatula.
Serve at once. A cooled cachapa loses its softness and turns into a dense cake.
Soften the onion and garlic in half the olive oil for eight minutes.
Add the diced potato, cover with a litre and a half of water and boil twenty minutes, until completely soft.
Blend the soup to a smooth purée and season it.
Fry the chouriço slices in a dry pan until they colour and drain them on paper.
Roll the kale leaves tightly and cut across them into threads.
Bring the purée to the boil, add the kale and cook it exactly three minutes.
Ladle it out, add the sausage slices and pour over raw olive oil.
Wash the leaves, strip the tough stems and chop them coarsely.
Fry the onion and garlic in butter until soft.
Add the leaves, okra, pumpkin, thyme and the whole scotch bonnet, and cover with water two fingers above.
Simmer forty minutes covered. No less: raw taro leaves burn the mouth.
Remove the chilli and thyme, add the coconut milk and warm it five minutes without boiling.
Break the soup down with a swizzle stick or a masher to a thick but not perfectly smooth purée.
Cut deep slashes to the bone on both sides of the fish, every three centimetres.
Grind the garlic, ginger, chilli, stock cube, lemon juice and oil into a paste and work it into the cuts.
Leave the fish to marinate for an hour in the cold.
Slice the onions and sweat them in oil over a low heat for thirty minutes, to a caramel colour.
Stir the mustard and lemon juice into the onions and season; that is the yet sauce.
Grill the fish over indirect heat, twenty minutes a side.
Fry the plantain and serve the fish under the onion sauce, with the plantain and lemon.
Dry the meat and brown it in butter in batches until dark. Set it aside.
In the same fat sweat the onion for twenty minutes until soft and gold: it gives the sauce its sweetness and body.
Return the meat, pour in the beer and add the syrup, vinegar, thyme and bay. The liquid should nearly cover the meat.
Spread the bread with mustard and lay it mustard side down on top of the meat. Do not stir it in.
Cover and cook three hours on the lowest heat or at 150 °C in the oven. The bread dissolves on its own.
Stir the sauce, check the balance of sweet and sour and serve with chips.
Peel the cassava, strip the woody core and boil it in salted water until completely soft.
Mash the cassava hot and work it with the egg and salt into a pliable dough.
Fry the onion, pepper and garlic, add the mince, cumin and tomato paste and cook it through.
Stir the culantro into the filling and cool it completely.
Take a lump of dough with wet hands, flatten it on your palm and put the filling in the centre.
Seal it and draw it into a torpedo with pointed ends.
Fry at 175 °C for four minutes, to a deep golden crust, and serve them hot.
Marinate the chicken in lime juice, garlic, Salsa Lizano, salt and pepper for twenty minutes.
Cook the rice loose and warm the beans with a spoon of their liquid.
Dice the chayote and carrot small and stew them with garlic for ten minutes; that is the picadillo.
Fry the chicken over medium heat, six minutes a side.
Fry the ripe plantain slices to a caramel colour.
Toss the shredded cabbage with tomato, coriander, lime juice and salt.
Build the plate in sectors: rice, beans, chicken, picadillo, salad, plantain — unmixed.
Boil the potatoes in their skins until completely soft, peel them hot and press them through a ricer.
Work the purée by hand for five minutes, until it is even and elastic.
Cool the purée to room temperature, then work in the ají paste, lime juice, oil and salt.
Mix the tuna with the mayonnaise, finely chopped red onion and coriander.
Press half the purée into a mould in a layer a centimetre and a half thick and level it.
Spread the filling and the avocado slices and cover with the other half of the purée.
Chill it two hours, garnish with egg and olives and serve cold.
Grate the raw potato finely and wring it out in a cloth. Collect the liquid in a bowl.
Let the liquid stand ten minutes, pour off the water and stir the settled starch back into the grated potato.
Mash the boiled potato and combine it with the grated, adding the starch and salt. The mass should shape without sticking.
Mix the mince with half the finely chopped onion, marjoram, salt and pepper and roll four firm balls.
With wet hands take a lump of dough, flatten it on your palm, set the filling in it and seal it into an elongated oval.
Lower them into barely simmering salted water and cook twenty-five minutes. Do not stir; just rock the pot once in the first minute.
Render the pork fat with the remaining onion to crackling, spoon it over the cepelinai and serve with soured cream.
Combine all three minces with the crushed garlic, bicarbonate, paprika, salt and pepper.
Work it by hand for ten minutes, adding the iced water a little at a time, until the mass turns tacky and even.
Press film onto the surface and refrigerate for at least twelve hours.
With wet hands roll sausages eight centimetres long and as thick as a thumb.
Grill over hot coals or on a griddle three minutes a side, turning once.
Split the warm somun, tuck the ćevapi inside and add a pile of raw onion and kajmak.
Soak the sliced onion in iced water for ten minutes and pat it dry: the harshness goes, the flavour stays.
Squeeze the limes by hand rather than in a press: pressure on the skin releases bitter oils.
Salt the fish, mix it with the chopped ají and coriander, pour the lime over and leave it exactly three to five minutes. The edges turn opaque and the middle stays translucent.
Add the onion, toss once and serve at once with the sweet potato and corn. Pour the juice from the bowl into small glasses.
Peel the prawns, boil the shells in a litre of water for twenty minutes and strain the broth.
Poach the prawns in that broth for exactly two minutes and drop them straight into iced water.
Chill the broth completely; it becomes the base of the dressing.
Slice the red onion thin, rinse it in cold water and cure it in lime juice with salt.
Blend two tomatoes to a purée and mix it with the ketchup, mustard, orange juice and the cold broth.
Combine the prawns, cured onion, chopped tomatoes and the dressing.
Chill it an hour, stir in the coriander and serve with popcorn and plantain crisps.
Grate the carrots coarsely and cut the peppers and onions into thin strips.
Fry the onion with the garlic, ginger and chilli in oil until soft, five minutes.
Add the curry powder and paprika and warm them a minute; the spices need to open up in the oil.
Add the peppers and carrot and cook five minutes over a high heat, stirring.
Add the tomatoes, season and cook seven minutes, until the sauce thickens.
Stir in the beans, warm them three minutes and take the pan off. The vegetables should still have bite.
Brown the chicken pieces in a dry heavy pot without fat, to a golden crust.
Lift out the meat, add the butter and soften the onion in the rendered fat.
Skin the tomatoes, grate them and add them to the onion.
Return the chicken, season, add the khmeli suneli and the whole chilli and cover the pot.
Stew thirty minutes on a low heat, never adding water.
Chop all the herbs and the garlic coarsely, not to a paste.
Stir in the herbs and garlic, cover the pot, take it off the heat and let it stand ten minutes.
Line a colander with two layers of close-woven cloth and pour in the katyk.
Knot the corners of the cloth and hang the bundle over a bowl somewhere cold.
Leave it draining a full day, until the mass is as firm as soft curd.
Pound the garlic with a pinch of salt into a smooth paste.
Chop the coriander, dill, basil and spring onion as fine as you can.
Fold the herbs and garlic into the strained mass with a spatula, without mashing it.
Salt it, smooth it in a bowl, press a hollow with a spoon and pour the oil into it.
Mix the flour with the salt and sugar, add the warm water and two spoons of oil.
Knead the dough fifteen minutes, until it is smooth and elastic.
Cover it with a damp cloth and rest it an hour at room temperature.
Divide it into eight balls, roll each into a thin round and brush it generously with oil.
Roll the round into a rope, coil it like a snail and press it flat with your palm.
Rest the coils fifteen minutes and roll each one out into a round again.
Cook them in a dry pan a minute and a half a side, brushing with oil, to browned spots.
Mix the mince with the cornmeal, egg, onion, chilli, coriander leaf, crushed coriander seed, pomegranate seeds and salt.
Fold in the tomatoes last so they do not weep too early, and chill the mixture for twenty minutes.
With wet hands shape flat patties twelve centimetres across and a centimetre thick.
Heat half a centimetre of ghee and fry them three or four minutes a side over medium heat, uncovered.
Serve with flatbread, onion rings and lemon. Traditionally an egg is broken over each patty in the pan.
Separate the fresh noodles into individual strips by hand, trying not to tear them.
Set everything out beside the hob — the cooking takes four minutes and there will be no time to fetch anything.
Heat the wok until it smokes, melt the lard and fry the garlic and sausage for twenty seconds.
Add the prawns and cockles and cook thirty seconds, without stirring constantly.
Push everything to the side, break the eggs into the centre, let them set for ten seconds and break them up.
Add the noodles, both soy sauces, the sambal and sugar and toss them for a minute and a half.
Throw in the sprouts and chives, toss for twenty seconds and serve immediately.
Beat the eggs with chopsticks without raising foam; the movement should cut rather than whip.
Add the cooled dashi, soy, mirin and salt and stir without whisking.
Strain the mixture twice through a fine sieve; that is the only route to smoothness.
Divide the prawn, a piece of chicken, a mushroom and a slice of kamaboko between the cups.
Pour in the custard, lift any bubbles off the surface with a spoon and cover with foil.
Steam gently for fifteen minutes with the steamer lid propped open a centimetre.
Test with a skewer: the liquid that rises should run clear. Scatter with herbs and serve hot.
Toast a hundred and fifty grams of the sesame and the almonds in a dry pan and grind them to a coarse paste.
Mix the flour with the nut paste, aniseed, cinnamon, saffron, yeast and salt.
Add the melted butter, orange blossom water, vinegar and warm water and knead fifteen minutes to a smooth dough.
Rest the dough an hour under film.
Roll it thin, cut it into rectangles and make four lengthways slits in each.
Thread your fingers through alternate slits and twist each piece into a flower, pinching the ends.
Fry at 165 °C for four minutes to golden, drop them straight into warm honey for five minutes and scatter with sesame.
Fry the onions in ghee to a deep gold — twenty minutes over medium heat. Set half aside: that is the birista, and the main flavour of the dish.
Marinate the chicken in the yoghurt with the ginger, garlic, spices, half the fried onion, mint and salt. Give it an hour, better three.
Boil the rice in plenty of salted water with the whole spices for exactly five minutes and drain. A grain should snap but stay white in the middle.
Spread the marinated chicken over the bottom of a heavy pot and the rice over it in an even layer. Pour the saffron milk over in patches and scatter the rest of the onion and the herbs.
Cover as tightly as you can, sealing the rim with foil if you like. Five minutes on a high flame, then forty on the lowest. Do not lift the lid once.
Let it stand for ten minutes, then fold once from the bottom up, lifting the chicken into the rice rather than stirring everything to a mush.
Char the peppers over a flame or under a grill until blistered black all over, close them in a bag for ten minutes and peel the skin away.
Make a lengthways slit, ease the seeds out leaving the stalk in place, stuff with cheese and pin the slit with a cocktail stick.
For the sauce, blend the tomatoes with the onion and garlic, fry the purée in a spoon of oil for ten minutes with the oregano, and season.
Whip the whites to firm peaks, add a pinch of salt and fold in the yolks one at a time, trying not to knock the air out.
Dust a pepper in flour, dip it in the batter and lower it into oil at 180 °C. Fry two minutes a side, spooning oil over the top.
Drain on a rack, remove the sticks and serve with the hot tomato sauce beneath the pepper rather than over it.
Joint the crab: lift the shell, cut the body into four and crack the claws with the back of a knife.
Pound the garlic, ginger and chillies to a paste and fry it in oil for three minutes, until fragrant.
Add the sambal, ketchup, sugar and vinegar and cook two minutes, until the sauce darkens.
Pour in the stock, bring it up and add the crab pieces. Cover and cook eight minutes.
Slake the cornflour in cold water and stir it in to thicken the sauce.
Turn off the heat and pour in the beaten eggs in a thin stream, stirring once in a circle.
Scatter with coriander and serve with the fried mantou.
Dissolve the salt in the warm water: that spreads it evenly instead of leaving it on the bottom of the jar.
Rub the dried oregano between your palms and steep it in the vinegar for five minutes: it softens and releases its scent.
Chop the parsley and garlic fine with a knife. The garlic is chopped rather than crushed: crushed it gives a sharpness that never leaves.
Mix everything together, pour in the oil and stir. Let it stand two hours at room temperature.
Heat the oven to 220 °C in advance; the dough has to go into a hot one.
Beat the softened fat with the eggs and salt until smooth.
Work in the grated cheese and the aniseed, rubbing the mass with your hands until the cheese is evenly distributed.
Add the starch a little at a time, with the milk, until the dough is firm and pliable.
Roll ropes and join the ends into rings about eight centimetres across.
Bake twenty-five minutes, to browned patches. Serve warm.
Pound the beef under film to four millimetres and season it.
Fry the bacon crisp and drain it on paper.
Get the pan very hot and sear the steaks forty-five seconds a side.
Lay the cheese on the meat in the pan and cover it for thirty seconds so it softens.
Fry the eggs with runny yolks and toast the cut buns in a dry pan.
Spread mayonnaise on both halves and layer lettuce, tomato, the steak with its cheese, ham, bacon and the egg.
Close it, spear it with a cocktail stick and an olive, and serve with chips.
Brown the meat with the onion and celery in ghee for ten minutes.
Add the grated tomato, tomato paste, cinnamon, salt and pepper and cook five minutes.
Pour in two litres of boiling water, add the chickpeas and simmer forty minutes.
Rinse the freekeh, add it and cook twenty minutes more, stirring; the grain settles and catches.
Stir in the coriander five minutes before the end and loosen with water if the soup has gone too thick.
Ladle out, crumble dried mint over each bowl and add lemon juice.
Cut the kernels from the cobs with a knife, running the blade down the core.
Grind the kernels in a blender in short pulses to a grainy mass.
Work in the egg, sugar, salt and corn flour to the consistency of thick cream.
Heat a pan with butter over medium until it just wisps.
Pour in a ladle of batter and spread it into a fifteen-centimetre round.
Fry three minutes a side, to golden patches and a springy centre.
Serve them hot with natilla and a slice of fresh cheese.
Knead a stiff dough from the flour, egg, water and salt and work it fifteen minutes.
Cover the dough and rest it forty minutes at room temperature.
Chop the mutton fine with a knife and mix it with the grated onion, cumin, salt and pepper.
Roll the dough a millimetre thick and cut it into three-centimetre squares.
Put a pea of filling on each square, fold it into a triangle and join two corners into a ring.
Bring the broth to the boil with the tomatoes and the whole chilli and drop the chuchvara in batches.
Cook five minutes after they surface, divide them between bowls with the broth, and add suzma and coriander.
Rinse the tripe several times in cold water, rub it with salt and rinse it again.
Boil the tripe in water with half the vinegar for ten minutes and throw away that first water.
Cover it with fresh water along with the bones and root vegetables and simmer four hours.
Lift out the tripe, cut it into fine strips and return it to the strained broth.
Crush the garlic with salt into a paste and let it down with a ladle of the broth.
Whisk the yolks with the cream and ladle in hot broth, stirring without stopping.
Pour the mixture into the pot off the heat, add the garlic and the remaining vinegar, and warm it through without boiling.
Scrub the clams and steam them in a cup of water, covered, for five minutes, until they open. Discard any that stay shut. Strain the liquor through muslin: sand settles in it.
Take the meat from the shells and chop it coarsely. Set it aside; it returns at the very end.
Render the bacon in the pot, add the butter, onion and celery, and sweat them for eight minutes until soft.
Stir in the flour, cook it two minutes, pour in the strained clam liquor and the milk, and add the potato, thyme and bay.
Simmer for fifteen minutes until the potato is soft. Crush a few pieces against the side: the soup thickens without more flour.
Pour in the cream, return the clams and warm through for two minutes without boiling. Check the salt and serve with crackers.
Slake the achiote paste with the juice of two oranges, the grapefruit and the lime to a thin slurry.
Add the crushed garlic, oregano, cumin, salt and pepper and mix it smooth.
Coat the pork in the marinade, working it in by hand, and refrigerate overnight.
Pass the banana leaves over a flame and line a deep dish with them, overlapping and with an overhang.
Put in the pork with its marinade, fold the leaves over and seal the dish with two layers of foil.
Bake at 150 °C for four hours without opening it.
Pickle the sliced red onion with the habanero in the juice of the remaining oranges. Shred the meat and serve with tortillas.
Boil the potatoes in their skins in salted water until completely soft, twenty-five minutes.
Warm the milk and cream with the sliced spring onion until hot and leave it to infuse ten minutes.
Shred the cabbage and cook it in half the butter for eight minutes, until soft.
Peel the potatoes hot and mash them with a masher, never a blender.
Strain the hot milk into the mash and work it smooth, then season.
Fold in the cooked cabbage and the infused spring onion from the milk.
Mound it up, make a well in the centre and put the remaining butter into it.
Mash the avocados with a fork, salt and lemon juice into a coarse purée, not smooth.
Dice the tomatoes small, salt them and drain them in a sieve to lose the excess water.
Poach the frankfurters in water on a low heat for five minutes, without letting them split.
Warm the buns in steam or in the oven for two minutes; they should be soft and hot.
Put a frankfurter in each bun and spread the drained tomato over it in an even layer.
Pile the avocado over the tomato, covering it completely.
Finish with a generous stripe of mayonnaise and serve the ají sauce separately.
Cover the chicken with the wine, carrot, garlic and herbs and leave it in the fridge overnight. In the morning lift the meat out and dry it, keeping the wine.
Render the bacon in a casserole and lift it out. In that fat, brown the chicken hard on all sides, in batches.
Dust with the flour, stir and cook for two minutes. Pour in the marinade with its vegetables and the stock, bring to the boil and skim.
Braise covered over a low flame or at 160 °C for an hour. The sauce should barely tremble.
While it braises, fry the onions in butter until golden, and separately the mushrooms over a high flame until they colour.
Add the onions, mushrooms and bacon to the pot, give it ten minutes over a low flame and check the sauce for salt.
Brown the meat with the onion in the base of the couscoussier, add the tomato paste, spices and chickpeas and cover with water. Cook an hour.
Sprinkle the couscous with water and oil and rub it between your hands so the grains separate. Steam it fifteen minutes.
Turn the grain into a wide dish, sprinkle again, rake it apart and let it cool five minutes.
Return it to the steam for fifteen more minutes. Meanwhile add the carrot and turnip to the broth.
Rake it a third time, working in the butter, and steam it a final ten minutes.
Add the courgette and pumpkin to the broth for the last twenty minutes; they cook faster than the roots.
Mound the couscous, meat and vegetables on top. Serve the broth in a separate bowl and the harissa in a third.
Poach the chicken in salted water for twenty minutes, lift it out and pull it into threads. Keep the broth.
Fry the onion and garlic, add the chicken, tomato paste, parsley and salt and cook five minutes.
Bring the broth and butter to the boil, add all the flour at once and work it on the heat for five minutes.
Turn the dough onto the table and knead it by hand until it is smooth and stops sticking.
Flatten a piece of dough on your palm, add filling and a little catupiry, seal it and draw it into a teardrop with a point.
Coat in egg and crumbs, repeat once more and chill them twenty minutes.
Fry in batches at 175 °C for four minutes, to a deep gold.
Split the vanilla, scrape the seeds into the cream and heat it to just below boiling. Take it off and let it infuse for fifteen minutes.
Work the yolks and sugar together without whipping air in — foam is not wanted here. Pour the warm cream in a thin stream, stirring all the while.
Strain through a sieve and skim any foam off the surface. Divide between ramekins and stand them in a deep tray.
Pour boiling water into the tray to halfway up the ramekins and bake at 150 °C for forty minutes. The centre should wobble.
Cool completely and refrigerate for at least four hours. Only then dust with sugar and burn it with a blowtorch.
Fry the onion and garlic in olive oil until soft, add the cuttlefish and cook five minutes; it releases water.
Add half the wine and the tomato paste and stew covered for twenty-five minutes, topping up with stock, until the cuttlefish softens.
Add the rice and toast it two minutes, until the grains turn translucent at the edges. Pour in the rest of the wine.
Add hot stock a ladle at a time, stirring, for eighteen minutes. Each addition goes in when the last has nearly been absorbed.
Five minutes before the end stir in the ink. The risotto turns black within seconds.
Off the heat, beat in a spoon of olive oil and the parsley, cover for two minutes and serve.
Mix the flour, cold milk, yeast, sugar, salt and softened butter for five minutes. No longer: strong gluten fights the rolling later.
Flatten the dough into a rectangle, wrap it and refrigerate at least four hours, better overnight.
Beat the cold butter with a rolling pin into a centimetre-thick square and keep it cold. It should bend without cracking or melting.
Roll the dough to twice the size of the butter square, lay the butter in the middle and fold the edges over it like an envelope, sealing the seams.
Roll it into a long rectangle and fold it in three. Chill forty minutes. Repeat twice more — three folds in all.
Roll the dough to four millimetres, cut triangles with a ten-centimetre base and roll each from the base to the tip, stretching gently.
Prove two hours at 25 °C — no warmer, or the butter runs out. Glaze with egg and bake at 200 °C for eighteen minutes.
Melt the butter with the olive oil, soften the onion until translucent, add the ham and warm it for a minute so the fat renders into the pan.
Add the flour and cook, stirring, for four or five minutes, until it smells nutty and just begins to colour.
Add the warm milk a ladle at a time, stirring smooth before the next goes in. Cook for ten minutes more, until the mixture pulls away from the sides.
Season with nutmeg and salt, spread into a dish two centimetres deep, press cling film onto the surface and chill for at least four hours.
Shape cylinders with wet hands and coat in egg then breadcrumbs. For a sturdier shell, do the coating twice.
Deep-fry at 180 °C for two minutes in small batches. A crowded pan drops the temperature and the croquetas drink oil instead of crisping.
Scrub the shellfish through several changes of water and discard any that are already open.
Boil half the potatoes, mash them and work them with the flour and lard into firm chapalele cakes.
Line the bottom of the pot with two layers of cabbage leaves.
Lay the shellfish in as the first layer, add the wine and cover with more cabbage leaves.
Arrange the ribs, chicken, sausage and onion as the second layer and cover with leaves again.
Put the whole potatoes and the cakes on top, cover with leaves and close the lid tightly.
Cook over medium heat for an hour without opening it. Serve in layers, with the broth from the bottom in separate bowls.
Rinse the lentils and boil them in a litre of water with the turmeric for thirty minutes, until they collapse completely. Skim for the first five minutes.
Start the rice. While it cooks, fry the onion, add the potato and cauliflower with a little turmeric and water, and cook fifteen minutes: that is the tarkari.
Fry the greens with garlic over a high flame for two minutes; they should stay bright.
For the jhaneko, heat the ghee and throw in the ajwain, cumin, dried chilli and garlic, frying twenty seconds to the smell.
Pour the sizzling spiced fat straight into the dal — it hisses. Stir, season and serve at once.
Build the plate: rice in the middle, dal in a small bowl, tarkari and greens around it, achar at the edge.
Cover the lentils with three cups of water, add the turmeric and simmer covered for thirty minutes, until the grains collapse into a soft mass.
Mash some of the lentils against the side of the pot and season. The consistency should be that of a thick soup.
Separately fry the onion until golden, add the tomatoes and cook until they break down into a sauce. Stir that into the lentils.
Heat the ghee in a small pan until it is just short of smoking. Add the mustard seeds; they should crackle within seconds.
Add the cumin at once, the garlic and chillies ten seconds later, the asafoetida twenty seconds after that. The whole thing takes under a minute and cannot be left alone.
Pour the sizzling tadka straight into the lentils — it should hiss. Stir once and serve with rice or flatbread.
Whisk the eggs and sugar over a water bath until warm, then beat them eight minutes to a thick foam.
Fold in the sifted flour with a spatula in three additions, trying not to knock the air out.
Draw six circles on parchment and spread a thin layer of batter on each.
Bake the layers at 200 °C for six minutes each, to golden edges, and lift them off the parchment at once.
Whisk the eggs with the icing sugar over a water bath until thick, cool it and work in the softened butter and melted chocolate.
Melt the caramel sugar with lemon juice to amber and pour it over the flattest layer.
Cut the caramel layer into twelve wedges with a hot oiled knife, assemble the cake and set the wedges on top.
Cover the mutton with cold water, bring it up and skim thoroughly.
Simmer two hours with the bay, until the meat comes away from the bone.
Lift out the meat, cool it and pull it into threads by hand, discarding bones and sinew.
Crumble the flatbread by hand into pieces the size of a fingernail. Do not cut it.
Slice the onion thin and work it with a pinch of salt so it softens.
Mix the bread, meat and onion dry in a large bowl, and season.
Divide between bowls and pour over the strained boiling broth immediately before serving.
Scald fresh leaves for a minute; soak preserved ones half an hour in cold water.
Rinse the rice and mix it with the mince, finely chopped onion, salt, pepper and cinnamon.
Chop all the herbs fine and work them into the filling; their volume should be obvious.
Put a teaspoon of filling on each leaf, tuck in the sides and roll it into a tight cylinder a finger thick.
Line the bottom of the pot with torn leaves and pack the dolma in tight layers, seam down.
Dot the top with ghee, add water level with the top layer and cover with a weighted plate.
Cook an hour on a low heat and serve with matsoni whisked with crushed garlic and salt.
Rinse the rice and mix it with the mince, chopped parsley, tomato paste, baharat, oil, salt and pepper.
Cut lids off the peppers and tomatoes and hollow them. Blanch the onions whole and separate them into layers.
Roll the filling in vine leaves into tight cylinders — the rice doubles, so leave it room.
Fill the vegetables two-thirds full and put their lids back on.
Line the pot with tomato slices, then layer the parcels and stuffed vegetables, the heaviest at the bottom.
Mix water with the pomegranate molasses, lemon juice and salt and pour it in until it reaches the top layer.
Cover with a weighted plate and cook on a low heat for an hour and fifteen minutes. Serve by inverting the pot onto a platter.
Marinate the chicken in lemon juice and salt for half an hour.
Cook the onion in a dry pot over medium heat for forty minutes, stirring. It weeps, reduces and turns into a dark paste. Add neither oil nor water.
Add the spiced butter, garlic and ginger, cook five minutes, then stir in the berbere and fry five more: the spices have to open in the fat.
Pour in the wine and a cup of water, add the chicken and braise covered for forty minutes over a low flame.
Score the boiled eggs in several places and slip them into the sauce for the last ten minutes.
Serve with injera. The sauce should be thick and dark red, with oil separated on top.
Dissolve the yeast and sugar in warm water, add the flour, turmeric and salt and knead a soft dough.
Let the dough rise somewhere warm for an hour, until doubled.
Boil the chickpeas with garlic for an hour, until completely soft.
Fry the onion, add the curry powder and cumin, warm them a minute and stir in the chickpeas with half their liquid.
Mash a third of the chickpeas in the pot and cook ten minutes to thicken the sauce.
Divide the dough into small balls, rest them twenty minutes and flatten them by hand into discs.
Fry the baras twenty seconds a side in hot oil; they must stay soft. Put the channa between two baras and serve with tamarind.
Grate the potato and onion finely into the same bowl.
Let the mass stand three minutes and pour off the water that gathers on top, leaving the sediment.
Season with salt and pepper. Add nothing else.
Heat the oil over medium and drop the mixture in by the spoonful, flattening it to half a centimetre.
Fry three to four minutes a side, to a deep golden crisp crust.
Drain on paper and serve immediately with soured cream and dill.
Simmer the beef with onion, stock cube and salt for forty minutes. Keep the broth.
Soak the stockfish in boiling water for twenty minutes and break it into pieces, removing bones.
Mix the ground egusi with a little water into a thick paste that holds its shape.
Heat the palm oil until clear and fry the onion and ground scotch bonnet for three minutes.
Drop the egusi paste into the oil by the spoonful without stirring and let the lumps set for five minutes.
Pour in the broth and add the meat, both fish, the crayfish and the locust beans, and cook twenty minutes.
Stir in the greens for the last five minutes and serve with fufu or eba.
Quarter the chillies lengthways. The seeds stay in; in Bhutan they are not removed.
Put the chillies, sliced onion, garlic and tomato in a pan and add water to the same level.
Bring it up and cook ten minutes, until the chillies soften.
Crumble the cheese in, drop the heat and leave it two minutes; it should begin melting on its own.
Stir it into a creamy sauce, add the butter and salt cautiously; the cheese is salty.
Serve with the red rice Bhutanese cook to a slightly sticky texture.
Fry the onion in the lard over medium heat for fifteen minutes, until soft and translucent, without letting it colour.
Add the chopped beef, paprika, cumin and chilli and cook five minutes: the meat should only lose its pink, no more.
Season, take it off the heat and cool it completely, then refrigerate for at least four hours.
Fold the chopped egg, olives and spring onion into the cold filling.
Put a tablespoon of filling on each disc, wet the rim, fold it over and crimp it into the plaited repulgue, folding the corners over one another.
Brush with yolk and bake at 220 °C for twenty minutes, until browned.
Dice the onion and sweat it in fat for twenty minutes over a low heat; it should turn sweet, not brown.
Add the meat, paprika and cumin and stew twenty minutes. By volume there should be at least as much onion as meat.
Chill the filling for at least three hours, ideally overnight.
Knead a dough from the flour, melted fat, warm milk and salt. Work it ten minutes and rest it half an hour.
Roll out twenty-centimetre rounds. On each go two spoons of filling, an olive, a quarter egg and a pinch of raisins.
Fold into a parcel, seal the edges and turn them over twice. Prick the top with a toothpick so steam can escape.
Brush with yolk and bake at 200 °C for twenty-five minutes, to a deep gold.
Cure the onion in the juice of two limes with salt and leave it at least fifteen minutes.
Fry the garlic and tomatoes with the cumin for five minutes, add a litre and a half of water and bring it up.
Lower in the tuna whole and poach it fifteen minutes on a low heat. Fish does not tolerate a hard boil.
Lift out the fish, strain the broth and return it to the heat. Cook the cassava in it for twenty minutes, until soft.
Flake the tuna coarsely, discarding the dark parts, and return it to the pot for two minutes.
Ladle it out and top with the cured onion and its juice and coriander. Serve with a wedge of lime.
Simmer the beef and tripe with the onion and a stock cube for an hour, until tender.
Soak the dried fish in hot water twenty minutes and flake it, taking out the bones.
Shred the eru leaf as fine as you can, rolling it tight before cutting.
Rinse the waterleaf and cut it coarsely; it wilts right down as it cooks anyway.
Put the waterleaf into the pot with the meat and let it wilt, giving up its juice.
Add the eru, fish, crayfish and chilli and stew twenty minutes with the lid on.
Pour in the palm oil, stir it through and cook ten minutes more uncovered.
Rinse the peas and cover them, with the ribs and belly, in two and a half litres of cold water.
Bring it up, skim and simmer an hour, until the peas start breaking down.
Add the potato, carrot, celeriac and onion and cook another hour, stirring so nothing catches.
Lift out the meat, strip it from the bones and return it to the soup in pieces.
Add the sliced leek and celery leaves and cook twenty minutes.
Cool it completely and leave it overnight in the fridge; the soup thickens.
Reheat it, add the sliced sausage for five minutes and serve with rye bread.
Soak the beans twelve hours in cold water and drain them.
Put the beans, cured meats, onion, garlic and olive oil in a pot and cover with cold water by three fingers.
Bring it up, skim, and drop the heat until the surface barely trembles.
Cook two and a half hours, adding half a cup of cold water every thirty minutes.
Lift out the onion and garlic, crush them with the saffron and paprika and return them to the pot.
Salt it at the very end and let it stand half an hour before serving.
Lift out the meats, slice them and serve them on a separate platter, with the beans in a tureen.
Cover the ground fenugreek with cold water and leave it six hours, changing the water twice.
Simmer the lamb with the onion and salt for an hour and a half, keeping the broth.
Break the meat into small pieces and return it to the strained broth.
Pound the garlic, chilli and coriander into a sahawiq paste in a mortar.
Add the tomatoes, hawaij and half the paste to the stew and reduce it to a thick body.
Drain the fenugreek and whip it with a spoon of cold water into a white froth.
Ladle the stew into scorching bowls, spoon the froth over and serve it boiling with flatbread.
Soak the cod for a day with four changes of water and poach it in milk for twenty minutes.
Boil the beans, lupini, broad beans, lentils and peas separately until soft.
Grind the peanuts with milk to a smooth mass; it is the soup's thickener.
Fry the onion in annatto oil, add the pumpkin and courgette and stew twenty minutes.
Blend the pumpkin and courgette and return them to the pot with the cod's milk.
Stir in all the cooked pulses, the rice, corn and peanut mass and cook thirty minutes.
Add the cream, cheese and pieces of cod, and serve with halved eggs and fried plantain.
Lay a layer of meat fat side down in the pot, season it and scatter peppercorns over.
Add a layer of cabbage, more salt and pepper, and a dusting of flour if you want body. Alternate the layers until everything is used.
Pour the water down the side; it should reach halfway up, no higher.
Bring it to the boil, cover and cook two hours on the lowest heat. Do not stir: the layers are meant to stay layers.
It is done when the meat comes away from the bone. Serve with boiled potatoes, spooning broth from the pot over.
Boil the chickpeas in unsalted water for ninety minutes, until completely soft, and keep the water.
Tear the pitas into two-finger pieces and fry them in oil to a golden crisp.
Whisk the yoghurt with the tahini, crushed garlic, lemon juice and salt until smooth.
Let the yoghurt mixture down with a couple of spoons of the chickpea water to the body of thick cream.
Fry the pine nuts in the ghee until golden and take them off the heat.
Spread the fried bread in a dish and top it with the hot chickpeas and a spoon of their liquid.
Pour over the yoghurt, spoon on the butter and nuts, dust with paprika and parsley and serve at once.
Tear the bread by hand into two-finger pieces and fry them in olive oil until browned.
Drain the bread on paper and dust it with half the sumac while it is still hot.
Cut the tomatoes, cucumbers and radishes into large uneven pieces; the salad should be rough rather than neat.
Tear the lettuce by hand and chop the herbs and spring onion.
Whisk a dressing from the lemon juice, pomegranate molasses, crushed garlic, the remaining sumac, oil and salt.
Toss the vegetables in the dressing, add the bread and serve at once.
Boil the salted meat in fresh water for twenty minutes and drain: the last stage of getting the salt out.
Cover the beans with water three fingers above, add the bay, the ribs and the salted meat, and simmer for an hour and a half.
Add the belly and the sausage and give it another hour. The beans should be collapsing and the liquid thickening on its own.
Fry the onion and garlic until golden, add a ladle of beans, mash them and return it all to the pot. That thickens the stew and deepens it.
Fry the greens over a high flame for two minutes with garlic — they should stay bright green and crisp.
Serve the beans and meat with the rice, greens and orange segments alongside. Everyone builds their own plate.
Char the peppers over a flame or under a grill until the skins blacken.
Put the hot peppers in a bag for ten minutes and peel them.
Soften the onion and garlic in butter and stir in a spoon of flour.
Add the chopped tomatoes and reduce them to a thick base with no loose liquid.
Cut the peeled peppers into strips and stir them into the tomato base.
Mash the curd cheese with the feta and work it into the hot mixture.
