Transfer it to a clay pan and bake at 200 °C for twenty minutes, until it bubbles.
Toast the walnuts in a dry pan for five minutes, cool them and grind them almost to a paste.
Fry the onion until golden, add the turmeric and the meat and brown it all over.
Lift out the meat, add the walnut paste to the pot and pour in a litre of hot water.
Cook the sauce an hour on a low heat, stirring every ten minutes; it darkens and starts releasing oil.
Add the pomegranate molasses, cinnamon, sugar and saffron and return the meat to the pot.
Stew an hour more, until the sauce turns dark brown and thick and oil shows at the edges.
Taste and adjust the balance of sour and sweet, and serve with rice and pomegranate seeds.
Pound the lemongrass, galangal, turmeric, garlic, shallot and half the lime leaves in a mortar to a smooth paste.
Warm the paste in a pan with half the coconut milk for five minutes, until it smells right.
Take it off the heat, cool it to warm and whisk in the eggs, fish sauce, palm sugar and the rest of the milk.
Fold the fish pieces through and leave them to marinate fifteen minutes.
Fold cups from the banana leaves, or use ramekins. Line the bottom with spinach leaves.
Divide the fish and sauce between them without filling to the brim and steam for twenty minutes.
Spoon over the coconut cream, scatter with shredded lime leaves and serve with rice.
Rinse the cut potatoes of their starch, dry them thoroughly and fry at 140 °C for six minutes. They should turn soft but stay pale. Set them aside to cool.
Mix the flour, cornflour and baking powder. Pour in the ice-cold beer and whisk only a few strokes — lumps are fine, an over-mixed batter turns tough.
Dry the fish, dust it in plain flour and shake off the excess. Without that the batter slides off in the oil.
Heat the oil to 190 °C. Dip the fish, let the excess run off and lower it in, holding it for a couple of seconds so it does not stick to the bottom. Fry six minutes.
Lift the fish out and finish the chips in the same oil for three minutes, until gold. Salt them at once, while hot.
Whisk the flour with the water and salt into a smooth thin batter — thicker than for pancakes, but pourable.
Let the soured cream down with cold water to the consistency of thin cream and salt it.
Butter a round tin and pour the batter in stripes from the centre outwards, like the spokes of a wheel.
Put it under the top grill for four minutes, until the layer sets and spots appear.
Sprinkle with the thinned cream and pour the next layer into the gaps between the previous stripes.
Repeat, alternating the direction of the stripes, until the batter runs out — usually twenty to twenty-five layers.
Pour over melted butter, rest it ten minutes and serve with yoghurt or honey.
Rub the inside of the pot with a cut clove of garlic and leave it in.
Toss both grated cheeses with the cornflour by hand until every shred is coated.
Warm the wine with the lemon juice until bubbles appear at the edge, but not to a boil.
Add the cheese a handful at a time, stirring in a figure of eight until each is fully melted before the next goes in.
When the mass turns even and strings from the spoon, add the kirsch and season with nutmeg and pepper.
Move it to the burner and keep the flame at its lowest. The bread is speared through the crust rather than the crumb.
Cut the chicken along the backbone, open it out and press it flat.
Blend the chillies, garlic, the juice of two lemons, paprika, vinegar, oregano, oil and salt.
Pour half the sauce into a separate bowl; that half is for basting.
Coat the chicken with the rest, working it under the skin, and refrigerate overnight.
Light the coals and rake them to the sides; the heat has to be indirect.
Grill the chicken skin up for thirty minutes, then turn it and give it fifteen more.
For the last five minutes baste with the reserved sauce mixed with melted butter. Serve with lemon.
Melt the butter in a heavy pot, add the onions and a pinch of salt, and keep them over medium heat, stirring every few minutes. For the first twenty minutes the onions give up water.
Then the caramelisation proper begins: another twenty-five minutes to take the onions to the colour of strong tea. If they catch, lower the heat and add a spoonful of water.
Stir in the flour and cook it out for a couple of minutes so it loses its raw taste.
Pour in the wine and scrape everything stuck to the bottom back into the pot. Let it reduce by half.
Add the stock and thyme, bring to the boil and simmer for twenty minutes. Season at the end, since the stock may already be salty.
Ladle into ovenproof bowls, top each with a slice of baguette, cover with cheese and put them under the grill until bubbling and browned, about three minutes.
Mix both minces with the grated onion, egg, flour, salt, pepper and allspice.
Work it for five minutes, adding the milk in stages. The mixture should turn tacky and string off the spoon.
Chill it for half an hour: cold farce holds its shape better.
Melt the butter over medium heat. With a spoon dipped in water, scoop the mixture into the pan and flatten each one.
Fry six minutes a side, to a dark brown crust. Do not hurry: the colour is the flavour.
Serve with boiled potatoes, pickled red cabbage and the gravy from the pan.
Soak the raisins in the rakija for twenty minutes, so they swell and give up their aroma.
Dissolve the yeast in the warm milk with a spoon of sugar and leave it until it foams.
Beat the eggs with the remaining sugar, the zests, vanilla and salt.
Combine with the yeast mixture and the flour and whisk to a smooth loose batter.
Stir in the raisins with their rakija and let the batter rise an hour somewhere warm.
Heat the oil to 170 °C and drop the batter in with two teaspoons, shaping irregular balls.
Fry three minutes, turning them, to a deep gold, and dust them with icing sugar while hot.
Drain the soaked beans, cover them with fresh water three fingers above and bring to the boil. Skim.
Drop to the lowest possible heat and cook covered for three or four hours, until the beans start to collapse. Top up the water as needed.
Mash about half the beans in the pot with a masher, leaving the rest whole.
Stir in the crushed garlic and season. Divide between bowls.
Into each bowl: olive oil generously, lemon juice, cumin, tomato, parsley and chilli to taste. Serve with flatbread.
Drain the soaked beans, cover them with fresh water and boil ninety minutes, until completely soft.
Pour off most of the water, leaving half a cup, salt the beans and mash them about halfway.
Crush the garlic with salt and cumin and stir it through the beans.
Turn them into a wide bowl and pour the sesame oil over without stirring it in.
Scatter over the crumbled cheese, chopped tomato, onion, chilli and halved eggs.
Serve with lemon and flatbread. It is eaten by hand from the shared bowl.
Cut the tomatoes into large wedges, skins and seeds left in.
Heat the olive oil in a wide pan and soften the onion in it.
Add the crushed garlic and the whole green chillies and warm them a minute.
Tip in the tomatoes, salt them and stew over a medium heat, stirring now and then.
Crush the tomatoes with a spoon once the skins start to lift from the flesh.
Reduce it fifteen minutes more, until the oil rises at the edges as a separate layer.
Scatter with dried mint and serve it in the pan with flatbread.
Soak the ribs in cold water for an hour, changing it twice, until the water runs clear.
Blanch the ribs in boiling water for five minutes, drain and rinse them under cold water.
Blend the pear, onion, garlic and ginger to a smooth purée.
Mix the purée with the soy, sugar, mirin and sesame oil and pour it over the ribs.
Bring it up, skim, and braise covered for an hour and a half on a low heat.
Add the carrot, daikon, mushrooms, chestnuts and jujubes and braise twenty-five minutes more.
Uncover and reduce the sauce to a gloss, spooning it over the ribs. Scatter with spring onion.
Fry the finely chopped onion, pepper and garlic in oil until soft, five minutes.
Add the beans with a ladle of their liquid and warm them three minutes.
Add the cold rice and stir, breaking up lumps with a spatula.
Add the Salsa Lizano, season and fry over medium heat for seven minutes, stirring occasionally.
Stir in the chopped coriander and take it off the heat.
Serve with fried eggs, fried plantain and, if you like, soured cream or fresh cheese.
Fry the onion, garlic and pepper in oil until soft, five minutes.
Add the beans with a ladle of their liquid and warm them three minutes.
Add the cold rice and stir, breaking up lumps with a spatula.
Fry over a high flame for eight minutes, leaving it undisturbed for the last three so a crust forms underneath.
Season and stir in the coriander.
Serve with fried plantain, cuajada cheese and a fried egg.
Cut the tuna into large pieces and rinse them under cold water.
Cover with a litre and a half of cold water, salt it and bring it up.
Skim for the first five minutes; the clarity of the broth depends on it.
Add the curry leaves and pandan and cook twenty minutes on the lowest heat.
Remove the leaves, check the salt and take it off the heat.
Serve with rice, sliced onion, chilli and lime, each person adding them to their own bowl.
Knead a dough from the flour, softened butter, soured cream, yeast and salt and work it ten minutes.
Wrap the dough in film and chill it an hour.
Rub the filling flour with the cold butter, sugar and vanilla to a damp crumb.
Roll the dough into a rectangle, brush it with butter, fold it in three and chill it twenty minutes.
Repeat the rolling and folding once more, then roll it out a centimetre thick.
Spread the filling over half the sheet, fold the other half over and seal the edges.
Score a pattern with a fork, brush with yolk and bake at 180 °C for forty minutes, to a deep gold.
Soak the bread crumb in cold water for ten minutes and squeeze it dry.
Blend the tomatoes, cucumber, pepper, garlic and bread until completely smooth. It takes longer than you expect — a good two minutes at full speed.
With the blender still running, pour the oil in a thin stream. The soup pales and thickens: that is the emulsion.
Add the vinegar and salt, taste and season again. Pass it through a sieve for a silkier texture and chill for at least two hours.
Cut lids off the tomatoes and scoop out the flesh with a spoon without piercing the walls.
Blitz the flesh and add the sugar; it takes the edge off the tomato acidity.
Soften the onion in olive oil for ten minutes, until sweet.
Mix the raw rice with the onion, herbs, half the tomato purée, salt and pepper.
Fill the vegetables two-thirds full, cap them with their lids and set them in a dish.
Tuck potato wedges between them, pour over the remaining purée and douse it all with oil.
Bake covered with foil at 180 °C for an hour, then uncover and give it twenty minutes more.
Cut the top off the pumpkin with its stalk; that is the lid. Scoop out the seeds and loose flesh with a spoon, leaving a wall two fingers thick.
Boil the rice in salted water for seven minutes, to half done, and drain.
Cover the dried fruit with boiling water for ten minutes, drain, and chop the apricots and prunes coarsely. Chop the nuts.
Mix the rice with the fruit, nuts, melted butter, honey and cinnamon. Salt it: a sweet filling without salt tastes flat.
Fill the pumpkin, without packing it down, put the cut lid back on and set it on a baking tray.
Bake at 180 °C for an hour and a half. Test at the side with a knife: it should go into the wall without resistance.
Rest fifteen minutes, carry it out whole and cut it into wedges from the crown to the base.
Fry the onion with the turmeric until gold, add the meat and brown it on all sides.
Cover with water, add the beans and simmer for an hour.
Meanwhile chop all the herbs fine and fry them in the oil for twenty minutes, stirring. They shrink to a quarter and darken; that is correct. Add the fenugreek for the last two minutes.
Stir the herbs into the pot, prick the dried limes with a fork and drop them in whole. Simmer for another hour.
Crush the limes against the side of the pot, season and let it stand fifteen minutes. The sauce should be dark and thick, with oil separated on top.
Mash both cheeses with a fork and mix them with the eggs, kefir, soured cream and half the oil.
Stir in the sparkling water; it lightens the custard and keeps it from setting dense.
Taste the custard for salt: brined cheese varies, and it has to be adjusted rather than measured.
Oil the tin and lay two whole filo sheets flat on the bottom, uncrumpled.
Dip each remaining sheet in the custard, crumple it like a concertina and lay it in the tin.
Pour the remaining custard over, cover with two whole sheets and brush them with oil.
Bake at 190 °C for fifty minutes, sprinkle it with water and cover it with a cloth for ten minutes.
Simmer the pork belly in salted water for thirty minutes, cool it and slice it thin.
Boil the prawns two minutes, cool them and split each one lengthways.
Boil the vermicelli, rinse it in cold water and drain it well.
Let the peanut butter down with the hoisin, garlic and water to the thickness of pouring cream.
Dip a sheet of rice paper in warm water for two seconds and lay it on a damp cloth.
Lay two prawn halves cut side down in the upper third, and below them the lettuce, noodles, pork and herbs.
Fold the bottom up, tuck the sides in and roll it tight. Serve with the peanut sauce.
Mix the chicken with the egg white, a spoon of cornflour, a spoon of soy and a pinch of salt, and leave it twenty minutes.
Mix the sauce in advance: vinegar, the rest of the soy, the sugar and the rest of the cornflour with two spoons of water. Keep it within reach — there is no time to mix it later.
Heat the oil and fry the chillies with the Sichuan pepper for twenty seconds, until dark but not black. Burnt chilli turns bitter.
Add the chicken and leave it alone for a minute, then toss and cook through — two minutes more.
Throw in the garlic, ginger and the white of the spring onion, then after half a minute pour in the sauce. It thickens in seconds. Off the heat, add the peanuts and the green of the onion.
Sweat the onion in the lard over a low flame for twenty minutes, until soft and golden. It feels long and pointless, and it is where the sweetness of the sauce comes from.
Take the pan off the heat, add the paprika and caraway and stir. Half a minute later return it to the flame and add the meat.
Cook the meat with the onion covered for half an hour without adding water: it gives up its own. Only then pour in water to the level of the meat.
Simmer for an hour and a half. Add the peppers, tomatoes and garlic forty minutes before the end, the potatoes twenty-five.
Salt it at the very end and let it stand fifteen minutes before serving.
Run your fingers over the fillet for pin bones and pull them with tweezers. Leave the skin on: it holds the shape while curing.
Mix the salt, sugar and crushed pepper. Sprinkle the fish with aquavit and rub the mixture into the flesh.
Lay half the dill in a dish, the fish on it skin down, and bury it under the rest of the dill.
Cover with film, set a board and a kilo weight on top and refrigerate for forty-eight hours.
Every twelve hours pour off the brine that has collected and turn the fish over.
Scrape off the cure, pat the fish dry and slice it thinly on the diagonal, stopping at the skin. Serve with a mustard sauce of mustard, sugar, vinegar and oil.
Grate the potatoes, onions and shallots coarsely into one bowl.
Wring the mixture out in a cloth, but not bone dry; a little moisture is needed.
Mix in the eggs, flour, chopped parsley, salt and pepper.
Heat the oil to 175 °C. Hotter, and the edges burn before the middle is hot.
Drop the mixture in by the spoonful, flattened to half a centimetre, and fry three minutes a side.
Drain on a rack, salt them and serve hot with apple sauce.
Dissolve the yeast with a spoon of sugar in the warm milk and leave it ten minutes.
Knead a dough from the flour, yeast mixture, remaining sugar, oil and salt, working it fifteen minutes.
Blanch the belly two minutes, rinse it and braise it in the soy, wine, sugar and star anise for ninety minutes.
Let the dough rise an hour, roll it into ovals and fold each in half with a strip of parchment inside.
Prove the buns thirty minutes and steam them for twelve.
Pound the peanuts with two spoons of sugar into a coarse crumb.
Open a bun and lay in a slice of belly, the pickled greens, the peanut crumb and coriander.
Halve the avocados, remove the stones and scoop the flesh into a bowl. A ripe avocado gives under a finger without collapsing.
Add the lime juice and the salt straight away. The acid needs to reach the flesh before it starts to brown.
Crush with a fork to a coarse, uneven mass. Lumps of avocado should remain — that is the texture you want.
Fold in the onion, the jalapeño and the coriander, taste, and adjust the salt or lime. The tomato goes in last and gently, so it does not water everything down.
Serve at once. If it has to wait, press cling film directly onto the surface — air is what darkens it.
Pat the beef dry, season it and dust it with flour on all sides.
Brown the meat in batches in hot oil to a dark crust and lift it out.
Soften the onion in the same fat, add the tomato paste and cook it three minutes.
Pour in the stout, bring it up and scrape everything caught on the bottom; that is where the flavour is.
Return the meat, add the stock, thyme and bay and braise covered at 160 °C for two hours.
Add the carrot, parsnip and potato and braise forty-five minutes more.
Stir in the honey, taste for the balance against the bitterness and serve with soda bread.
Soak the gundruk in warm water for ten minutes and squeeze it out, keeping the water.
Toast the soybeans in a dry pan until they darken in patches and crack.
Heat the mustard oil until it smokes, take it off and let it cool a minute; raw mustard oil is acrid.
Fry the onion, garlic, ginger and turmeric, add the tomatoes and cook five minutes.
Add the gundruk, soybeans and potato, and pour in the soaking water and a litre of water.
Cook twenty-five minutes, until the potato and beans are soft, and season.
Sizzle the dried chillies, fenugreek and timur in a spoon of oil and pour it into the soup.
Dissolve the yeast with the sugar in the warm water and leave it ten minutes, until it foams.
Whisk in the flour and salt to a smooth, loose batter without lumps.
Add the oil and beat another minute, until the batter goes glossy.
Cover it and leave it warm for an hour, until bubbles break the surface.
Heat a dry pan over medium and pour in a ladle of batter.
Cover it and cook five minutes, until the top sets and turns matt.
Lift it out without turning it and stack the breads under a cloth.
Bring the dashi with the soy, mirin, sake, sugar and grated ginger to the boil in a wide pan.
Add the onion and simmer for five minutes over medium heat, until it turns translucent.
Lay the beef over the surface slice by slice rather than in a heap, and cook two or three minutes. Skim any foam.
Take it off the moment the beef loses its pink. Left longer it toughens within a minute.
Divide the rice between bowls, spoon the beef and onion over with two or three spoons of the broth, and serve with the pickled ginger.
Boil the soaked beans in fresh water for an hour, until completely soft.
Blend the beans with some of their liquid to a smooth mass.
Press the mass through a sieve with a spoon and discard the skins left behind.
Return it to the heat and add the coconut and evaporated milk, cinnamon, cloves and sugar.
Cook twenty minutes on a low heat, stirring so it does not catch.
Add the sweet potato in pieces and the raisins and cook twenty minutes more, until the potato is tender.
Stir in the vanilla, butter and a pinch of salt, chill it and serve it cold with biscuits.
Rub the chicken with salt inside and out and stuff the cavity with half the ginger and the spring onions.
Bring a pot of water to the boil, lower the whole chicken in, bring it back up and turn the heat off immediately.
Keep it covered for forty minutes without lifting the lid. It is done when the juices from the thigh run clear.
Move the chicken into iced water for ten minutes, then pat it dry and brush it with sesame oil.
Skim the fat from the broth, fry the chopped garlic and ginger in it, add the rinsed rice and toast it three minutes.
Add broth to the rice at one and a half to one, drop in the pandan leaf and cook covered for fifteen minutes.
Pound the chillies with garlic, ginger and lime into a sauce. Joint the chicken and serve with the rice, cucumber, sauce and a bowl of the broth.
Cut the carp into steaks, salt them and chill them an hour; the salt firms the flesh.
Put the small fish, heads, backbones and all the sliced onion into the cauldron and cover with water.
Cook an hour over medium heat, until the fish and onion have completely broken down.
Press the broth through a sieve, working the flesh through, and return it to the cauldron. Discard the bones.
Take the cauldron off the fire and stir in both paprikas until the colour is even.
Return it to the fire, add the tomato, pepper and the hot chilli and bring it up.
Lower in the carp steaks and the roe and cook twelve minutes, only rocking the cauldron. Serve with white bread.
Soak the wheat overnight and the chana dal and barley for four hours, then rinse them.
Fry three onions in ghee until deep brown and set half aside for serving.
Brown the meat with the remaining onion, the ginger garlic paste and all the spices.
Cover with water and braise three hours, until the meat starts falling into threads.
Boil the wheat, barley and both dals in a separate pot for three hours, until completely broken down.
Remove the bones, combine the two and beat with a wooden masher for forty minutes, until uniform.
Serve with the fried onion, ginger, chilli, coriander and lemon scattered on top.
Warm the annatto seeds in the lard for five minutes and strain it; the coloured fat goes into both dough and guiso.
Fry the onion and pepper in the annatto fat, add all three meats and brown them.
Add the wine and stock and stew an hour, until the meat is tender and the sauce thick.
Cool the guiso completely, ideally leaving it overnight in the fridge.
Knead a dough from the masarepa, warm stock, annatto fat and salt until pliable.
Warm the banana leaves, spread a disc of dough on each and add guiso, olives, raisins and capers.
Wrap in two leaves, tie them crosswise with string and boil them for an hour and twenty.
Soak the halloumi in cold water for fifteen minutes, drain it and pat it completely dry.
Cut the cheese into centimetre slices — thinner and it dries out, thicker and it will not heat through.
Cut the chilled watermelon into large cubes and keep it in the fridge until serving.
Heat a dry pan hard and sear the halloumi two minutes a side, to dark stripes.
Whisk the olive oil with the lemon juice, honey and pepper.
Arrange the watermelon, rocket and hot cheese, spoon over the dressing and scatter with mint. Serve at once.
Rub the chicken with smoked salt and pepper and leave it half an hour.
Cut the sweet potato, potato and pumpkin into large pieces and the cabbage into quarters.
Wrap the wood chips in foil, pierce it in a few places and put the packet at the bottom of a deep tray.
Lay the vegetables on a rack above the chips, the chicken over them, season and dot with butter.
Seal the tray tightly with two layers of foil; no steam may escape.
Bake at 160 °C for two hours without opening it.
Take off the foil and let the chicken colour for ten minutes at 200 °C.
Soak the wheat overnight in cold water and rinse it.
Cover the meat with three litres of water, bring it up and skim.
Add the wheat, cinnamon and cardamom and simmer two hours.
Remove the bones and whole spices, season, and cook an hour more, stirring and topping up with boiling water.
Beat the mass with a wooden spoon or a mixer until entirely smooth — twenty minutes of work.
Spread it in a dish, make a hollow, pour in melted ghee and scatter with fried onion.
Fry the lamb with the onion, ginger and cinnamon for five minutes, add the chopped celery and herbs and give it two more.
Add the grated tomato and the chickpeas, pour in two litres of water and simmer for an hour, until the chickpeas are soft.
Add the lentils and give it twenty minutes more.
Whisk the flour into a cup of cold water until completely smooth and pour it in as a thin stream, stirring without stopping. Cook five minutes: the soup thickens and turns matt.
Add the vermicelli and cook until done. Serve with lemon and dates — that pairing is not accidental: sweet and sour at once.
Drop the pork cubes into boiling water for two minutes, drain and rinse them under cold water.
Dry the meat thoroughly. Wet, it spits in the caramel and cools it.
Melt the sugar in the oil over medium heat to an amber colour, stirring; it takes three or four minutes.
Add the meat and turn it for two minutes, until every cube is coated in the caramel.
Add the wine, both soy sauces, the ginger, spring onion and spices.
Add hot water level with the meat and braise covered for an hour on a low heat.
Uncover and reduce the sauce hard to a glaze, spooning it over the meat.
Dissolve the yeast and sugar in the warm water and leave it ten minutes, until it foams.
Mix the rice flour with the yeast mixture and half the coconut milk to a smooth batter.
Cover it and leave it to ferment overnight at room temperature, about eight hours.
In the morning stir in the remaining coconut milk and salt; the batter should be as thin as pouring cream.
Mix the finely chopped onion, chilli flakes, Maldive fish, lime juice and salt; that is lunu miris.
Heat a small wok, oil it and pour in a ladle of batter, swirling the pan immediately.
Break an egg into the centre, cover and cook three minutes to crisp edges. Serve with the lunu miris.
Cut the tomatoes into large wedges and salt them straight in the bowl. Leave them five minutes: the juice they give up becomes the base of the dressing.
Add the cucumber, pepper and onion. Mix with your hands rather than a spoon — nothing breaks that way.
Scatter the olives over, lay the slab of feta on top and pour the oil over everything at once. Sprinkle the oregano straight onto the feta, where the oil will open it up.
Drain the soaked chickpeas, cover with fresh water and the bicarbonate and boil for an hour or ninety minutes, until they collapse. Skim off the foam and the floating skins.
Drain, keeping a cup of the cooking water. Rub the chickpeas between your palms under cold water and the remaining skins float free.
Blend the tahini with the garlic, lemon juice and salt — it pales and thickens. Add the iced water and blend again: it turns light and aerated.
Add the warm chickpeas with the cumin and blend for at least three minutes, loosening with the cooking water. Three minutes is not an exaggeration; that is where the texture comes from.
Spread it on a plate, sweep a channel round it with the back of a spoon, flood it with olive oil and dust with cumin.
Knead a stiff unleavened dough from the flour, water and salt and rest it under a cloth for thirty minutes.
Dice the mutton and fat small with a knife, and chop the onion as fine as you can.
Mix the meat, fat, onion, cumin, salt and pepper. Add no water; the onion supplies the juice.
Divide the dough in two, roll the larger piece into a round and line an oiled tin, leaving an overhang.
Spread the filling evenly, cover with the second sheet and seal the edges in a firm rope.
Make a small steam hole in the centre, brush with butter and cover with foil.
Bake at 180 °C for an hour under the foil, then uncover and give it ten more minutes to colour.
Chop the dates and put them in a pan with the zests, aniseed and liqueur.
Cook the filling over a low heat for twenty minutes, to a thick even paste.
Cool the filling completely; warm, it tears the pastry as you wrap it.
Cut the margarine into the flour with salt to a crumb and bring the dough together with cold water.
Roll the dough into a long strip twelve centimetres wide.
Lay a rope of the date paste down the centre, fold the edges over and press the seam.
Cut it on the diagonal into diamonds and fry them at 180 °C, two minutes a side.
Simmer the brisket with an onion and salt for an hour and a half, until fully tender.
Lift out the meat, keep the broth and pull the beef into fine threads by hand.
Fry the onion, garlic, pepper and tomatoes with the annatto to a thick base.
Slake the masa in cold broth until smooth, without a single lump.
Add the shredded meat to the vegetable base and warm it five minutes.
Pour in the slaked masa in a thin stream, stirring constantly, and cook twenty minutes.
Add the orange juice, stir in the chopped mint and serve it with rice.
Mix the teff flour with water to the consistency of pouring cream, without lumps.
Cover it with a cloth and leave it at room temperature for three days, without stirring.
Pour off the liquid that has separated on top; it is bitter and must not be left in.
Take a cup of the batter, cook it in boiling water to a thick paste and stir it back in.
Let the batter stand another two hours and let it down with water to a very thin cream.
Heat a wide pan, oil it lightly and pour the batter in a spiral from the rim to the centre.
Cover for two minutes, until eyes appear all over the surface, and lift it off without turning.
Simmer the chicken with onion, pierced black lime and baharat for forty minutes. Keep the broth.
Rinse the rice until the water runs clear and soak it twenty minutes.
Fry the vermicelli in ghee to a deep brown, stirring.
Fry the potato, carrot, almonds and raisins separately and drain them on paper.
Joint the chicken and fry the pieces with the tomato paste until browned.
Cook the rice with the fried vermicelli in the strained broth for twenty minutes, covered.
Mound the rice on a platter and lay the chicken and all the fried components on top, unmixed.
Put the meat into the pot raw, add the onion, carrot and the first lot of potatoes cut large.
Pour in the stock, bring it to the boil, skim and cook covered for an hour and a half on the lowest heat.
Crush the collapsed potato against the side of the pot: the broth thickens and turns milky white.
Add the second lot of potatoes in large pieces and cook another forty minutes.
Season, and let it stand fifteen minutes. Scatter parsley over before serving.
Slice the lamb very thin, season it and leave it twenty minutes.
Fry the onion and garlic in oil, add the pepper paste and warm it a minute.
Add the passata and oregano and cook the sauce fifteen minutes to thicken it.
Cut the pide into cubes and dry them in the oven at 180 °C for eight minutes.
Sear the lamb slices over a very high flame in batches, a minute and a half each.
Spread the bread on the plates, spoon over some of the sauce, then the meat and the rest of the sauce.
Melt the butter until it sizzles and pour it over the meat. Put the yoghurt at the side and serve with fried peppers.
Mix the flour with turmeric, curry powder and salt and rub in the cold fat in large pieces, not to a fine crumb.
Add the iced water and bring the dough together without kneading, then chill it half an hour.
Roll it out, fold it in three and repeat twice more, chilling between folds.
Fry the onion, spring onion, thyme and chopped scotch bonnet, add the mince and cook it through.
Add the stock, allspice and breadcrumbs and cook ten minutes to a juicy but not runny filling.
Cool the filling completely, roll out the dough and cut fifteen-centimetre rounds.
Put filling on half of each round, fold it over, crimp with a fork and bake at 200 °C for thirty minutes.
Soak the cracked wheat in cold water for two hours and rinse it.
Fry one onion in ghee, add the meat and brown it.
Add the tomatoes, baharat and pierced limes, cover with water and cook forty minutes.
Add the wheat, top up with water two fingers above and cook ninety minutes on a low heat, stirring.
Remove the bones, stir in the yoghurt and beat the porridge with a spoon or a mixer until creamy and uniform.
Fry the remaining onion dark brown and spoon it over the jareesh with its oil.
Chop the chicken through the bone into pieces about the size of a matchbox.
Pound the ginger and garlic to a coarse paste.
Fry the onion in oil until soft, add the paste and cook it two minutes.
Add the chicken and fry five minutes, until it whitens all over.
Add the tomatoes and chillies, pour in water a finger above and season.
Simmer twenty minutes; the broth should stay thin.
Stir in the coriander and serve in deep bowls with red rice.
Blend the chillies, allspice, spring onion, thyme, ginger, garlic, soy, lime juice, sugar, nutmeg and oil into a thick paste.
Cut deep slashes into the chicken down to the bone and rub the marinade in with gloved hands, filling the cuts.
Refrigerate for at least eight hours, better a full day.
Bank the coals to one side of the grill and throw soaked allspice berries and wood chips on them. Put the chicken on the far side, away from direct heat.
Cook covered at 150-160 °C for an hour and a half, turning every half hour and adding more chips.
For the last ten minutes move it over direct heat for colour. Serve with lime and festival bread.
Knead a dough from the flour and warm water for eight minutes and rest it under film for half an hour.
Salt the shredded cabbage and leave it fifteen minutes, then squeeze it dry by hand.
Work the pork with the ginger, soy and sesame oil in one direction, trickling in the stock until the mass turns tacky. Fold in the cabbage and spring onion.
Roll eight-centimetre rounds, thinner at the edge and thicker in the middle. Add filling and pleat one side shut.
Heat the oil in a pan, set the dumplings in seam up and fry three minutes to a golden base.
Pour in a hundred millilitres of water and cover at once. After seven minutes take the lid off and let the water go, back to a crisp base.
Blend the tomatoes, peppers, one onion and the scotch bonnet until smooth.
Fry the second onion in the oil until soft, add the tomato paste and cook five minutes, until it darkens.
Pour in the purée and reduce it for twenty-five minutes over medium heat, stirring. It darkens, thickens and the oil begins separating at the edges.
Add the curry powder, thyme, bay and stock, season and bring it to the boil.
Stir in the rinsed rice once, cover with foil and a lid, and cook on the lowest heat for twenty-five minutes. Do not lift the lid or stir.
Take it off and let it stand ten minutes. Fork it through from the bottom up, lifting the lower layer.
Grind the saffron with a pinch of sugar and steep it in three spoons of warm water for fifteen minutes.
Grate the onions finely and squeeze the juice through muslin, discarding the pulp.
Mix the onion juice, half the saffron infusion, the juice of two lemons, the yoghurt, oil, salt and pepper.
Cut the chicken into four-centimetre pieces, coat it in the marinade and refrigerate it eight hours.
Thread the pieces onto flat skewers packed tight and get the coals to an even strong heat.
Grill eight minutes a side, turning the skewer every two minutes.
Mix the melted butter with the remaining saffron and brush the kebabs before serving. Serve with rice, tomatoes and sumac.
Boil the soaked beans in a separate pot until soft, an hour. Keep the water.
Simmer the smoked ribs in a litre and a half of water for forty minutes with the bay.
Add the soured turnip or sauerkraut with some of its brine and cook twenty minutes.
Add the diced potato and sausage and cook twenty minutes more.
Fry the onion and garlic in oil until golden and stir them into the soup.
Add the beans with their water, mash some of the potato in the pot and cook five minutes.
Strip the meat from the bones, return it to the soup and season with salt and pepper.
Soak the meat in cold water for four hours, changing the water twice.
Cover it with fresh water, bring it up, boil ten minutes and drain.
Cover it again, add the bay leaves and simmer an hour and twenty, until tender. Keep the broth.
Pod the beans, scald them for a minute and slip the skin off each one.
Render the bacon, fry the onion in its fat, stir in the flour and cook two minutes.
Add two ladles of the broth and the cream, then the savory and the beans, and stew ten minutes.
Cut the meat into thick slices and serve with the beans and boiled potatoes.
Rinse the rice until the water runs clear and soak it twenty minutes.
Fry the onion in ghee until golden, then add the garlic, cardamom and cinnamon.
Brown the chicken on all sides, then add the tomato paste, tomatoes, carrot and baharat.
Pierce the dried limes, drop them in, add water and simmer thirty minutes.
Lift out the chicken, pat it dry and put it under the grill for ten minutes, to a browned skin.
Add the rice to the broth at one and a half times its volume in liquid, season, and cook twenty minutes covered.
Fry the almonds and raisins in ghee, mound the rice on a platter, set the chicken on it and scatter the nuts over.
Soak the rice in salted water for two hours and rinse it until the water runs clear.
Fry the onion in oil until deep gold, add the meat and brown it.
Add a litre of water, the cardamom and salt and simmer an hour, until the meat is tender. Strain the broth.
Melt two spoons of sugar in a dry pan to a dark caramel and let it down carefully with a ladle of broth.
Fry the carrot with the rest of the sugar for five minutes until glossy, add the raisins and nuts and take it off.
Parboil the rice for five minutes and drain it.

Layer the rice over the meat in the pot, spoon over the caramel broth, dust with char masala, pierce to the bottom and hold covered thirty minutes on a low heat. Serve with the carrot and raisins on top.
Boil the cut potatoes in salted water for twenty minutes, until completely soft.
Without draining, rain in the maize flour in a thin stream, stirring constantly.
Cook on a low heat for fifteen minutes, stirring with a wooden paddle; the porridge catches quickly.
Mash the potato in the pot together with the porridge until uniform.
Work in the crumbled cheese and kajmak, adding hot milk, and beat with the paddle for five minutes.
Turn it into a bowl, make a hollow and pour in melted butter. Serve at once.
Mix the flour, eggs, water, salt and nutmeg and beat the dough with a spoon for a good five minutes, until bubbles rise and it starts to string off the spoon.
While the dough rests, fry the onion in butter over medium heat until deep gold. That is twenty minutes, not five — the sugars need the time to caramelise.
Press the dough into boiling salted water through a spätzle grater or a wide-holed colander. They float within a minute; lift them out with a slotted spoon.
Layer them into a warm dish: spätzle, cheese, spätzle, cheese. The heat of the noodles melts it; no oven is needed.
Bury it under the fried onion and serve at once. The classic side is a green salad with a vinegar dressing, and it is a counterweight rather than a garnish.
Simmer the turkey with an onion in three litres of water for ninety minutes, skimming.
Seed the chillies and char them on a dry pan for ten seconds a side.
Char the tomatoes, tomatillos, onion and garlic on the same pan until blackened in patches.
Toast the coriander, achiote and mace on a dry pan until fragrant.
Blend everything with two ladles of the broth to a smooth red mass.
Strain the mass through a sieve into the pot with the turkey and cook twenty-five minutes.
Add the samat and mint for the last five minutes and serve with corn tamalitos.
Whisk the kefir with the sugar and a pinch of salt until the sugar has dissolved.
Add the kama a little at a time, whisking; all at once it lumps, and the lumps never break up.
Leave it fifteen minutes for the flour to swell, then check the consistency and let it down with more kefir if needed.
Stir in the honey and divide between glasses.
Chill for an hour and serve with berries and, if you like, a spoon of whipped cream.
Warm the milk to thirty-seven degrees and dissolve the yeast. Mix with the flour, sugar, salt and cardamom and knead for ten minutes.
Work in the soft butter piece by piece until the dough turns smooth and glossy. Prove for an hour.
Beat the butter with the sugar and cinnamon to a paste. Roll the dough into a half-centimetre rectangle and spread the filling over all of it.
Fold the sheet in three, cut two-centimetre strips, twist each one and tie it in a knot. Space them on a tray.
Prove them for forty minutes, brush with egg and scatter with pearl sugar.
Bake at 220 °C for twelve minutes. Short and hot is what keeps the middle moist.
Soak the mushrooms in a cup of warm water for twenty minutes. Keep the water.
Simmer the smoked ribs in two litres of water for forty minutes with the bay.
Squeeze the kraut and set the brine aside. Add the kraut, the mushrooms with their water and the prunes to the broth and cook thirty minutes.
Fry the onion, take it off the heat, stir in the paprika and flour and let it down with a ladle of broth until smooth.
Pour the roux into the pot, add the sausage and cook fifteen minutes more.
Strip the meat off the bones, return it to the soup and bring the sourness up with the brine to taste. Serve with soured cream.
Simmer the oxtail in water for three hours on a low heat, skimming. Keep the broth.
Toast the rice in a dry pan until brown and grind it to a fine powder.
Warm the annatto seeds in oil for three minutes and strain it; the coloured oil is where the dish gets its colour.
Fry the onion and garlic in the annatto oil, add the peanut butter and let it down with broth.
Stir in the rice powder and cook the sauce fifteen minutes, stirring, to the body of soured cream.
Return the oxtail to the sauce and warm it ten minutes so the meat takes it up.
Blanch the vegetables separately until just tender, lay them over the meat and serve with rice and bagoong.
Cook the rice in the milk over a low flame for forty minutes, to a slightly loose porridge. Season it and cool it.
Knead a dough from the rye flour, water and salt for five minutes. It comes out firm and not sticky.
Divide it into sixteen balls and roll each into an oval half a millimetre thick. Dust with rye flour rather than wheat.
Spoon porridge into the middle, leaving the edges bare, and crimp them into a frill with the filling left open.
Bake at 250 °C for fifteen minutes — short and very hot, or the thin pastry dries out.
Melt half the butter with an equal amount of hot water and dip the hot pies in it. Cover them with a cloth for ten minutes.
Mash the boiled eggs with the rest of the butter, softened, and salt: this is munavoi, egg butter. Serve it with the pies.
Nick the fat rim of each cutlet in a few places so they do not curl, season them and coat in flour, then egg, then panko.
Deep-fry at 170 °C for three minutes a side until golden. Drain on a rack rather than paper, so the underside stays crisp.
Cut the cutlets into strips a centimetre and a half wide without moving them apart — the shape matters when you serve.
In a small pan bring the dashi, soy, mirin and sugar to the boil, add the onion and cook for three minutes until soft.

Slide the cutlet into the broth, pour two thirds of the loosely beaten egg around it and cover for a minute. Add the rest, cover for twenty seconds more and take it off — the top layer of egg should stay loose.
Slide everything in the pan onto the rice in one movement, sauce and all.
Brown the diced pork in oil on all sides.
Add the onion and peppers and fry seven minutes, until soft.
Add the mushrooms and cook over a high flame until their water has gone.
Take it off the heat, stir in the paprika and savory, add the wine and return it to the heat for three minutes.
Add the chopped tomatoes, season, and divide everything between the pots.
Bake at 180 °C for forty-five minutes, covered.
Take the lids off, break an egg into each pot, scatter the cheese and give them eight minutes more.
Knot the pandan leaves and warm them with the coconut milk until hot, without boiling.
Whisk the eggs with the sugar until it dissolves and strain the mixture through a fine sieve.
Pour the warm coconut milk into the eggs in a thin stream, stirring without stopping.
Cook the mixture over a water bath for forty minutes, stirring with a wooden spoon, to the thickness of jam.
Remove the pandan leaves and cool the kaya completely; it thickens further.
Boil the eggs exactly six minutes and serve them in a bowl with soy sauce and white pepper.
Toast the bread crisp, spread it with kaya and lay a cold slice of butter between two pieces.
Cut the onion, tomatoes, aubergines and pepper into large pieces.
Put the chicken and all the vegetables into the pot with the garlic, ginger, thyme, bay, salt and pepper.
Lay the whole scotch bonnet on top, uncut.
Cover it and seal the join with a rope of flour-and-water dough, or wrap it in foil.
Set it over the lowest heat or in a 160 °C oven for an hour and twenty.
Every fifteen minutes shake the pot, holding the lid down. Do not open it once.
Break the seal, remove the chilli and serve with attiéké or rice.
Crush the crackers to fine crumbs and mix them with the melted butter, sugar and a pinch of salt.
Press the crumbs into a tin, working them up the sides, and bake at 175 °C for ten minutes.
Beat the yolks with the zest of two limes until pale, about three minutes.
Add the condensed milk and beat three minutes more, until the mixture thickens.
Pour in the lime juice in a thin stream with the mixer running; the mixture thickens in the bowl.
Pour the filling into the base and bake at 160 °C for fifteen minutes, until the edges set and the centre still wobbles.
Cool it and chill it four hours, then top with cream whipped with the icing sugar.
Stir the yeast and sugar into the warm matsoni and leave it ten minutes to foam. No foam means dead yeast, so start again.
Add the egg, the melted butter, the salt and the flour. Knead a soft dough: it should stay slightly tacky, and no more flour goes in.
Cover it and leave it somewhere warm for an hour, until it has doubled.
Mix both cheeses together by hand until even and divide into four balls. Divide the dough into four as well.
Roll each piece of dough into a disc, set a ball of cheese in the middle, gather the edges to the centre and pinch them shut. Turn it seam down and roll it gently to about a centimetre thick.
Cook in a dry pan over medium heat for about four minutes a side, until dark spots appear. Brush the finished bread with butter.
Set a fifth of the noodles aside, separate the strands and deep-fry them to a golden crisp.
Heat the thick part of the coconut milk in a pan, without stirring, until the oil separates out.
Fry the curry paste, curry powder and turmeric in that oil for three minutes, until deeply fragrant.
Add the chicken and turn it in the paste until it is coated all over.
Add the rest of the coconut milk and some water, the fish sauce and the sugar, and simmer thirty minutes.
Boil the remaining noodles and divide them between bowls.
Ladle over the curry and chicken, top with the fried noodles, shallot, pickled greens, coriander and a wedge of lime.
Knead a dough from the flour, water and a pinch of salt. It should come out noticeably stiffer than a dumpling dough — hard work to knead. Wrap it and rest it for forty minutes.
Chop the meat by hand into pieces a few millimetres across. Mix it with the onion, coriander, cumin, salt and pepper.
Work the iced water into the filling a little at a time until the mixture turns sticky and stops taking any more. Chill it for twenty minutes.

Roll out discs 12 cm across and about two millimetres thick. Put a tablespoon of filling in the middle and gather the edge in pleats all the way round — eighteen at the least. Twist the top and pinch it shut.
Drop them into a large pot of salted boiling water, swirling the water with a slotted spoon first so they do not stick. Boil for seven or eight minutes after they float.
Boil the beetroot until tender with a spoon of vinegar so it keeps its colour, and cool it completely.
Cook the sorrel in a little water for five minutes, until it darkens, and cool it.
Grate the cooled beetroot coarsely and cut the cucumbers into matchsticks.
Mix the beetroot, the sorrel with its liquid, the cucumber and herbs with the soured cream and salt it.
Add the cold kefir and stir to an even pink.
Chill it an hour so the soup infuses and turns genuinely cold.
Boil the potatoes and serve them hot on a separate plate, with halved eggs in the soup.
Knead an unleavened dough from the flour, water and salt and work it ten minutes to smoothness.
Cover the dough and rest it thirty minutes.
Chop the lamb fine by knife, fat and all, and mix it with the onion and garlic.
Pour the broth into the filling and work it to a loose but not runny mass.
Divide the dough into balls and roll each into a twelve-centimetre round.
Put filling on one half, fold it over and crimp the edge tightly and evenly.
Fry them in a centimetre of oil, three minutes a side, to a blistered crust.
Soak the bulgur in cold water for twenty minutes and squeeze it completely dry.
Blitz the lean beef with one onion to a paste and work in the bulgur, salt and half the spices.
Knead the mass five minutes, wetting your hands, until it is smooth and tacky.
Fry the remaining onion, add the minced lamb, the spices and the pine nuts and cook ten minutes.
Press half the mass into an oiled tray in a one-centimetre layer, smoothing it with a wet palm.
Spread the filling and cover with the other half of the mass, smoothed the same way.
Cut it into diamonds down to the base, pour over the olive oil and bake at 200 °C for forty minutes, to a browned crust.
Soak the bulgur in cold water for ten minutes, drain and squeeze it dry. Chill the bowl — everything for nayyeh must stay cold.
Trim the lamb of fat and silverskin down to clean muscle and cube it. Blitz with the onion to a smooth paste without letting the bowl warm up.
Add the bulgur, spices, mint and salt. Knead, wetting your hands with iced water, until the paste is smooth and glossy.
Spread the paste over a cold plate about a centimetre and a half thick, press grooves with the back of a spoon and pour the olive oil over generously.
Serve at once, with mint leaves, white onion wedges and flatbread. Nayyeh is not kept: leftovers are fried as patties the same evening.
Fry the pork in the sesame oil over medium heat until the fat has rendered and the meat has colour, about five minutes.
Add the kimchi and fry for five minutes, until the edges darken. This step takes the raw edge off the acidity and rounds the flavour out.
Stir in the gochugaru, gochujang and garlic, pour in the kimchi liquid and the water, and bring it to the boil.
Simmer for twenty minutes, add the onion and tofu and give it five more. Do not stir the tofu; it falls apart.
Off the heat, scatter over the spring onion and serve it in the pot, with a separate bowl of rice.
Melt the butter over a low heat with the ginger, garlic, cardamom, cinnamon and fenugreek.
Hold it twenty minutes without boiling, until the foam settles and the butter turns clear.
Strain the niter kibbeh through muslin and keep it warm.
Trim every membrane and sinew from the beef and chop it very fine with a knife, almost to a paste.
Work the warm niter kibbeh, mitmita and salt into the meat by hand for two minutes.
Warm the mixture in a pan for thirty seconds to body temperature, without letting it whiten.
Serve it on injera with the ayib cheese and stewed greens alongside.
Cover the meat with three litres of cold water, bring it up and skim carefully.
Simmer for an hour and a half, never letting it boil hard; the broth has to stay clear.
Add the barley and onion and cook forty minutes more.
Add the carrot, swede and potato in large pieces and cook twenty minutes.
Add the cabbage for the last ten minutes and season with salt and pepper.
Divide the meat between bowls, ladle over the broth and vegetables and serve with rye bread.
Work the mince with the starch, salt, pepper, ginger and nutmeg for five minutes.
Add the iced water a spoon at a time, still working the mixture, until it turns tacky and even.
Fold in the grated onion and chill the mixture twenty minutes.
Shape flat oval patties with wet hands, about a hundred grams each.
Fry the patties in butter four minutes a side and move them to a pot.
Stir the flour into the pan with the remaining fat, cook it to a nutty brown and add the stock.
Pour the sauce over the patties and stew twenty minutes. Serve with potatoes, peas and lingonberry.
Cut deep slits into the lamb and push a sliver of garlic into each.
Rub the meat with salt, pepper, oregano, olive oil and lemon juice.
Leave the lamb to marinate in the fridge for at least four hours.
Cut the potatoes into large wedges and lay them in the base of a clay dish.
Set the meat on the potatoes and add the bay, cinnamon and lemon halves.
Cover it and seal the join with a strip of dough or a double layer of foil.
Bake at 160 °C for five hours without opening it and rest it twenty minutes.
Dissolve the yeast in the warm milk and leave it ten minutes, until it foams.
Rub the flour with the melted ghee, mahlab, fennel, nigella and salt.
Add the yeast mixture and knead a soft dough, working it ten minutes.
Cover it and rest it an hour at room temperature.
Work the date paste with a spoon of ghee and the cardamom until pliable.
Roll the dough into a rectangle, spread the paste in a thin layer and roll it into a tight log.
Cut the log into centimetre slices, brush them with yolk, scatter with sesame and bake at 180 °C for twenty minutes.
Soak the bread in a hundred millilitres of the cream for ten minutes and mash it to a paste.
Fry the onion in butter until soft and cool it completely: warm onion starts cooking the meat.
Mix both minces with the panade, onion, egg, allspice and salt, and work it for five minutes until tacky.
Roll walnut-sized balls with wet hands and fry them in butter in batches, shaking the pan so they roll and colour evenly.
In the same pan whisk the flour into the remaining fat, pour in the stock and the rest of the cream, add the soy and cook five minutes to a sauce.
Return the meatballs to the sauce and warm them through for five minutes. Serve with mashed potato, lingonberry and pickled cucumber.
Push the curd through a fine sieve twice, until not a single grain remains.
Beat the softened butter with the icing sugar, vanilla and salt until fluffy.
Combine the curd with the butter mixture and work in the cream to the body of a firm cream.
Fold in the raisins and shape twelve finger-sized bars.
Lay the bars on parchment and freeze them two hours, until solid.
Melt the chocolate with the coconut oil over a water bath until smooth and cool it to lukewarm.
Dip the frozen bars on two forks, let them drain and set them on parchment to harden.
Soak the beans four hours, then rub them between your hands so the skins come away.
Rinse the beans several times, pouring off the floating skins, until the grains are clean and white.
Grind the beans with the onion and chilli into a thick paste, adding water a spoon at a time.
Beat the mass by hand or with a spatula for ten minutes, until it lightens and turns airy.
Warm the palm oil and work it into the mass to an even orange.
Pass the banana leaves over a flame until pliable and spoon the mass onto them with the greens.
Fold the parcels, tie them and steam them an hour and a half, until firm.
Soak the dried mushrooms in warm water for twenty minutes and chop them fine.
Fry two onions with the mince and mushrooms, add the marjoram, salt and pepper and cool it completely.
Grate the potatoes and the remaining onion finely into one bowl.
Let the mass stand three minutes and pour off the water that gathers, leaving the sediment.
Work in the egg and season the potato mass.
Put a spoon of the mass on your palm, add filling and cover it with a second spoon, sealing the edges.
Fry them three minutes a side, move them to a pan, pour over the soured cream and stew fifteen minutes.
Fry the onion in the oil over medium heat for twenty-five minutes to a deep brown, stirring. Drain it on paper; it crisps as it cools.
Boil the lentils for twenty minutes to soft but not collapsing, and drain.
Cook the rice in the onion oil: fry it two minutes, add water at one and a half to one and cook covered for fifteen minutes.
Boil the pasta and drain it. For the sauce, fry the garlic in a spoon of oil to gold, pour in the vinegar and let it reduce by half.
Add the tomatoes, cumin and chilli and cook twenty minutes to a thick sauce. Season.
Build it in the bowl in layers: rice, lentils, pasta, chickpeas, sauce, fried onion. The mixing happens at the table.
Cut the roti into centimetre strips: that makes the chopping easier later.
Heat a large pan with the oil, fry the onion, leek and chilli two minutes, add the carrot and cabbage and cook three more.
Push the vegetables aside, break the eggs into the cleared space, let them set and break them up.
Add the chicken, curry powder and strips of roti and start chopping with two spatulas, mixing as you go. Three minutes of real work.
Pour the curry sauce down the side and keep chopping a minute more. The mixture should be moist but not wet.
Scald the vine leaves for a minute and spread them on a cloth.
Mix both minces with the raw rice, grated onion, tomatoes and herbs.
Work in the cinnamon, mint, salt, pepper and half the olive oil.
Put a spoon of filling on a leaf, fold the sides in and roll it into a tight cylinder.
Line the pot with torn leaves so the rolls do not catch.
Pack the rolls in tight layers seam down and weight them with a plate.
Pour in water with lemon juice and oil and cook them an hour, covered, over a low heat.
Dice the pork and fat and chill them to just above freezing.
Put the meat through the coarse plate of a mincer and the fat through the medium one.
Work in the curing salt, crushed garlic, pepper and iced water and knead the mixture until tacky.
Leave the mixture in the fridge for a day so the salt distributes and the colour sets.
Fill the casings tightly but without air pockets and tie them in twenty-centimetre pairs.
Air-dry the sausages two hours and cold-smoke them if you can.
Lower them into water at 75 °C and hold them twenty-five minutes without letting it boil. Serve with horseradish and mustard.
Cover the bone-in lamb with cold water, bring it up and skim. Add the chickpeas and simmer for an hour.
Work a grated onion, the rice, salt and pepper into the mince and knead for five minutes, until the mass pulls back at your hand.
Divide the mince into four. Hide a plum and an apricot in each and shape a tight ball with no cracks.
Lower the kufta into the barely simmering broth and cook thirty minutes without stirring. For the first five minutes do not touch it at all.
Add the potatoes whole and the turmeric and cook twenty minutes more, until the potatoes are tender.
Into each bowl goes one kufta, one potato and some chickpeas; ladle over the broth and crumble dried mint on top.
Render the bacon to crackling, add the chopped onion and fry it golden.
Grate the potatoes finely and squeeze them lightly, collecting the liquid in a bowl.
Let the liquid stand ten minutes, pour off the water and stir the settled starch back in.
Add the hot milk and the hot fat with the onion and crackling, stirring quickly.
Work in the eggs, salt, pepper and marjoram to an even thick mass.
Pour it into a greased dish in a four-centimetre layer and level it.
Bake at 180 °C for an hour and a half, to a deep golden crust, and rest it twenty minutes.
Boil the diced potato in a litre and a half of water with the caraway and bay for fifteen minutes.
Fry the sliced mushrooms in butter until their water has gone and add them to the pot.
Cook them together ten minutes so the mushrooms give their flavour to the broth.
Whisk the soured cream with the flour until smooth and lump-free.
Take the soup off the heat, stir in the cream mixture, return it to a low flame and warm it five minutes without boiling.
Add the vinegar, sugar, salt, pepper and most of the dill and taste for the balance of sour against creamy.
Poach the eggs in acidulated water and set one into each bowl, scattered with the remaining dill.
Boil a syrup of sugar, water and lemon juice for ten minutes, take it off, add the flower waters and cool it completely.
Soak salted cheese in cold water for two hours, changing it three times, and cut it into cubes.
Pull the kataifi apart into separate strands by hand and shorten them with scissors.
Pour the melted ghee over the pastry and rub it through with your hands until every strand glistens.
Press half the pastry into a greased tin, spread the cheese short of the edges and cover with the other half.
Bake at 190 °C for forty minutes to a deep gold underneath — check by lifting an edge with a spatula.
Turn it out onto a platter, pour the cold syrup over at once and scatter with ground pistachios.
Cover the qurut with hot water for twenty minutes and rub it by hand into an even liquid.
Pass it through a sieve to remove any grains. The liquid should be like thin soured cream.
Slice the onion into rings and fry it in oil until golden, ten minutes.
Tear the fatir into large pieces into a wide dish.
Pour the qurut over the bread and leave it five minutes to soak.
Top with the fried onion and its oil, then the tomato, cucumber and herbs.
Dice the tail fat and render it in a cauldron to golden crackling.
Lift out the crackling with a slotted spoon and set it aside; it goes back at the very end.
Cut the meat into walnut-sized pieces and fry it in batches to a dark crust.
Return all the meat to the pot, salt it, add the cumin and cover it for fifteen minutes.
Add the onion in thick half-moons and fry until it turns translucent.
Add the potatoes in large pieces and cook twenty minutes more, covered.
Return the crackling, add the garlic and coriander and serve it straight from the pot with bread.
Dissolve the yeast with the sugar in the warm milk and leave it ten minutes, until it foams.
Steep the saffron in a spoon of hot water and knead a dough with the flour, egg, half the butter and cardamom.
Let the dough rise somewhere warm for an hour, until doubled.
Warm the date paste with the remaining butter and cardamom until soft.
Roll the dough into a rectangle half a centimetre thick and spread the date paste over it.
Roll it up tight and cut it into two-centimetre rounds.
Set them cut side up, prove them twenty minutes and bake at 180 °C for twenty-five minutes.
Rinse the cracked wheat and soak it in cold water for an hour.
Fry two of the onions in ghee until soft and add the baharat.
Brown the chicken with the onion and add the tomatoes, tomato paste, cinnamon and pierced dried lime.
Pour in two litres of water, salt it and cook forty minutes, until the chicken is tender.
Lift out the chicken, tip the wheat into the broth and cook it an hour over a low heat.
Mash the porridge until the grain breaks down into a uniform mass.
Fry the remaining onion to deep brown, plate the porridge with the chicken and pour the onion and its butter over.
Soak the kidneys in cold water for an hour, changing it twice, and trim out every duct.
Render the tail fat in the cauldron to cracklings and lift them out with a slotted spoon.
Sear the mutton hard to a dark crust, five minutes.
Add the heart and fry eight minutes more, stirring.
Add the kidneys, then the liver three minutes later, and fry three more; the liver must not overcook.
Add the diced onion and potato, season, add the cumin and cook covered for fifteen minutes.
Stir in the garlic and herbs, take it off the heat and serve straight from the cauldron with flatbread.
Leave the whites in an open bowl at room temperature for twelve hours.
Toast the nuts ten minutes, chop them coarsely and mix them with the flour and part of the sugar.
Whip the whites to a foam, adding the rest of the sugar a spoon at a time, to firm glossy peaks.
Fold in the nut mixture with a spatula in three additions and divide it between two tins.
Dry the layers at 150 °C for two hours and leave them in the switched-off oven until completely cold.
Cook a syrup of milk, yolks and sugar to thickness, cool it completely and beat it into the softened butter.
Split the cream: vanilla and brandy into the larger part, cocoa into the smaller. Assemble the cake and chill it six hours.
Knead a dough from the flour and warm salted water and work it fifteen minutes until smooth.
Divide it into ropes, oil them generously, coil them in a bowl and leave them an hour under film.
Stretch a rope, folding it in half and swinging it, until the strands are the thickness of a matchstick.
Sear the beef in very hot oil, then add the onion, cumin and ground coriander.
Add the vegetables in order: radish, beans, pepper, and the tomatoes and paste last.
Add a cup of boiling water, season and stew ten minutes; the vegetables should keep their bite.
Boil the noodles in plenty of water for three minutes, drain and divide between bowls. Vaja and coriander on top.
Knead a dough from the flour, water, yeast and salt for eight minutes and prove it an hour.
Blend the onion, pepper and tomato and press the purée through a sieve: the spare water is not wanted.
Mix the lamb with the vegetable purée, the pepper paste, chopped parsley, flakes and salt. It should be as thick as a pâté.
Heat the oven with a stone at full power for forty minutes.
Roll the balls of dough paper-thin, twenty-five centimetres across, and spread the topping thinly right to the edges.
Bake on the stone three or four minutes. The edges should colour and the middle stay soft: a lahmacun is rolled up to eat.
Fry the garlic slices in oil until golden and lift them out at once; a few seconds more and they turn bitter.
Toast the sesame in a dry pan until fragrant, two minutes, stirring.
Rinse the tea paste in cold water if it is very salty and squeeze it dry.
Shred the cabbage fine, cut the tomatoes into wedges and the chilli into rings.
Combine everything in a bowl with the peanuts, beans, sesame, garlic oil, fish sauce and lime juice.
Toss it with your hands immediately before serving and scatter the fried garlic over the top.
Soak the dried chillies in boiling water for fifteen minutes, then blend them with the shallots, lemongrass, galangal, turmeric and belacan to a smooth paste.
Fry the paste in the oil over medium heat for fifteen minutes, stirring. It is ready when the oil starts separating and rising at the edges.
Pour in the stock, bring it to the boil and simmer ten minutes. Add the prawns and tofu for three minutes.
Add the coconut milk and warm it through without letting it boil hard. Season.
Divide the cooked noodles between bowls, ladle the broth over and serve the sprouts, cucumber and lime alongside.
Peel the prawns, fry the shells and simmer them in a litre of water for twenty minutes, then strain.
Soak the dried chillies and dried shrimp in boiling water for twenty minutes.
Blend the chillies, shallot, garlic, lemongrass, galangal, turmeric, candlenuts and belacan into a paste.
Fry the paste in oil for twenty minutes over medium heat, until the oil breaks out at the edges.
Add the prawn broth and the laksa leaf and cook fifteen minutes.
Add the coconut milk, season and warm it five minutes without letting it boil.
Cut the cooked noodles into short lengths, divide them between bowls with the prawns and sprouts and ladle over the broth.
Beat the butter and sugar pale, add the eggs one at a time, then the vanilla.
Fold in the sifted flour with the baking powder and salt, alternating with the milk.
Pour into a square tin and bake at 180 °C for twenty-eight minutes, until a skewer comes out clean.
Cool it completely and leave the sponge uncovered overnight.
Cut it into five-centimetre cubes.
Whisk the icing sugar with the cocoa and hot milk to a thin icing that runs off a spoon in a stream.
Dip each cube on two forks, let it drain and roll it in coconut. Leave them to set for an hour.
Fry the fish steaks three minutes a side and let them cool.
Lift the flesh off the bones, picking out every small bone.
Fry the onion, add the cauliflower florets and stew them ten minutes.
Add the spinach, tomato paste, olives, capers, sultanas and walnuts and cook it dry.
Cool the filling completely and fold the fish into it in pieces.
Line a tin with pastry, add the filling and cover it with a second sheet, crimping the edge.
Glaze it with egg, cut vents and bake at 190 °C for forty-five minutes, to a golden crust.
Dissolve the yeast and sugar in the warm milk and leave it ten minutes, until it foams.
Mix the flour, mashed potato, salt and the yeast liquid and knead for eight minutes to a smooth soft dough. It stays a little tacky; that is right.
Cover and prove for an hour in the warm: the dough should double.
Divide into four, stretch each by hand into a twenty-centimetre round, leaving the edges thicker.
Deep-fry at 175 °C for ninety seconds a side. It balloons; that is correct, do not press it down.
Rub the hot bread with a cut clove of garlic, spread it with soured cream and pile on the cheese.
Toast the raw sticky rice in a dry pan for ten minutes, to a deep gold, stirring.
Grind the cooled rice in a mortar or mill to a coarse powder.
Chop the pork fine with a knife, but not to a paste; the pieces should stay distinguishable.
Cook the meat in a pan with two spoons of water over medium heat for five minutes, breaking up lumps.
Take it off the heat and let it cool to warm, about five minutes.
Stir in the fish sauce, lime juice, chilli, shallot and rice powder.
Add the herbs, toss and serve with sticky rice and raw vegetables.
Render the pancetta, add the soffritto and sweat it twenty minutes over a low flame until completely soft. There is no hurrying this: the vegetables have to dissolve.
Add both minces and cook over a high flame, breaking up the lumps, until every drop of water has gone and the meat starts to brown.
Pour in the milk and let it cook away entirely, about twenty minutes. Then the wine, likewise to dryness.
Add the tomato paste and the stock, bring it to the boil and simmer three hours on the lowest heat, topping up with water as needed.
Make the béchamel: melt the butter, whisk in the flour, cook it a minute and pour in warm milk in a thin stream, whisking. Cook to the thickness of cream and season with nutmeg.
Build the layers: béchamel, pasta, ragù, béchamel, parmesan — six times over. The top layer is béchamel with parmesan.
Bake at 180 °C for forty minutes, the last ten uncovered. Let it stand twenty minutes before cutting.
Melt the sugar with the water to an amber caramel and pour it into the moulds, tilting them to coat the base.
Let the caramel set in the moulds while you make the custard.
Work the yolks with a whisk without beating them to a foam; air bubbles leave holes.
Stir in both milks, the vanilla and the zest, mixing slowly.
Strain the mixture twice through a fine sieve and lift any foam off the surface with a spoon.
Pour it into the moulds over the caramel and seal each one tightly with foil.
Steam for forty minutes at a gentle simmer, chill four hours and turn out onto a plate.
Slash the fish at the sides and rub it with salt, pepper and lemon juice.
Grind the garlic, ginger and chilli to a paste and work it into the cuts and the cavity.
Pass the banana leaves over a flame so they turn pliable and stop cracking.
Lay tomato and onion slices on a leaf, the fish on them, then more tomato and spring onion.
Wrap in three leaves into a tight parcel and tie it with a strip of the same leaf.
Set the parcels on the coals and bake them fifteen minutes a side.
Serve them still in the leaf, with boiled cassava or rice.
Boil the potatoes in their skins, peel them hot and mash them dry. Add no liquid at all.
Warm the achiote in a spoon of oil for a minute and work the coloured oil into the mash with salt.
Roll balls, press a cube of cheese into each, close them up and flatten into cakes a centimetre thick.
Chill the cakes for half an hour; that is what holds their shape in the pan.
For the sauce fry the onion, add the peanut butter and milk and simmer five minutes to the thickness of cream.
Fry the cakes over medium heat, four minutes a side, to a golden crust.
Serve with a fried egg, the sauce and an avocado salad.
Cover the head and bones with a litre and a half of water, add the allspice and bay, and simmer twenty-five minutes, skimming. Strain it.
Fry the leek and carrot in butter for five minutes without letting them colour.
Pour in the strained stock, add the potato and cook fifteen minutes until soft.
Add the cream and warm it without boiling. Season.
Slip in the pieces of salmon and hold them at a bare simmer for exactly five minutes. The fish should stay in whole pieces.
Ladle into bowls and add a knob of butter and a generous handful of dill to each.
Marinate the beef in the oyster and soy sauces with garlic, sugar and half the pepper for twenty minutes.
Mix the lime juice with the remaining pepper and a pinch of salt; that is the dipping sauce.
Arrange the lettuce, tomato and cucumber slices and red onion rings on a platter.
Heat a pan as high as it goes and sear the beef in batches, a minute and a half each, without stirring constantly.
Fry the eggs, keeping the yolks runny.
Pile the beef on the vegetables, top with the eggs and give everyone their own small bowl of the dip.
Marinate the beef in the soy, vinegar and garlic for fifteen minutes, then pat it dry: a wet surface will not scorch.
Heat the pan until it smokes and sear the beef in two batches, ninety seconds each, leaving it alone for the first forty seconds. Set it aside.
In the same pan fry the onion and ají for ninety seconds — the onion should stay crisp inside.
Return the beef, pour in what is left of the marinade, add the tomatoes and warm through for half a minute. Take it off and stir in the coriander.
Serve with hot chips — some tossed into the pan so they take up the sauce — and a separate helping of rice.
Dice the belly into one-centimetre cubes, keeping the fat with the meat.
Fry the sliced shallots in oil to a deep golden crisp and set half aside for serving.
In the same oil brown the pork, rendering some of its fat, for ten minutes.
Add the wine, let it cook off for a minute, then add both soy sauces, the sugar, spices and garlic.
Add water level with the meat, bring it up and braise covered for ninety minutes on the lowest heat.
Add the boiled eggs to the sauce for the last twenty minutes; they take on the colour and flavour.
Serve over rice with half an egg, blanched greens and the fried shallots on top.
Steep the saffron in a spoon of warm water and leave it.
Mix the flour, cornflour, yeast, sugar, cardamom and salt.
Add the yoghurt, warm water and saffron infusion and whisk to a smooth loose batter.
Leave it somewhere warm for an hour; the batter should rise and bubble.
Heat the oil to 170 °C and drop the batter in by the teaspoon, dipping it in water each time.
Fry in batches for three to four minutes, moving them with a slotted spoon, to a deep gold.
Drain on paper, pour over the date syrup and scatter with sesame. Serve at once.
Brown the pork well, add the onion and fry until soft.
Add the sliced sausage and ribs, pour in a cup of water, add the bay and stew twenty-five minutes.
Whisk the flour into the soured cream until smooth and stir it into the pot.
Simmer ten minutes on a low heat, until the gravy thickens to the consistency of pouring cream.
Whisk a pancake batter from the flour, milk, eggs and salt and let it stand fifteen minutes.
Cook thin unsweetened pancakes in a dry pan.
Serve the machanka in a deep bowl with the pancakes stacked beside it. You tear off a piece and dip.
Rinse the rice until the water runs clear and soak it twenty minutes.
Fry the onion in ghee to a deep gold, fifteen minutes, and set a third aside.
Add the garlic, ginger, bizar and turmeric and warm them a minute, until fragrant.
Add the tomatoes and the pierced limes, pour in water at one and a half times the volume of the rice, and season.
Bring it up, add the rice, cover and cook fifteen minutes on a low heat.
Lay the prawns over the rice, cover and give it five more minutes; they cook in the steam.
Rest it ten minutes and scatter with the reserved onion, coriander and chilli.
Rub the semolina with the olive oil and salt by hand until it is damp all through.
Leave the mixture half an hour so the grain takes up the oil and swells.
Add the warm water with the orange blossom water a little at a time, gathering the dough without kneading.
Steam the dates soft and pound them with the cinnamon and zest into a smooth paste.
Roll the dough into a strip, lay a rope of date paste down the centre and close the edges over it.
Press the strip flat and cut it on the diagonal into four-centimetre diamonds.
Deep-fry at 170 °C until golden and drop them hot into cold honey for five minutes.
Slake the cornflour in a cup of cold milk until completely dissolved and lump-free.
Heat the rest of the milk with the cream and sugar until hot, without letting it boil.
Pour in the starch mixture in a thin stream, whisking without stopping.
Cook over medium heat for five minutes, until the mixture thickens to the body of double cream.
Take it off the heat, stir in the rose water and pour it straight into glasses.
Press film onto the surface so no skin forms and chill for four hours.
Before serving pour over the syrup and scatter with chopped pistachios, peanuts and coconut.
Cover the jointed rabbit with the wine, half the garlic and the bay leaves and refrigerate for a day.
Lift out the meat, dry it and brown it in olive oil. Keep the marinade.
Fry the onion and remaining garlic until soft, add the tomato paste and cook three minutes.
Return the meat, pour in the marinade, season and stew covered for an hour on a low heat.
Add the potato and carrot and stew twenty-five minutes more.
Add the peas for the last ten minutes.
Ladle off some of the sauce and dress spaghetti with it as a first course. The meat follows.
Bring the salted water to the boil. Set aside a handful of the meal; it is wanted at the end.
Pour the meal in as a thin stream, whisking without stopping. Do not pause until all of it is in.
Drop to the lowest heat and cook thirty minutes, stirring with a wooden spoon every three or four minutes. The mass pulls away from the sides.
Add the reserved handful of meal and work it in: it gives the light graininess mămăligă is valued for.
Stir in the butter, turn it out onto a board and let it stand five minutes. Cut it into slabs with thread and serve with the cheese and soured cream.
Warm the coconut milk and dissolve the yeast in it with a spoon of sugar.
Mix the flour with the remaining sugar, the cardamom and the salt.
Work in the egg, melted butter and the coconut yeast mixture and knead a soft dough.
Let it rise somewhere warm for an hour, until doubled.
Divide the dough into four, rolling each piece into a round a centimetre thick.
Cut each round into four triangles and let them rest fifteen minutes.
Fry at 170 °C for two minutes a side, to a golden colour.
Peel the plantains under water, halve them and boil in salted water for twenty minutes, until soft.
Set aside a cup of the cooking water and cool it.
Pickle the sliced onion in vinegar with salt and leave it fifteen minutes.
Mash the hot plantain with butter, adding the cold water, to a smooth purée.
Fry slices of salami and cheese in a dry pan until browned.
Fry the eggs and build the plate: purée, the onion and its vinegar on top, salami, cheese and egg alongside.
Soak the jameed in warm water for four hours, break it up by hand and pass it through a sieve to an even liquid.
