Simmer the lamb with the cardamom for an hour and twenty minutes, skimming. Keep the broth.
Pour the jameed liquid in with the meat and bring it up, stirring continuously in one direction.
Drop the heat to its lowest and hold it forty minutes. The sauce thickens and turns creamy.
Cook the rice in the meat broth with turmeric and a spoon of ghee.
Fry the almonds and pine nuts in ghee until golden and set them aside.
Line a platter with the bread, moisten it with sauce, spread the rice, lay the meat on top, spoon over more sauce and scatter the nuts and parsley.
Knead a stiff dough from the flour, eggs, water and salt and work it fifteen minutes.
Cover it and rest it forty minutes, or the dough springs back as you roll it.
Mix the mince with the grated onion, salt and pepper and squeeze out the excess juice.
Roll the dough a millimetre thick and cut it into two-centimetre squares.
Put a knife-tip of filling on each square and pinch the four corners up into a knot.
Boil the mantı in salted water for eight minutes and drain, keeping a ladle of the water.
Whisk the yoghurt with the garlic, plate the mantı, spoon the yoghurt over and pour on the paprika and mint butter.
Knead a dough from the flour, water and salt, work it ten minutes and rest it forty under film.
Mix the mince with the finely chopped onion, salt, pepper and coriander. Add no water.
Boil the split peas forty minutes until soft, with a spoon of tomato paste and salt.
Crush the garlic with salt, stir it into the yoghurt and thin it with water to pouring consistency.
Roll the dough thin and cut it into eight-centimetre squares.
Add the filling and bring the corners together crosswise, leaving four open corners.
Steam twenty-five minutes. Set them on a layer of yoghurt, spoon over the pea sauce, more yoghurt, and dust with mint.
Slip the tofu into barely simmering salted water for three minutes and drain it gently.
Fry the pork until browned and its fat has rendered, then push it aside. Add the doubanjiang and fry for a minute, until the oil turns red.
Add the garlic, ginger and black beans, warm for half a minute and pour in the stock. Bring it to the boil.
Slide the tofu in and simmer for three minutes without stirring — swirl the pan instead, or the cubes break up.
Slake the cornflour in cold water and add it in two goes, letting the sauce come back to the boil each time. Off the heat, scatter over the ground Sichuan pepper and spring onion.
Cut the lamb into two-finger strips along the grain.
Rub the strips all over with salt and turmeric, sparing neither.
Hang the meat in shade with a draught and dry it three to five days, until fully hard.
Soak the dried meat in cold water for two hours, changing the water once.
Boil the meat forty minutes, until it softens and starts to come apart in threads.
Fry the onion with the garlic, cumin and chilli in ghee until golden.
Add the shredded meat and fry ten minutes more, to browned edges. Serve it with rice.
Simmer the chicken with the onion, cinnamon and baharat for forty minutes. Lift out the meat and strain the broth.
Soak the rice in warm water for twenty minutes and rinse until the water runs clear.
Slice the aubergines into rounds, salt them and leave fifteen minutes, then pat dry and fry until browned.
Fry the cauliflower florets and potato slices until golden and drain them on paper.
Lay the potato on the bottom of the pot, aubergine up the sides, then chicken, cauliflower and rice on top. Do not press it down.
Pour in hot broth to a finger above the rice, bring it up and cook covered on a low heat for forty minutes.
Take it off the heat, rest it ten minutes, cover with a platter and invert in one movement. Scatter with pine nuts.
Knead a dough from the flour, water, a spoon of oil and salt and rest it twenty minutes.
Chop the onion, chillies and curry leaves as fine as you can.
Work the onion, chilli and salt with your hands until the onion releases its juice and softens.
Add the grated coconut and the flaked tuna and keep working it with your fingers until even.
Squeeze in the lime juice and mix again. Taste and adjust for salt and acidity.
Roll the dough into thin flatbreads and cook them on a dry pan a minute a side.
Serve the mas huni with the hot roshi and black tea.
Soak the rice separately and the dal with the fenugreek separately, six hours each.
Grind the dal to a light fluffy paste, then the rice to a slightly grainy one, and combine them.
Salt it, cover it and leave it somewhere warm for eight to twelve hours, until it rises and smells sour.
Pop the mustard seeds in oil, then add the curry leaves, onion, chillies and ginger.
Add the turmeric and the crushed potato, season and warm it five minutes; that is the filling.
Heat a flat pan, wipe it with the oiled onion and pour a ladle of batter, spreading it in a spiral from the centre.
Drizzle oil around the edge and cook until the underside browns, two minutes. Add the filling and fold it over.
Cut the fish along the back without separating the belly, gut it and open it out like a book. Leave the spine in.
Mix the oil, turmeric, tamarind, curry powder, salt and pepper and paint the flesh with it. Leave the skin alone.
Leave the fish half an hour at room temperature; cold, it cooks unevenly.
Light the fire and let it settle to a steady flame. Stand the fish upright, flesh towards the fire, half a metre away.
Cook for an hour, turning as needed. The flesh should whiten and dry at the edges without scorching.
Move the fish skin down onto the coals, lay the onion and tomato over it and give it ten more minutes.
Serve it on the board, with flatbread, lemon and raw onion.
Heat the thick part of the coconut milk without stirring until the oil separates.
Fry the massaman paste in that oil for four minutes, until it darkens and smells right.
Add the beef and turn it in the paste, then add the cinnamon, cardamom and bay.
Add the rest of the coconut milk and stew gently for an hour, until the meat is tender.
Add the potato and onion in large pieces and cook twenty minutes more.
Stir in the tamarind, palm sugar and fish sauce and taste: it should read sweet, sour and salty at once.
Add the peanuts, warm them five minutes and serve with jasmine rice.
Wash the leaves, strip the tough stems and pound them to a paste in a mortar.
Fry the onion and garlic in oil until soft and add the tomatoes.
Stir in the leaves, add water to the same level and cook forty minutes on a low heat.
Add the ground peanuts and cook twenty minutes more, stirring.
Add the prawns, the whole piri-piri and salt and stew ten minutes.
Pour in the coconut milk and warm it five minutes without letting it boil.
Serve with rice or with xima, the maize porridge.
Peel the bananas with oiled hands; their sap stains the skin black.
Pass the banana leaves over a flame for ten seconds so they turn pliable.
Line the bottom of the pot with the leaf ribs; they keep the parcel off the water.
Wrap the bananas in the leaves into a tight parcel and set it on that platform.
Add water two fingers deep, cover and steam for an hour and twenty, topping up with boiling water.
Without unwrapping, press the parcel through the leaves into an even purée and return it to the steam for ten minutes.
Serve with peanut sauce or stewed beef, straight onto the leaf.
Mix the cassava starch with the corn flour and salt in a wide bowl.
Rub the soft fat into the dry mix with your fingers until it looks like damp sand.
Work in the grated cheese, still rubbing the mixture by hand.
Add the milk a spoon at a time, until the crumb just holds when squeezed in your fist.
Heat a dry pan over medium without adding a drop of oil.
Tip in a centimetre of crumb and press it down with a spatula across the whole surface.
Cook it five minutes, flip it with a plate and colour the second side.
Rub the fish steaks with salt and half the curry powder and leave them fifteen minutes.
Fry the fish two minutes a side to a crust and lift it onto a plate.
Soften the onion in the same pan and add the garlic and ginger.
Add the remaining curry powder and warm it a minute, until the aroma lifts.
Add the tomatoes and chilli and reduce them to a thick base without loose liquid.
Pour in the coconut milk with the tamarind and warm it without letting it boil.
Return the fish to the sauce, let it sit five minutes and serve with rice and coriander.
Brown the beef in batches so it does not release its juices, and set it aside.
Fry the onion until soft, stir in the flour and cook it two minutes.
Return the meat, add the stock, Worcestershire sauce and tomato paste and stew forty minutes, until thick.
Cool the filling completely, ideally in the fridge.
Line the tins with shortcrust, trim the edges and fill them with the cold filling.
Cover with rounds of puff pastry, seal the edges and cut a vent in the middle.
Glaze with egg and bake at 200 °C for twenty-five minutes, to a deep golden lid.
Slice the aubergines lengthways half a centimetre thick, salt them and press them under a weight for half an hour.
Pat the slices completely dry; wet ones spit in the oil and never crust.
Fry the aubergine in batches in olive oil, two minutes a side, and drain them on a rack.
Fry the garlic, add the tomatoes and cook the sauce twenty minutes to thicken, salting at the end.
Slice the mozzarella and leave it on paper to drain for ten minutes.
Layer it: sauce, aubergine, mozzarella, parmesan, basil — four times over.
Bake at 190 °C for forty minutes and let it stand twenty before cutting.
Rub the flour with the cold butter, a spoon of sugar and an egg into a dough and chill it half an hour.
Line a tin with the pastry and blind-bake it at 180 °C for fifteen minutes, to a pale gold.
Heat the milk with the cinnamon stick until hot and leave it to infuse ten minutes.
Whisk the remaining eggs with the sugar, flour, cornflour, vanilla and salt until smooth.
Pour in the hot milk in a thin stream, whisking constantly, and return it to the heat.
Cook over medium heat for eight minutes, until the filling thickens to the body of double cream.
Pour the filling into the base, chill it three hours and dust it with ground cinnamon before serving.
Slice the peppers into rings and fry them in the two fats for three or four minutes, until the edges start to darken.
Add the tomatoes, salt them and cook over medium heat for ten minutes. Wait for the oil to separate and glisten at the edges — that is the sign the water has gone.
Lower the heat, break the eggs straight into the sauce and scatter the pepper flakes. Stir slowly and only two or three times, leaving streaks of yolk.
Take it off when the white has set and the yolk is still loose: the pan finishes the job. Scatter over the oregano and the cheese.
Fry the onion and carrot in a spoon of butter until soft, add the tomato paste and give it another minute, until it darkens.
Add the lentils, potato and water, bring to the boil and simmer for twenty-five minutes, until the lentils have collapsed completely.
Blend until entirely smooth. The soup should be thick but still pourable; loosen it with boiling water if it is not.
Melt the rest of the butter, take it off the heat and stir in the mint and paprika. Ladle out the soup, spoon the butter over and serve with a wedge of lemon.
Pound the meat to five millimetres and season it.
Beat the eggs with crushed garlic and chopped parsley; that garlic in the egg wash is the Uruguayan touch.
Dip the pieces in the egg, then press them firmly into the breadcrumbs.
Let the coating set for fifteen minutes in the fridge.
Fry in hot oil three minutes a side, to a golden crust, and drain on a rack.
Lay the milanesas on a tray, spoon on the tomato sauce, cover with ham and cheese and dust with oregano.
Grill for four minutes, until the cheese melts and colours.
Cook the onion dry in a pot for thirty minutes over medium heat, stirring, until it becomes a dark paste.
Pour in the oil, add the garlic and ginger and cook three minutes.
Stir in the berbere and tomato paste and fry five minutes: the mixture darkens and turns fragrant.
Add the lentils, pour in the water and simmer twenty-five minutes, stirring, until the lentils fall apart.
Season at the end, cook it down to a porridge-thick stew and serve with injera or flatbread.
Cover the kombu with cold water and set it over low heat. Bring it to the edge of a boil over about ten minutes and lift the seaweed out before bubbles appear.
Bring the water to the boil, add the bonito flakes, take it off the heat at once and let it stand for two minutes until the flakes sink.
Strain the stock through a sieve without pressing the flakes — pressed flakes turn it bitter.
Soak the wakame in cold water for five minutes; it swells several times over.
Warm the dashi, add the tofu and the wakame and hold it at a low heat for a couple of minutes.
Whisk the miso smooth in a ladle of the hot stock, stir it back in and take the pan off the heat immediately. Scatter over the spring onion.
Poach the fish with the lemongrass and turmeric for fifteen minutes, lift it out and pick the flesh, discarding bones and skin. Strain the broth.
Pound the onion, garlic and ginger to a paste and fry it in oil with the paprika until dark and fragrant.
Mash the fish with a fork and stir it into the paste, frying five minutes; it should break down into threads.
Transfer everything to the pot with the broth, add the fish sauce and simmer twenty minutes.
Slake the rice and chickpea flours in cold water to a thin slurry and pour it into the soup in a stream, stirring.
Cook twenty minutes more, until the broth thickens to the consistency of thin cream.
Boil the noodles, divide them between bowls, ladle the soup over and serve with egg, split peas, coriander and lime.
Simmer the chicken with an onion and garlic for forty minutes. Strain and keep the broth.
Seed the chillies and toast them on a dry pan ten seconds a side, stopping short of blackening.
Cover the chillies with boiling water for twenty minutes to soften.
Fry the almonds, peanuts, sesame, raisins and bread in lard, one at a time and separately.
Char the tomatoes, tomatillos and garlic on a dry pan until blackened in patches.
Blend everything with broth in batches and pass it through a sieve twice.
Cook the sauce for an hour on a low heat, stirring, stir in the chocolate and salt, add the chicken and heat it through.
Simmer the chicken with the onion, cardamom and bay for forty-five minutes and strain the broth.
Chop the molokhia leaves finely with a mezzaluna or blitz them to an even green mass.
Bring the broth to the boil, add the leaves and immediately drop the heat to its lowest.
Hold the soup just below a simmer for ten minutes, stirring; it thickens and turns slippery.
Crush the garlic with salt into a paste and fry it in ghee with the coriander until deep gold.
Pour the tempering into the soup — it will hiss — and cover the pot immediately for a minute.
Serve with boiled rice, the chicken and lemon, each in its own dish.
Knead a dough from the flour, cold water and a pinch of salt for eight minutes and rest it under film for half an hour.
Mix the chopped meat with the onion, ginger, garlic, coriander, timur, a spoon of oil and salt. Do not work it to a paste; pieces should remain.
Char the tomatoes over a flame until blackened, toast the chillies and sesame in a dry pan, and blend everything with salt into a sauce.
Roll eight-centimetre rounds, thinner at the edges. Add a spoon of filling and pleat all the way round, twisting the top shut.
Oil the steamer and cook the momo ten minutes over a fierce steam, keeping them from touching.
Dissolve the yeast and sugar in the warm water and leave it ten minutes, until it foams.
Knead a dough from the flour, yeast mixture, eggs, oil and salt and work it fifteen minutes until elastic.
Let it rise somewhere warm for an hour and twenty, until doubled.
Divide it into twelve, roll each into a rope and join the ends into a ring with a large hole.
Bring a large pot of water to the boil with the honey and lower the rings in three or four at a time.
Boil them a minute a side and roll them in sesame or poppy seed at once.
Bake at 230 °C for twenty minutes, to a deep golden crust, turning them once halfway.
Strip the husks from the cobs whole and rinse them in warm water.
Cut off the kernels and grind them in a blender with the juice they release.
Beat the lard with salt and sugar and work in the corn mass until even.
Simmer the chicken until tender, pull it into threads and keep the broth.
Fry the onion, pepper and tomatoes with the annatto and add the chicken, olives and capers.
Spoon dough onto a husk, add filling, fold it over and tuck the ends under.
Stand the parcels upright in a pot and steam them an hour and a quarter.
Rub the fish with salt, pepper, crushed garlic and lime juice and leave it twenty minutes.
Slice the onion, tomatoes and peppers into rings of the same thickness.
Line the bottom of the clay pot with half the onion, tomato and pepper rings.
Lay the fish in a single layer, the prawns and remaining vegetables over it, and season.
Pour the coconut milk and dendê oil down the side, without dousing the fish from above.
Cover and cook twenty minutes over medium heat, rocking the pot but never stirring.
Scatter with coriander and spring onion and serve straight from the pot, with rice and farofa.
Boil the beans in three litres of water with the bay for an hour, to nearly done. Do not drain: the liquor is the base of the dish.
Fry the onion and pepper in the olive oil for fifteen minutes until soft, adding the garlic, cumin and oregano for a minute.
Measure the bean liquor: two parts liquid to one part rice by volume. Top up with water if there is not enough.
Combine the rice, beans, liquor, half the sofrito and the vinegar, season and bring it to the boil.
Lower the heat, cover and cook twenty minutes without lifting the lid. Let it stand ten minutes and fork the rest of the sofrito through.
Sort the mussels: discard any that are cracked or that will not close when tapped. Pull away the beards and rinse them under the tap.
Melt the butter in a wide pot and sweat the shallot, celery and garlic for five minutes without letting them colour.
Pour in the wine, add the thyme and bay and bring it to the boil.
Tip in the mussels, cover at once and hold them over a fierce flame for five minutes, shaking the pot a couple of times.
Lift the lid: the shells should be open. Throw out any that are not. Scatter parsley, add pepper and serve with chips and the broth in a separate cup.
Salt the aubergine slices and leave them in a colander for half an hour, then pat them dry. Brush with oil and roast at 200 °C for twenty minutes until soft and golden.
Fry the onion until soft, add the mince and cook, breaking up the lumps, until every drop of water has gone and the meat starts to brown. Pour in the wine and let it cook away.
Add the garlic, tomatoes and cinnamon and simmer for twenty minutes. The sauce is right when a spoon drawn across the bottom leaves a track behind it.

Melt the butter, whisk in the flour and cook for a minute. Pour in warm milk in a thin stream, whisking without stopping, and cook to the thickness of soured cream. Off the heat, add nutmeg, the yolks and half the cheese.
Layer it up: potato, aubergine, meat sauce, aubergine again. Pour the béchamel over and scatter the rest of the cheese.
Bake at 180 °C for forty-five minutes until the top is golden. Let it stand for half an hour before cutting: hot moussaka does not slice, it slumps.
Dissolve the yeast with a spoon of sugar in the warm milk and leave it to foam.
Knead a dough from the flour, sponge, eggs, sugar, zest, vanilla, salt and softened butter.
Let it rise somewhere warm for an hour and a quarter, until doubled.
Divide the dough into twelve and roll each into a forty-centimetre rope.
Twist each rope into a figure of eight, joining the ends, and set it on a tray.
Prove them thirty minutes and bake at 180 °C for twenty minutes, until golden.
Brush the hot mucenici with honey and cover them thickly with ground walnuts.
Char the peppers over a flame or under the grill until the skin blackens all over.
Put them in a bowl, cover it with film for fifteen minutes and remove the skin and seeds.
Toast the walnuts in a dry pan for five minutes, until they smell nutty.
Pound the walnuts in a mortar or pulse them briefly to a coarse crumb.
Blitz the peppers with the garlic, pomegranate molasses, lemon, cumin and Aleppo pepper.
Fold in the walnuts and breadcrumbs by hand and season, keeping the mass grainy.
Pour in the olive oil in a thin stream, stirring, and chill it an hour before serving.
Rinse the barley and boil it in salted water for an hour, until soft.
Add the roughly cut potato to the same pot and cook twenty minutes more.
Render the pork belly to crackling, add the onion and fry until golden.
Drain most of the water from the barley and potato, keeping half a cup.
Mash with the butter and milk, leaving the barley grains still visible. Season with salt and pepper.
Serve into bowls and spoon the crackling, onion and rendered fat over the top.
Peel the prawns and keep the shells and heads.
Fry the shells in a spoon of ghee for five minutes, cover with a litre of water and simmer twenty minutes. Strain.
Rinse the rice and soak it twenty minutes.
Fry the onion in ghee until golden, then add the garlic, turmeric and bizar.
Add the tomatoes, the pierced limes and half the dill, pour in the prawn broth and season.
Add the rice, cover and cook fifteen minutes on a low heat without opening it.
Lay the prawns and the rest of the dill on top, cover and give it five minutes. Rest ten and serve.
Mix the yoghurt with half the ginger, garlic and spices, season it and marinate the chicken for at least an hour, better overnight.
Roast the chicken at 220 °C for twenty minutes, or sear it in a screaming-hot pan until it takes dark scorch marks. It can stay slightly underdone inside — the sauce will finish it.
Melt the butter and fry the onion with the rest of the ginger and garlic until golden. Add the tomatoes and the spices and cook for fifteen minutes.
Blend the sauce with the soaked cashews until completely smooth and return it to the pan. It is the cashews, not flour, that give the sauce its body.
Return the chicken to the sauce, pour in the cream and warm it through for five minutes without letting it boil. Crush the kasuri methi between your palms, stir it in and take the pan off.
Strip the tough stems from the leaves, roll them up and shred them fine.
Fry the onion and garlic in oil until soft, five minutes.
Add the chopped tomatoes and cook seven minutes, until they collapse into a paste.
Let the peanut butter down with a cup of hot water until smooth and lump-free.
Stir in the greens and the slackened peanut butter, season and stew covered for twelve minutes.
Uncover and drive off the excess liquid; the sauce should cling to the leaves.
Rub the chicken with salt, pepper, allspice, cardamom and cinnamon and leave it half an hour.
Slice the onions into thin half-moons; a kilo and a half takes about twenty minutes.
Stew the onions in the olive oil over a low heat for forty minutes, until translucent and sweet.
Stir two-thirds of the sumac and salt into the onions and give them five more minutes.
Brown the chicken and roast it at 200 °C for twenty-five minutes.
Toast the pine nuts in a dry pan until golden, watching that they do not scorch.
Lay down the bread, the onions on it, the chicken on top, spoon over the pan oil and scatter with sumac and nuts.
Marinate the pork overnight in sour orange juice, achiote, garlic, salt and pepper.
Soak the rice two hours and drain it.
Slake the masa harina with warm water, add the melted lard, achiote and salt, and work it fifteen minutes until smooth.
Pass the banana leaves over a flame so they turn pliable.
On a leaf place a large spoon of dough, then pork, rice, potato slices, onion, pepper, tomato, an olive and a mint leaf.
Wrap in two leaves into a tight parcel and tie it crosswise with string.
Boil them in a large pot for three hours, topping up with boiling water as it goes.
Pound the shallot, garlic, chilli and terasi to a paste in a mortar. It smells aggressive; that is correct, frying softens it.
Heat the wok and fry the paste in the oil for two minutes, until it darkens and the smell turns deep.
Add the chicken and fry three minutes, then the prawns and cabbage for two more.
Tip in the cold rice, breaking up the lumps with the spatula, pour in the kecap manis and fry over a high flame for three minutes, tossing constantly.
Fry the eggs separately until the edges are lacy and the yolks loose. Serve the rice with an egg on top, slices of cucumber and fried shallots.
Rinse the rice until the water runs clear and cover it with coconut milk let down with water, salt and pandan.
Add slices of ginger and cook covered for fifteen minutes, then let it stand ten.
Soak the dried chillies in boiling water for twenty minutes and blend them with the shallot, garlic and belacan.
Fry the paste in oil for twenty minutes over medium heat, until oil breaks out at the edges.
Add the tamarind, palm sugar and salt and cook the sambal ten minutes more to thicken it.
Fry the anchovies and peanuts separately until crisp and hard-boil the eggs.
Build the plate: a mound of rice, a spoon of sambal, anchovies, peanuts, half an egg and cucumber slices.
Brown the beef, add the onion, garlic and ginger and fry until soft.
Add the tomatoes and curry powder and cook five minutes, until the tomatoes break down.
Add water level with the meat, season and stew thirty minutes, covered.
Peel the bananas under running water and cut them into thick rounds.
Add the bananas to the pot and cook twenty minutes, until tender.
Pour in the coconut milk and warm five minutes without letting it boil. Scatter with coriander.
Boil the leaves in salted water for ten minutes, wring them out and repeat twice more with fresh water.
Boil the peanuts twenty minutes until soft and blend them with water into a thick paste.
Brown the beef, then add the onion, garlic, ginger and chilli.
Add water and the dried shrimp and stew forty minutes, until the meat is tender.
Stir in the peanut paste and cook fifteen minutes, stirring; it catches easily.
Add the drained leaves and the fresh prawns and stew ten minutes more.
Serve with fried plantain or boiled cassava.
Fry the onions in ghee to a deep gold, about twenty minutes. Set half aside for serving.
Add the ginger and garlic, the spices and the chilli, warm them a minute, then the meat and bones, and sear until the raw colour goes.
Cover with water three fingers above, bring to the boil, skim and cook on the lowest heat for four or five hours. The meat should fall apart at a touch.
Whisk the flour into a cup of cold water until smooth and pour it in as a thin stream, stirring constantly. Cook ten minutes: the gravy thickens and turns glossy.
Lift out the bones and set the marrow aside separately. Serve with the fried onion, matchsticks of ginger, coriander, green chilli and lemon — everyone adds their own.
Cut the potatoes into large pieces and soak them ten minutes in cold water to lose the surface starch.
Fry the onion in oil for two minutes, add the thinly sliced beef and cook until it loses its pink.
Add the potato and carrot and turn them so they take on the fat from the meat.
Add the dashi, sake and sugar, bring it up and skim.
Cover with an otoshibuta or a foil disc with a hole in it and simmer ten minutes over medium heat.
Add the soy and mirin and simmer fifteen minutes more, until only a little liquid is left at the bottom.
Add the beans for the last three minutes, take it off the heat and let it stand twenty minutes.
Cut each piece along its length, stopping short of the far edge, and open it like a book.
Beat the opened meat lightly under film and season the inside.
Lay in a slice of prosciutto and a slab of cheese, close it and press the edges together.
Coat in flour, egg and crumbs, then repeat the egg and crumbs a second time.
Chill for twenty minutes; the coating sets and will not slide off in the pan.
Fry over medium heat, six minutes a side, to a deep gold.
Drain on a rack, rest it five minutes and serve with fried potatoes and lemon.
Poach the fish in salted water for ten minutes, lift it out and pick it by hand, removing every bone.
Pound the lemongrass, galangal, turmeric and lime leaves in a mortar into a kroeung paste.
Work the picked fish into the paste in the mortar, keeping the threads distinguishable.
Warm the fish and spice mixture in a pan for five minutes, then add the prahok and the fish broth.
Add the coconut milk and warm it ten minutes without letting it boil.
Shred all the vegetables fine and pile them on a large platter.
Boil the noodles, rinse them in cold water and serve them cold under the warm curry.
Rub the meat with salt, pepper, the juice of two lemons, crushed garlic and oil. Leave it an hour.
Light the coals and let them ash over. The heat is right when you can hold a palm above the grate for five seconds.
Lay the meat on in whole pieces and grill, turning every ten minutes, for an hour and twenty.
Mix the diced tomato, onion, coriander and chilli with lemon juice and salt; that is kachumbari.
For the ugali bring a litre of water to the boil, rain in the flour, stirring constantly with a wooden spoon, and work it fifteen minutes into a firm mass.
Rest the meat ten minutes, cut it small across the grain and serve with ugali, kachumbari and salt.
Pound the onion, garlic and ginger to a paste and fry it in oil with the turmeric and paprika.
Add the chicken in small pieces and fry it until it whitens all over.
Add a litre of water and the fish sauce and simmer twenty minutes.
Slake the chickpea flour in a cup of cold water until completely smooth and lump-free.
Pour the slaked flour into the broth in a thin stream, whisking without stopping.
Cook ten minutes to thicken, add the coconut milk and warm it five minutes without boiling.
Boil the noodles, divide them between bowls, ladle over the broth and serve with egg, lime and chilli.
Rinse the trout, pat them dry and cut two slashes on each side.
Rub the fish with salt, pepper, paprika and olive oil inside and out.
Tuck lemon slices, garlic, parsley and thyme into each cavity.
Slice the potatoes thin and lay them overlapping on an oiled tray.
Set the fish on the potatoes and pour over the wine and the remaining oil.
Bake at 200 °C for twenty-five minutes, until the skin colours.
Test at the spine and serve straight from the tray with a wedge of lemon.
Fry the merguez in olive oil until browned all over and lift them onto a plate.
In the same fat fry the sliced pepper and the garlic until soft.
Stir in the harissa, tomato paste and caraway and cook them two minutes.
Add the chopped tomatoes, season and cook fifteen minutes to thicken.
Return the sausages, cut into pieces, and warm them three minutes.
Drop the heat to its lowest, break in the eggs and stir with a spatula for three minutes into a creamy mass.
Scatter with parsley and serve straight from the pan with baguette.
Mix the flour, grated yam and dashi and rest it half an hour in the fridge: the batter comes together better.
Fold the eggs into the batter, then the cabbage, spring onion and tenkasu. Fold from underneath and briefly: the cabbage must not start weeping.
Mound a quarter of the mixture onto a hot pan in a fifteen-centimetre round and do not flatten it: the air inside is wanted.
Lay slices of pork belly on top and cook five minutes covered over medium heat.
Turn it with two spatulas in one decisive movement and cook five minutes more, this time uncovered.
Brush with okonomi sauce, pipe lines of mayonnaise and drag a cocktail stick across them. Scatter over katsuobushi and aonori.
Cover the shank with cold water, bring it to the boil and skim it thoroughly.
Add the onion, pepper and salt and simmer two hours, until the meat is tender.
Cut the cassava into large pieces, removing the woody core, and add it to the broth.
Twenty minutes later add the corn on the cob and the carrots.
Twenty minutes after that add the potatoes and squash in large pieces.
The plantain goes in last and cooks ten minutes, no longer.
Lift the solids out onto a platter, ladle the broth into cups and serve with rice, coriander and lime.
Slake the starch in half the cold water until completely smooth, with no lumps.
Boil a syrup from the sugar and the remaining water and bring it to a rolling boil.
Pour the starch mixture into the boiling syrup in a thin stream, stirring without stopping.
Steep the saffron in a spoon of hot water and add it to the mass with the cardamom.
Stir over a low heat for an hour and a half, adding the ghee a little at a time.
Work in the honey, rosewater and toasted cashews once the mass starts pulling from the sides.
Spread it in a tin in a three-centimetre layer, level it and cool it six hours.
Mix the tamarind, crushed garlic and ginger, all the spices, oil and salt into a marinade.
Cut the meat into one-and-a-half-centimetre cubes and coat it in the marinade.
Refrigerate for at least four hours, ideally overnight.
Thread the pieces onto skewers packed close, without gaps.
Get the coals hot — you should not be able to hold a palm above the grate for more than three seconds.
Grill a minute and a half on each of four sides, basting with the leftover marinade.
Slide the meat off the skewers into flatbread, add raw onion and serve at once.
Rinse the rice through seven changes of water and soak it an hour in warm salted water.
Render the mutton fat in the cauldron and lift out the cracklings.
Brown the meat hard, add the onion and fry it golden.
Add the carrot and cook ten minutes, leaving it undisturbed for the first five so it heats rather than weeps.
Add boiling water two fingers above, along with the chickpeas, cumin, barberries and salt, and simmer the zirvak forty minutes.
Spread the rice in an even layer, press in the garlic heads and add boiling water a centimetre above the rice.
Cook on a high flame until the water has gone, mound the rice, pierce it to the bottom, cover and hold twenty minutes on the lowest heat.
Tie each piece round its circumference with kitchen string so the meat stays on the bone.
Nick the membrane around the edge in two or three places, or the pieces curl as they brown.
Dust with flour and brown them in butter on both sides, four minutes a side.
Lift out the meat and soften the finely chopped onion, carrot and celery.
Add the wine and reduce it by half, scraping up what has caught on the bottom.
Return the meat, add stock to half the height of the pieces and braise covered for two hours on a low heat.
Mix the chopped zest, garlic and parsley and scatter it over the osso buco before serving.
Boil the beans with half the onion and some garlic until soft, an hour to ninety minutes. Salt at the end.
Simmer the beef whole in salted water for an hour and twenty minutes. Lift it out and cool it enough to handle.
Pull the meat into threads along the grain. Across the grain it shreds into crumbs.
Fry the remaining onion, pepper and garlic, add the tomatoes and cumin, then the meat, and stew twenty minutes with a ladle of the broth.
Cook the rice loose, without butter or spice; here it is the neutral part.
Slice the plantain on the diagonal and fry over medium heat until caramel on both sides.
Build the plate in sectors: rice, beans, meat and plantain side by side, unmixed.
Pound the garlic and chillies to a rough paste in a mortar. A mortar gives a different result from a knife: the juices come out and reach the oil.
Mix the oyster, fish and soy sauces with the sugar in a cup — there will be no time once the pan is hot.
Heat the wok with two spoons of oil, throw in the paste and fry for twenty seconds, to the smell.
Add the pork and leave it alone for a minute, then break it up and fry two minutes more. Pour in the sauce and let it coat the meat.
Off the heat, stir in the basil — the residual heat wilts it in seconds. In the same pan fry the eggs in the rest of the oil until the edges go lacy.
Soak the noodles in warm water for twenty minutes. They should bend but still feel firm when you bite one.
Dissolve the palm sugar in the tamarind and fish sauce, warming them together for a minute. Taste it: sour, salty and sweet should all land equally.
Get the wok hot, fry the tofu until crisp, add the garlic and shallot, then after half a minute the prawns. Cook until pink and push them to the side.
Break the eggs into the cleared space, let them set and break them up with the spatula. Add the drained noodles and pour in the sauce.
Fry, tossing constantly, for two minutes until the noodles drink the sauce and soften. Add the sprouts and chives, toss once and take it off.

Heat the oil in a wide pan and brown the chicken and rabbit on every side. This is not a five-minute job: it takes a good quarter of an hour, and there is no point rushing it — the flavour of the whole dish is laid down here.
Push the meat to the edges, put the green beans in the middle and fry them for a couple of minutes. Add the grated tomato and the paprika and cook until the tomato darkens and stops smelling raw.
Pour in the stock, add the rosemary, saffron and white beans, salt it noticeably harder than feels right and let it boil for ten minutes. This is the last moment you can correct the seasoning.
Scatter the rice in an even layer and level it once with a spoon. After that do not touch the pan again — no stirring, no smoothing.
Cook on a high flame for ten minutes, then drop to medium for another eight, until the stock is gone. The rice should be showing above the surface.
Turn the heat up for half a minute and listen: the moment the sound turns from bubbling to a dry crackle, take it off. That is the socarrat. Cover with a cloth and let it stand for five minutes.
Dissolve the yeast in the warm milk and knead a dough with the flour, yolks, a spoon of ghee and salt.
Let the dough rise an hour somewhere warm and divide it into eight equal balls.
Mix the ground walnuts with half the sugar and the cardamom; that is the filling.
Roll the first ball to the size of the tin, lay it in and brush it generously with ghee.
Alternate layers of dough and nut filling, buttering each, until the dough runs out.
Cut it into diamonds right down to the base, press a walnut half into each and brush with saffron infusion.
Bake at 180 °C for forty-five minutes and pour over a hot syrup of honey and the remaining sugar.
Drop the spinach into boiling water for ninety seconds and move it straight into iced water. Squeeze it out and blend it with the chilli to a purée.
Soak the paneer in hot salted water for ten minutes, then drain it.
Fry the cumin seeds in the ghee until they crackle, add the onion and cook it gold, then the ginger and garlic for a minute.
Add the tomatoes and cook seven minutes, until they break down and the fat starts separating at the edges.
Stir in the spinach purée, garam masala and salt, and warm it for exactly a minute. Add the paneer and cream and take it off the heat.
Bring the milk, water, oil and salt to just below boiling.
Pour all the hot liquid into the starch at once and stir with a spatula. The mixture looks lumpy and odd; that is correct. Let it cool to warm.
Work in the eggs one at a time, then both cheeses. Knead to an even sticky mass — hands are easier than a spoon.
With wet hands roll walnut-sized balls and space them three centimetres apart on a tray.
Bake at 200 °C for twenty minutes until golden. Do not open the door for the first fifteen: the steam escapes and they collapse.
Wring the curd in muslin and push it through a sieve to remove any grain.
Mix the curd with the eggs, sugar, zest, vanilla, bicarbonate and salt.
Work in the semolina and flour a little at a time, until the dough is soft but stops sticking.
Rest the dough twenty minutes; the semolina swells and shaping becomes easier.
Shape six ten-centimetre rings and six balls the size of a walnut.
Fry at 165 °C for three minutes a side, to a golden colour.
Set a ring on a plate, spoon over the soured cream and jam, and crown it with a ball.
Fry the finely chopped onion until translucent, add the mince, cumin, salt and pepper and cook through. Let the pino cool; warm, it will weep.
Blitz the corn with the basil and milk to a coarse but even mass.
Cook it down with the butter over medium heat, stirring, for about fifteen minutes, until a spoon stands up in it.
Divide the pino between earthenware dishes and top each with a piece of chicken, half an egg and a couple of olives with raisins.
Cover with a two-centimetre layer of the corn mass, level it and dust with sugar.
Bake at 200 °C for forty minutes, the last five under the grill, to a dark caramel crust.
Boil the sugar and water to 100 °C and take it off. Separately bring the milk, cream, cinnamon and lemon peel to just below boiling.
Whisk the flour into a little cold milk until smooth and stir it into the hot mixture. Cook, stirring, to the thickness of soured cream.
Pour the hot syrup into the milk base in a thin stream, take it off the heat and stir in the yolks. Strain it and cool completely.
Roll the pastry into a tight log, cut two-centimetre discs and press each into a tin with your thumbs, taking the walls above the rim.
Heat the oven as high as it goes, at least 250 °C. Fill the cases three-quarters full and bake twelve to fifteen minutes, until the tops blister black.
Fry the mince with the onion and annatto, add the finely diced potato and stew until soft.
Season the filling and cool it completely.
Shred the cabbage finely and pickle it in vinegar with salt for half an hour.
Mix the masa with warm water and salt to a pliable dough that does not stick to your hands.
Press a ball of dough between two sheets of film into a thin round.
Put a spoon of filling on one half, fold it over and seal the edge with a fork.
Deep-fry at 180 °C for three minutes a side and serve with the cabbage and sauce.
Braise the chicken with the onion, saffron, ginger, coriander and a little water for an hour, until tender.
Lift out the meat, shred it, and reduce the sauce with the onion to a thick paste.
Beat the eggs into the hot paste and stir over a low heat to coarse curds, then cool it.
Fry the almonds golden, cool them and grind them with half the icing sugar and a spoon of cinnamon.
Line a tin with overlapping sheets of pastry, buttering each, with a generous overhang.
Layer in the egg and onion mass, then the meat, then the almond layer, and sprinkle with orange blossom water.
Fold the edges in, cover with two more sheets, brush with butter and bake at 190 °C for forty minutes. Dust with icing sugar and cinnamon.
Knead a dough from the flour, water and salt, work it ten minutes and rest it half an hour.
Boil the split peas with the onion for forty minutes until completely soft, mash them and season.
Mix the ricotta with the eggs, parsley, salt and pepper.
Roll the dough very thin, spread it with fat, roll it up and chill it twenty minutes.
Cut the roll into pieces and flatten each into a round; the layers give the flakiness.
Add the filling and seal them: ricotta as an open-topped boat, peas as a closed diamond.
Bake at 220 °C for thirty minutes, to a deep gold, and serve hot.
Dice the pork into centimetre cubes, salt it generously and leave it two hours in the cold.
Dissolve the yeast in the warm water and leave it ten minutes, until it foams.
Knead a soft dough from the flour, sponge, oil and salt and work it ten minutes.
Let it rise an hour somewhere warm, until doubled.
Divide the dough into four and stretch each into an oval thirty centimetres long.
Fold the edges in to make a rim and spread the meat with paprika over the whole surface.
Bake at 250 °C for twenty minutes, crack an egg on top and give it five more.
Cut the potato into uneven chunks: broken faces give more crisp surface. Rinse off the starch and dry them thoroughly.
Fry at 140 °C for eight minutes until soft, without letting them colour. Set them aside to cool at least ten minutes.
For the sauce, fry the garlic in olive oil, take the pan off the heat, add the flour and both paprikas and stir. On the flame paprika burns in seconds.
Return it to a low flame, pour in the stock in a thin stream, stirring, and cook five minutes to a sauce. Add the vinegar and salt.
Raise the oil to 190 °C and fry the potato three minutes more, to a deep gold. Salt it at once.
Pile them on a dish and pour the hot sauce over immediately before serving.
Whisk room-temperature egg whites to soft peaks in a scrupulously dry, grease-free bowl.
Add the sugar a spoonful at a time, still whisking, until the meringue is stiff and glossy.
Rub some between your fingers: if you feel sugar grains, keep going, or the shell will weep syrup.
Fold in the cornflour, vinegar and vanilla with a spatula, in three movements at most.
Shape a twenty-two centimetre circle on parchment, raising the edges and leaving a hollow in the middle.
Bake at 120 °C for ninety minutes, then turn the oven off and leave the pavlova inside until completely cold.
Whip the cream, spoon it into the hollow and top with kiwifruit, berries and passionfruit pulp just before serving.
Build a fire of hardwood and let it burn down to substantial embers, about an hour.
Rub the meat with salt, pepper, garlic and rosemary and leave it half an hour.
Spread the potatoes, onion, carrot and tomatoes over the tray in one layer.
Lay the meat over the vegetables, pour on the olive oil and wine and add the bay leaves.
Cover with the bell and bury it in embers completely, until no metal shows.
Cook an hour and a half, then lift the bell, turn the potatoes and baste everything with the juices from the tray.
Replace the bell and embers and give it another hour and twenty. Serve straight from the tray.
Marinate the chicken in the green seasoning, ketchup, salt and pepper for at least an hour.
Heat the oil in a heavy pot and add the sugar, without stirring it with a spoon.
Wait until the sugar darkens almost to black and starts to smoke, and put the chicken in at once.
Fry the chicken, turning it in the caramel, until every piece is dark brown.
Add the onion, carrot, pumpkin and pigeon peas and warm them five minutes.
Add the rinsed rice, pour in the coconut milk and water to a finger above and drop in the whole chilli.
Cover and cook twenty-five minutes on a low heat without opening it. Serve with coleslaw.
Soak the peas twelve hours in cold water, changing it once.
Drain, cover with fresh water two fingers above and boil unsalted for an hour and twenty minutes, until soft.
Dice the pork belly and render it in a dry pan to golden crackling.
Add the chopped onion and fry it in the rendered fat until soft and golden.
Drain the peas, leaving a little liquid in the pot, and season with salt and pepper.
Stir the crackling, onion and fat into the peas and serve hot, with cold kefir in a glass.
Knead a stiff dough from the flour, eggs, iced water and salt and work it fifteen minutes.
Wrap it in film and refrigerate it forty minutes.
Chop the meat by hand or put it through a coarse plate, and mix it with the grated onion, salt and pepper.
Work the crushed ice into the filling and chill it twenty minutes.
Roll the dough a millimetre thick and cut six-centimetre rounds.
Put a teaspoon of filling on each round, fold it into a half-moon, seal it and join the ends into a ring.
Boil them in salted broth with bay for four minutes after they surface, and serve with butter and soured cream.
Simmer the chicken with an onion and salt for forty minutes. Keep the broth.
Toast the pumpkin and sesame seeds in a dry pan to a deep gold, stirring.
In the same pan char the chillies, tomatoes, tomatillos and garlic until blackened in patches.
Blend everything with two ladles of the broth and the cinnamon to a smooth sauce.
Pass the sauce through a sieve; the chilli skins left behind would spoil the texture.
Cook the sauce twenty minutes, stirring, until it thickens and darkens.
Add the chicken, potato and beans and stew fifteen minutes. Serve with rice and coriander.
Wash the basil and dry it completely: any water stops the oil binding to the leaves. Chill the mortar and pestle in the fridge.
Pound the garlic with the coarse salt to a paste. The salt works as an abrasive; without it the garlic just slides around.
Add the pine nuts and work them to a cream, then add the basil a handful at a time. The movement is a pressing circle rather than a pounding: the leaves are crushed against the wall, not smashed.
Work in both cheeses, then trickle the oil in while still grinding. The sauce should come together thick and even.
Cover the bones with cold water, bring to the boil and let them go for ten minutes. Throw the water away, rinse the bones under the tap and wash the pot. This step is what buys you a clear broth.
Halve the onion and ginger and char the cut faces in a dry pan or straight over the flame until they blacken in patches.
Toast the spices in a dry pan until they smell, then tie them in muslin. Return the bones to the clean pot with the brisket, onion, ginger and spices, and cover with water three fingers above.
Simmer for three hours at the barest tremble. Skim for the first half hour. Lift the brisket out after ninety minutes and let it cool.
Strain the broth through a fine sieve and season with fish sauce and sugar. Taste it: it should be slightly saltier than pleasant to drink on its own, because the noodles will take their share.
Cook the noodles and divide them between bowls. Lay the sliced brisket and the raw sirloin on top. Ladle boiling broth over so it covers the meat, and serve the herbs, lime and chilli alongside.
Pour the boiling water with the oil and salt over the flour, work it with a spoon and then, once it cools, by hand for eight minutes. Cover and rest it half an hour.
Fry two of the onions in butter to a deep gold. Half goes into the filling and half is kept for serving.
Mash the warm potato with the curd and the fried onion, and season generously. The filling has to be firm enough to hold its shape.
Roll the dough to two millimetres, cut discs with a glass, add a teaspoon of filling and pinch the edges dry — wet dough will not seal.
Boil in batches in a wide pot of salted water. Lift them out a minute after they float.
Serve with the rest of the fried onion and soured cream. Plenty of people fry the boiled pierogi in butter afterwards, which is equally correct.
Grate the pineapple and winter melon coarsely and press out the juice through muslin.
Reduce the pressed juice separately by half; it goes back into the filling as a concentrate.
Cook the pulp with the sugar and maltose on a low heat for an hour, stirring every five minutes.
Add the reduced juice and cook the filling until a spatula leaves a trail on the pan.
Beat the butter with the icing sugar, yolks, milk powder, cheese and salt, and work in the flour and cornflour.
Chill the dough half an hour, divide it into balls and flatten each in your palm.
Wrap a ball of filling in the dough, press it into a square mould and bake at 170 °C for twenty-five minutes, turning it halfway.
Cut the potatoes into thick batons and soak them in cold water for twenty minutes.
Dry the potatoes and fry them twice: at 150 °C until soft, then at 190 °C until crisp.
Sear the diced beef over a high flame in batches for two minutes each and set it aside.
Fry the sliced sausages until browned and add the onion and pepper for five minutes.
Return the meat to the pan, add the tomatoes and mustard and warm it three minutes.
Fry the eggs with runny yolks and cut the locoto into thin rings.
Pile the chips on a platter, top with the meat and vegetables, the eggs and the locoto rings, and drizzle with mayonnaise and ketchup.
Dissolve the yeast in the water, add the flour and mix to a rough dough. Rest it twenty minutes, then work in the salt and knead ten minutes to a smooth ball.
Leave it two hours at room temperature, divide it into four balls and refrigerate for a day.
Take the dough out three hours before baking. Crush the tomatoes by hand with a pinch of salt: the sauce is done.
Heat the oven with a stone or steel at full power for at least an hour. It takes longer than seems necessary and it is not optional.
Stretch a ball with your fingers from the centre outwards, leaving the rim untouched. No rolling pin: it drives the air out of the rim and the crust will not rise.
Spread a thin layer of sauce, lay on the mozzarella and trickle over the oil. Bake seven to nine minutes, until the rim is spotted, and add the basil to the finished pizza.
Knead a soft dough from the flour, warm water, a spoon of oil and salt, and work it ten minutes.
Divide it into six balls, oil them generously and leave them under film for forty minutes.
Mash the cheese with the egg and dill. Grate the pumpkin and mix it with sugar for the second filling.
Stretch a ball by hand on an oiled table into a thin round, until it turns translucent.
Put the filling in the middle and fold the edges to the centre, into a parcel or a round.
Flatten it with your palm to a centimetre and a half.
Cook in a hot dry pan four minutes a side, to a mottled crust.
Boil the potatoes in their skins until tender, peel them and cut them into large pieces.
Poach the cod in salted water for eight minutes, lift it out and flake it by hand, removing bones and skin.
Fry the onion in butter until soft, stir in the flour and cook it two minutes, stirring.
Pour in the milk in a thin stream, whisking continuously, and bring the sauce to the thickness of cream.
Stir in the mustard, salt and pepper, add the fish and potato and warm everything through for five minutes.
Mash with a fork to a coarse, uneven texture in which the pieces are still recognisable, and scatter with chives.
Rinse the rice until the water runs clear and cover it with warm salted water for as long as the zirvak takes.
Render the tail fat in the pot until only crackling is left and lift it out. Brown the meat hard over a high flame.
Add the onion and fry it gold, then the carrot — and leave it alone for five minutes so it sets. Then stir and fry ten minutes more.
Pour in boiling water to the level of the contents, add the chickpeas, cumin, barberries, chilli and the whole garlic bulbs. Simmer for forty minutes: this is the zirvak.
Salt the zirvak noticeably harder than seems right: the rice takes it. Spread the rice over in an even layer with a slotted spoon, without stirring, and pour boiling water two fingers above it.
Cook uncovered over a high flame until the water drops below the rice. Gather the rice into a mound, pierce it to the base in several places, cover and give it twenty minutes on the lowest heat.
Dissolve the yeast and sugar in half the warm milk and let it foam for ten minutes.
Mix both flours with the salt, pour in the yeast liquid, the egg and the rest of the milk, and whisk smooth.
Cover and leave it an hour in the warm. The batter turns bubbly and roughly doubles.
Heat a poffertjes pan or an ordinary one, butter it and spoon batter into the hollows without stirring what is left in the bowl.
After a minute, when the edges set, turn them with a fork and give them forty seconds more.
Serve them hot with a knob of butter on top and a generous dusting of icing sugar.
Pound the chilli flakes with the salt and the Maldive fish to a rough paste.
Add the onion and keep pounding: it should give up its juice and stain the paste.
Work the coconut in by hand, rubbing the mixture between your palms until it turns evenly red.
Add the lime juice, mix and taste. The sambol should be hot, sour and salty at once.
Wash the chicken with lime juice, rub it with oregano, garlic, salt and pepper and leave it an hour.
Melt the sugar in the oil over medium heat to a dark amber, without stirring with a spoon.
Put the chicken pieces into the caramel and brown them on all sides.
Add the onion, pepper and tomato paste and cook five minutes, stirring.
Add a cup of water, cover and stew twenty-five minutes on a low heat.
Add the potato in large pieces and stew twenty minutes more, until tender.
Stir in the olives and coriander, reduce the sauce to a coating consistency and serve with white rice.
Take the reindeer from the freezer and shave it into thin curls with a sharp knife.
Melt the butter in a cast-iron pan and heat it until it just smokes.
Add the frozen shavings and fry them hard until all the water has gone.
Add the chopped onion and fry five minutes more, to a good colour.
Add the beer and water, season, and stew covered for half an hour.
Boil the potatoes and mash them with hot milk to a smooth purée.
Serve the meat on the mash with a spoon of lingonberry and pickled cucumbers.
Dissolve the yeast in the warm milk with a spoon of sugar and leave it ten minutes, until it foams.
Knead a dough from the flour, the yeast mixture, yolks, sugar, softened butter, zest and salt. Work it fifteen minutes.
Leave it somewhere warm for an hour and twenty, until it has doubled.
Warm the cream with the honey, pour it over the ground walnuts, add the rum and cinnamon and cool it to lukewarm.
Roll the dough into a rectangle three millimetres thick and spread the filling, leaving two centimetres clear at the edges.
Roll it up tightly from the long side, lay it in a ring tin seam down and let it prove forty minutes.
Prick the roll in several places with a skewer and bake at 170 °C for an hour, to a deep gold.
Marinate the chicken in crushed garlic, ginger, thyme, salt and pepper for half an hour.
Fry the chicken in oil until browned all over and lift it out.
Cut the plantain into large pieces and fry it in the same oil, to caramelised edges.
Pour off most of the oil and fry the onion, tomatoes and pepper until soft.
Return the chicken, add the carrot, beans and the whole scotch bonnet, pour in a cup of water and stew twenty minutes.
Remove the chilli, fold in the plantain and warm it three minutes. Serve at once.
Rub the chicken with salt, pepper, garlic and lemon juice and leave it twenty minutes.
Brown the chicken in oil on all sides and lift it out.
Fry the onion with the ginger until soft, add the palm pulp and let it down with a cup of water.
Cook the sauce twenty minutes, stirring, until a layer of red oil rises to the surface.
Return the chicken, add the aubergine and the whole pili-piri and stew thirty minutes.
Stir in the spinach for the last five minutes and remove the chilli.
Serve with rice or with fufu made from cassava.
Cut the potatoes into one-centimetre batons and soak them twenty minutes in cold water to lose the surface starch.
Dry the batons thoroughly. Wet potato spits in the fryer and never crusts.
Melt the butter, stir in the flour and cook the roux to a nutty brown, four minutes.
Add both stocks, the Worcestershire sauce and the vinegar and simmer the gravy fifteen minutes, until thick.
Fry the potatoes at 150 °C for six minutes, until soft, and drain them on a rack.
Bring the oil to 190 °C and fry them a second time for three minutes, to a crisp shell. Salt them.
Pile the chips into a bowl, scatter the curds over them and pour on the boiling gravy. Serve at once.
Cover the pork with water, add half the onion, three cloves of garlic and the bay, and simmer two hours, skimming.
Seed the chillies, toast them in a dry pan twenty seconds a side and cover them with boiling water for twenty minutes.
Blend the chillies with the remaining onion, garlic and a cup of the broth, and pass the result through a sieve without fail.
Fry the strained sauce in a spoon of fat for five minutes: it darkens and thickens. Pour it into the pot with the meat.
Add the rinsed hominy and the oregano and cook another forty minutes. Pull the meat into shreds and return it.
Serve with bowls of sliced radish, cabbage, onion, lime wedges, oregano and tostadas. Everyone builds their own bowl.
Dissolve the yeast and sugar in the warm water and leave it ten minutes, until it foams.
Whisk in the flour, nutmeg and salt to a smooth loose batter without lumps.
Cover it and leave it somewhere warm for an hour; it should double and bubble all over.
Heat the oil to 170 °C and test with a drop of batter; it should surface within two seconds.
Take batter in your palm and squeeze a ball out between thumb and forefinger straight into the oil.
Fry three minutes, turning them with a slotted spoon, to an even golden brown.
Drain them on paper and serve warm, dusted with icing sugar.
Mix the paprika, sugar, mustard and garlic powders, cayenne, salt and black pepper.
Smear the shoulder with mustard as a binder and coat it all over in the dry rub.
Leave the meat in the fridge overnight, covered with film.
Bring the smoker or oven to 110 °C and take the meat out an hour ahead so it warms up.
Smoke it fat side up for six hours, spritzing with the vinegar and apple juice mix every hour.
When the internal temperature reaches 75 °C and stalls, wrap the meat in foil and return it to the heat.
Hold it to 95 °C inside, about four hours more, rest it an hour still wrapped, and pull it apart by hand.
Bring a large pot of water to the boil with the onion and bay. Do not salt it.
Hold the octopus by the head and dip the tentacles into the boiling water for five seconds, then lift it out. Repeat three times.
Lower the octopus in whole and cook at a bare simmer for forty minutes.
Test with a fork at the thickest part of a tentacle: it should go in without resistance.
Turn off the heat and leave the octopus in the water for fifteen minutes; it finishes and softens further.
Boil the potatoes in the same water and cut them into rounds.
Cut the tentacles with scissors into centimetre pieces, lay them over the potato, dust with paprika and salt and pour over the oil.
Dry the fish, cut two slashes on each side and rub it with salt and wine.
Lay a few spring onion stalks on a plate and set the fish on them, so steam reaches it from below too.
Tuck half the ginger into the slashes and the cavity.
Set the plate into a boiling steamer and cook eight minutes for every centimetre of thickness.
Pour off all the liquid from the plate and discard it; it is bitter.
Scatter the remaining ginger, shredded spring onion and coriander over the top.
Heat the oil until it smokes and pour it over the aromatics, then pour the soy and sugar around the edge of the plate.
Cut the cold butter into the flour with a pinch of salt to a crumb, add the egg and iced water and bring the dough together without kneading. Chill it an hour.
Roll the pastry out, line the tin, prick it and chill it again for twenty minutes: that is what stops it shrinking.
Line it with paper and weights and blind-bake at 190 °C for fifteen minutes, then remove the weights and give it five minutes more, to a dry base.
Render the bacon until browned and drain it on paper: spare fat splits the custard.
Whisk the eggs with the cream and milk without foaming, and season with nutmeg and pepper. It barely needs salt: the bacon is salty.
Scatter the bacon over the base, pour the custard in and bake at 170 °C for thirty-five minutes. The centre should still wobble slightly when it comes out.
Fry the aubergine over high heat in two spoons of oil until the edges brown, then set it aside. Aubergine drinks oil instantly — do not add more, it gives it back later.
In the same pan, fry the courgette until golden, about four minutes, and add it to the aubergine. It should stay firm.
Fry the pepper until soft with a few charred spots and set it aside as well.
In the remaining oil, sweat the onion until soft, add the garlic and thyme and give it half a minute, until fragrant.
Add the tomatoes and cook them down over medium heat into a thick sauce, about twenty minutes. It should hold on a spoon rather than run off it.
Return the vegetables to the pan, season and warm them through together for ten minutes over low heat. Take it off, add the basil and let it stand — ratatouille is better warm than hot.
Brown the pork in large pieces on all sides.
Add the onion, garlic and ginger and fry until soft.
Stir in the cassava leaves, add water to the same level and season.
Stew covered for an hour on a low heat, stirring every fifteen minutes.
Uncover and drive off the excess liquid; the dish should be thick rather than soupy.
Add the coconut milk and warm it five minutes without boiling. Serve with rice.
Knead a stiff dough from the flour, water, a spoon of oil and salt and work it fifteen minutes.
Roll the dough into a thin sheet and cut it into two-millimetre noodles.
Spread the noodles on a cloth, dust them with flour and dry them twenty minutes.
Simmer the chicken with the onion, chickpeas, cinnamon and white pepper in two litres of water for forty minutes.
Add the turnip in wedges and cook twenty minutes more, until tender.
Steam the noodles over the broth fifteen minutes, take them off, sprinkle with oil and toss them.
Repeat the steaming twice more, mound the noodles, top with the chicken and turnip and ladle broth over.
Boil the plantains in their skins for twenty minutes, until completely soft.
Peel them hot and mash them into a smooth purée with a pinch of salt and the flour.
Chill the purée for half an hour; warm, it will not hold as balls.
Mash the cooked beans and reduce them with the sugar, cinnamon and cloves to a thick paste.
Stir the chocolate into the hot bean paste and cool it completely.
Flatten a piece of purée on your palm, add the bean filling and seal it into a firm ball.
Fry at 170 °C for three minutes, to a browned crust, and serve with icing sugar and soured cream.
Soak the dried chillies in boiling water for fifteen minutes, then blend them with the shallot, garlic, galangal, ginger and turmeric to a smooth paste.
Toast the coconut in a dry pan until deep brown and pound it to an oily paste — this is kerisik, and it brings the nutty depth.
Fry the paste in a wide pot for five minutes, add the meat, coconut milk, bruised lemongrass and lime leaves, and bring it to the boil.
Simmer uncovered for two and a half hours, stirring every twenty minutes. The sauce gradually thickens and darkens.
Stir in the kerisik and carry on over medium heat for another hour, stirring more and more often. The milk splits, the oil separates and the meat begins to fry.
It is done when the meat is dark brown and nearly dry and the oil runs clear. Season and let it rest.
Boil the soaked beans in a litre and a half of water for an hour, until soft.
Add the coconut milk, garlic, spring onion, thyme and allspice and bring it to the boil.
Rinse the rice until the water runs clear, add it to the pot and level it with a spoon.
Lay the whole scotch bonnet on top, season, and check that the liquid covers the rice by a finger.
Cover and cook twenty minutes on a low heat, without lifting the lid once.
Take it off the heat and let it stand covered for ten minutes.
Remove the chilli and the thyme sprigs, fluff the rice with a fork and serve.
Beat the beef to five millimetres, season it and spread with mustard. Lay the bacon, strips of onion and a gherkin along the short edge.
Roll them up, tucking the sides in, and secure with a skewer or string. Firm but not tight — the filling expands.
Brown the rolls hard on every side and lift them out. In the same fat fry the remaining onion and the carrot, add the tomato paste and give it a minute.
Pour in the wine, let it reduce by half, add the stock and bay. Return the rolls, cover and braise over a low flame for an hour and a half.
Lift the rolls out and remove the skewers. Blend the gravy in the pot or crush it with a masher, then reduce it to the thickness you want.
Rinse the rice, cover it with the milk, vanilla and salt and cook an hour on the lowest heat, stirring.
Cool the rice completely; stand the bowl in cold water and stir so no skin forms.
Scald the almonds, slip off the skins and chop them coarsely, keeping one whole.
Stir the chopped almonds, sugar and sherry into the cold rice.
Whip the cream to soft peaks and fold it in with a spatula in three additions, without knocking it down.
Hide the whole almond in the mixture and chill the pudding at least three hours.
Cook the cherries with sugar for ten minutes, thicken with slaked cornflour and serve the sauce hot.
Steep the saffron in a ladle of hot stock and set it aside. Keep the rest of the stock at a bare simmer — cold stock stops the cooking.
Melt half the butter and sweat the onion over low heat until soft and translucent without letting it colour, about eight minutes.
Add the rice and stir for a couple of minutes until the grains are translucent at the edges and milky in the centre. This is the tostatura, and it keeps the grains intact.
Pour in the wine and let it evaporate completely — the smell of alcohol has to go.
Add the stock a ladle at a time, stirring, waiting until the rice has nearly absorbed it before the next. Around eighteen minutes, until the grain is soft outside with a slight bite in the middle.
Stir in the saffron infusion, take the pan off the heat and beat in the cold butter and parmesan, shaking the pan hard. The risotto should spread slowly across the plate.
Whisk the flour, eggs, milk and salt into a smooth batter and rest it an hour in the fridge.
Take the beef out of the fridge an hour before cooking, pat it dry and season it.
Sear the joint in a pan on all sides to a dark crust, two minutes a face.
Set it on the vegetables in a tray and roast at 200 °C for twenty minutes, then at 160 °C for forty more for a pink centre.
Lift the beef out, cover it with foil and rest it twenty minutes; it goes on cooking.
Heat the pudding tins with a spoon of dripping in each at 220 °C until the fat smokes.
Pour the cold batter halfway up the tins and bake twenty minutes without opening the door.
Boil the potatoes in their skins for twenty minutes, to the point where a knife meets resistance. Cool them completely and leave them overnight in the fridge.
Peel them and grate them coarsely straight into a bowl. Do not rinse and do not squeeze.
Season, and if you are using them, fold in the fried bacon and onion and the cheese.
Heat half the butter in a pan, spread the mixture in an even layer and press it once with the spatula.
Fry over medium heat for twelve minutes without touching it. Shake the pan now and then: the rösti should slide as one piece.
Cover with a plate, invert it, add the rest of the butter and fry the second side for ten minutes.
Warm the cardamom, cinnamon and cloves in the ghee until fragrant, one minute.
Add the asafoetida and the meat straight after, and brown it for ten minutes.
Take the pan off the heat and stir in the Kashmiri chilli; over a flame it burns in seconds and turns bitter.
Return it to a low heat and add the whisked yoghurt a ladle at a time, stirring between each.
Add the fennel and dry ginger, season, and pour in a cup of hot water.
Braise covered for an hour and twenty on a low heat, until the meat comes away from the bone.
Uncover and reduce the sauce until oil rises to the surface. Serve with rice.
Knead a soft dough from the flour, warm water, a spoon of oil and salt and rest it twenty minutes.
Roll a ball thin, brush it with oil, roll it into a rope, coil it like a snail and roll it out again.
Cook the chapatis over medium heat, a minute and a half a side, and keep them under a cloth.
Shred the cabbage, carrot, onion, tomatoes and chilli as fine as you can.
Beat the eggs with the vegetables, salt and pepper; the vegetables belong inside the omelette, not on top.
Pour a portion of egg into the pan, let it set and lay a chapati on top, pressing it down.
Flip the two together, slide them onto a board omelette up and roll it tight.
Fry the onion, garlic and ginger in oil until soft, five minutes.
Add both meats and the tomatoes and warm them through, without browning.
Add a litre and a half of water, season and simmer an hour.
Wash the greens and chop them coarsely, discarding tough stems.
Add the mustard greens and spinach and cook ten minutes.
Add the mafana for the last five minutes; long cooking weakens its effect.
Serve in deep bowls with a large helping of boiled rice.
Boil the beef whole in salted water with an onion for an hour and a half, until it pulls apart. Keep the broth.
Cool it and pull it apart along the grain into thin strands by hand.
Sweat the onion and peppers in the olive oil for twenty minutes to complete softness, then add the garlic, cumin and oregano for a minute.
Pour in the wine, reduce it by half, add the tomatoes and a cup of the broth. Simmer ten minutes.
Return the meat, add the olives and capers and cook another twenty minutes over a low flame. Serve with rice and fried plantain.
Simmer the beef whole in salted water with bay for an hour and a half. Keep the broth.
Cool the meat and pull it into long strands along the grain.
Fry the onion, pepper and garlic in oil until soft, eight minutes.
Add the tomatoes, tomato paste, cumin and oregano and cook ten minutes to thicken.
Fold in the meat, olives and capers and stew twenty minutes, adding broth a spoonful at a time.
Drive off any excess liquid uncovered; the sauce should coat the strands.
Scatter with culantro and serve with rice and fried plantain.
Knead a dough from the flour, water, egg, condensed milk and salt for fifteen minutes, until it is very elastic and smooth.
Divide into balls, coat each in oil and set them in a bowl covered with more oil. Leave them at least four hours.
On an oiled surface flatten a ball and stretch it from the centre, slapping it with your palms until the sheet turns translucent.
Brush the sheet with ghee, fold the edges to the middle and coil it into a tight spiral. Let it sit ten minutes.
Flatten the spiral into a round and fry it on medium heat, two minutes a side in ghee, until it takes golden spots.
Straight from the pan, crumple the bread between your palms from both sides and the layers open. Serve with dhal or curry.
Mix both flours with the sugar, baking powder, bicarbonate and salt in a large bowl.
Warm the milk with the syrup until the syrup dissolves.
Pour the liquid into the dry ingredients and stir with a spoon to an even thick batter.
Grease a tin, pour in the batter and fill it two-thirds full.
Seal the tin with two layers of foil and tie it with string so no steam escapes.
Stand the tin in a deep tray of water and bake at 100 °C for twelve hours.
Cool it completely in the tin and rest it a day before cutting. Serve with butter.
Mix the starter with half the water and half the flour and leave it overnight at room temperature.
In the morning take two hundred grams of the sponge back into a jar; that is the starter for next time.
Stir in the remaining flour, water, salt, malt and caraway with a wooden spoon until even.
Cover it and let it rise three hours; the dough roughly doubles and cracks appear on the surface.
Turn the dough into greased tins with wet hands, smoothing the top with a wet spoon.
Let it prove an hour and prick the top in several places with a fork.
Bake at 250 °C for fifteen minutes, then at 180 °C for forty-five more, and rest it a day before cutting.
Crumb the stale bread in a blender or by hand to a coarse crumb.
Mix the crumbs with the sugar and cinnamon and dry them in the oven at 160 °C for twelve minutes, stirring twice.
Cool the crumbs completely. On warm crumbs the cream collapses and the layers merge.
Whip the cold cream with the vanilla sugar to firm peaks.
Layer into glasses: crumbs, jam, cream, and repeat. Finish with cream.
Chill for at least four hours, ideally overnight. Serve with cranberries on top.
Cook the eggs at the barest simmer for an hour, then cool them in cold water and peel them.
Slice the aubergines a centimetre thick, salt them and press them under a weight for half an hour.
Pat the slices dry and fry them in oil to a deep gold on both sides.
Whisk the tahini with lemon juice, water and salt to the thickness of pouring cream.
Dice the tomatoes and cucumbers small and mix them with the parsley, lemon and salt.
Warm the pitas, cut them into pockets and spread tahini inside.
Layer in the aubergine, sliced egg and salad, and spoon over the amba, tahini and zhug.
Melt the sponge chocolate over a water bath and cool it to lukewarm.
Beat the butter with the icing sugar and vanilla until pale, add the yolks one by one, then the chocolate.
Whip the whites with the sugar to firm peaks and fold them in with a spatula, alternating with the sifted flour.
Bake at 170 °C for forty-five minutes, the first fifteen with the oven door propped open.
Cool it completely, split the sponge in two and spread the warmed sieved jam between the layers and over the sides.
Cook a syrup of sugar and water to 108 °C, take it off the heat and stir in the chocolate until smooth.
Cool the glaze to the body of cream, pour it onto the centre and spread it by tilting the cake. Let it set two hours.
Brown the meat, add the onion and garlic and fry until soft.
Add the tomatoes, cover with water to the same level, season and stew for an hour and twenty.
Shred the greens fine and stew them with tomato and peanut butter for fifteen minutes.
Slake a quarter of the maize meal in cold water and stir it into a litre of boiling water.
Cook that thin porridge for ten minutes, stirring with a wooden paddle.
Rain in the rest of the meal a little at a time, working it hard for fifteen minutes to a stiff mass.
Turn the sadza onto plates with a wet spoon and serve with the meat and greens.
Separate the whites from the yolks and whip the whites with half the sugar to firm peaks.
Beat the softened butter with the remaining sugar until pale, about eight minutes.
Add the yolks one at a time, still beating, then work in the soured cream, vanilla and zest.
Sift the flour with the starch and salt and fold it in with a spatula in three additions.
Fold in the whipped whites gently so the mixture does not collapse; the batter has to stay airy.
Heat the oven to 190 °C and pour the first thin layer onto a greased spit or into a tin.
Bake each layer three minutes to a golden colour and pour the next, until the batter runs out.
Dice the aubergines, salt them and leave them twenty minutes to draw out the bitterness.
Pat the cubes dry with paper; wet ones spit in the oil.
Fry the aubergine in batches to a dark brown crust and drain it on paper.
Pound the garlic with salt into a paste in a mortar.
Let the peanut butter down with lemon juice, the garlic and water to the body of soured cream.
Chop the tomatoes, onion and chilli fine and mix them with the cooled aubergine.
Pour over the peanut dressing, toss it and let it stand fifteen minutes.
Rinse the fat, dry it thoroughly and cut it into slabs ten centimetres wide.
Cut deep slits every two centimetres in each slab, stopping short of the skin.
Push a slice of garlic and a peppercorn into each slit.
Crush the remaining peppercorns and coriander and mix them with the salt and crumbled bay.
Roll the slabs in the mixture on all sides, pressing it into the slits.
Pack them into an enamelled dish skin down, cover and refrigerate for a week.
Scrape off the excess salt, roll the slabs in paprika and keep them in the freezer. Slice them thin and serve with rye bread.
Drain the soaked fenugreek, rinse it several times and grind it to a paste.
Whip the paste with cold water for ten minutes, by whisk or mixer, until it turns into a white froth.
Fry the onion and garlic, add the meat and brown it.
Add the tomatoes and potato, cover with water, season and stew an hour, until the meat is tender.
Heat a stone or cast-iron pot until very hot and transfer the boiling stew into it.
Break the eggs into the boiling stew and stir; they set into threads.
Spoon the hulba and a spoon of zhug on top and carry it to the table still bubbling. Serve with bread and rice.
