Fry the onion with the ají and cumin, add the beef and cook through. Pour in the stock and simmer ten minutes.
Dissolve the gelatine in a couple of spoons of hot water and stir it into the stew with the potato and peas.
Cool the filling and refrigerate it for at least four hours; it has to set to a firm jelly.
Knead a dough from the flour, softened butter, sugar, achiote, salt and warm water. Rest it half an hour.
Roll fifteen-centimetre rounds. On each go a spoon of the cold jelly, a wedge of egg and an olive.
Seal the seam in a plait along the top and stand the pastries seam-up. Any gap means the broth escapes.
Bake at 220 °C for twenty-five minutes. The high heat is what sets the pastry before the jelly melts.
Boil the beetroot until tender, cool it completely and grate it coarsely.
Cut the cucumbers into matchsticks and chop the dill and spring onion.
Mix the beetroot, cucumber and herbs with the soured cream and salt it now, before the kefir, so the salt disperses.
Pour in the cold kefir and stir. The soup turns an even pink.
Chill it for an hour. Warm šaltibarščiai makes no sense.
Boil the potatoes and serve them hot on a separate plate. Put halved eggs into the soup.
Soak the glutinous rice in cold water for two hours and drain it.
Rinse the birds, trim the excess fat at the cavity and pat them dry.
Fill each cavity two-thirds with rice, adding a ginseng root, garlic, a chestnut and a jujube.
Cross the legs and tuck one through a slit in the other; the cavity then closes without string.
Pack the birds into a pot and add cold water just to cover them.
Bring it up, skim, and simmer for an hour and a quarter.
Serve each bird in its own bowl of broth, with salt and pepper on a separate saucer.
Toast the rice in a dry pan to a deep gold and grind it to a fine powder.
Pound the lemongrass, galangal, turmeric and garlic into a kroeung paste.
Fry the paste in oil for five minutes, add the prahok and cook two minutes more.
Add the pork and brown it, then pour in a litre and a half of water.
Cook twenty minutes, then add the pumpkin, papaya and aubergine.
Add the rice powder, first stirred into a ladle of the broth, and cook ten minutes.
Add the beans and moringa leaves for the last five minutes and adjust with fish sauce and palm sugar.
Rub the ghee into the flour with the ajwain and salt until it looks like damp sand: squeezed in a fist it should hold its shape.
Add cold water a little at a time to a firm, tight dough — stiffer than a dumpling dough. Cover it and rest it half an hour.
Fry the cumin in a spoon of oil, add the chilli, spices, peas and coarsely crushed potato. Warm it five minutes and cool it.
Divide the dough into balls, roll each into an oval and cut it in half. Form a cone from each half, wetting the straight edge.
Fill the cone, pinch the top firmly shut and set it seam up. A weak seam opens in the oil.
Lower them into oil at 150 °C and fry twelve to fifteen minutes, raising it to 180 °C at the end. The pastry should carry fine blisters rather than large ones.
Knead a dough from the flour, warm water and salt for ten minutes and rest it under film for half an hour.
Roll the dough into a thin sheet, brush it with the melted fat, roll it into a tight log and chill it for half an hour.
Mix the chopped meat with the onion, cumin and pepper. Salt it immediately before shaping, not before that.
Cut the log into two-centimetre discs, set each cut side up and roll it into a round: the layers stay visible.
Add the filling and seal into a triangle, pressing the seams firmly. Set them seam down, glaze with egg and scatter with sesame.
Bake at 220 °C for ten minutes, then drop to 190 °C for twenty-five more, to a deep gold.
Fry the finely chopped onion, spring onion, tomato and garlic with the cumin and achiote down to a paste.
Put the chicken in the pot, add half the hogao and cover with four litres of water.
Bring it up, skim and simmer forty minutes.
Add the corn in halved cobs and the cassava in large pieces and cook twenty minutes.
Add the plantain and potato and cook twenty-five minutes more.
Mash a couple of pieces of cassava in the pot to thicken the soup and stir in the remaining hogao.
Scatter with coriander and serve with white rice and avocado on separate plates.
Marinate all the meats in lime juice, crushed garlic, oregano, salt and pepper for an hour.
Brown the meats in batches in a large pot.
Add the onion and pepper, cover with three litres of water and simmer an hour.
Add the cassava and yautía in large pieces and cook twenty minutes.
Add the sweet potato, plantain and corn and cook twenty minutes more.
Mash a couple of pieces of cassava in the pot so the soup thickens.
Stir in the coriander, check the salt and serve with white rice and avocado.
Rub the chicken with salt, garlic, oregano and lime juice and leave it twenty minutes.
Cover the chicken with three litres of cold water, bring it up and skim.
Add the onion and half the culantro and simmer an hour.
Peel the ñame, cut it into large pieces and add it to the pot with the corn.
Cook twenty-five minutes, until the ñame is soft.
Mash a couple of pieces of ñame in the broth so the soup thickens.
Stir in the remaining culantro, season and serve with a separate plate of white rice.
Rinse the sardines without gutting them and pat them dry on the outside.
Bury the fish in coarse salt on all sides and leave it half an hour at room temperature.
Light the coals and let them ash over; an open flame burns the skin within a minute.
Char the peppers on the coals, peel them and dress them with oil, garlic and vinegar.
Shake the excess salt off the fish and lay them on a hot, oiled grate.
Grill four minutes a side, turning them exactly once.
Lay the sardines on slices of bread and serve with boiled potatoes and the pepper salad.
Take the cabbage apart into leaves, rinse off the excess brine and pare down the thick ribs.
Fry the chopped onion in oil until soft and let it cool.
Mix both minces with the raw rice, the onion, a spoon of paprika, salt and pepper.
Roll the filling in the leaves into tight parcels, tucking the ends in.
Line the bottom of the pot with shredded cabbage trimmings and half the ribs.
Pack the sarma in layers with ribs and pork fat between them, and add water level with the top layer.
Stew two and a half hours on a low heat, adding a roux of flour, paprika and tomato paste at the end.
Take the cabbage apart into leaves and pare down the thick ribs. Rinse leaves that are too sour; soak overly salty ones for twenty minutes.
Fry the finely chopped onion in the oil until soft, add the tomato paste and cook two minutes. Cool it completely.
Mix the pork with the rice, the cooled onion, savory, salt and pepper.
Put a tablespoon of filling on each leaf, roll it up and tuck the ends in with a finger. The rolls should come out small, about two fingers wide.
Line the pot with shredded cabbage and the ribs, pack the rolls in tight layers with bay between them, and cover with the remaining cabbage and leaves.
Add water to the level of the top layer and cook three hours on the lowest heat or at 150 °C in the oven.
Take the head apart into leaves and pare down the thick rib at the base of each.
Fry the onion in oil until golden and cool it completely.
Mix the mince with the raw rice, onion, dill, thyme, salt and pepper.
Halve the larger leaves and roll parcels the size of a thumb.
Line the base of a pot with leaf trimmings and pieces of smoked rib.
Pack the sarmale in tight circles, laying ribs between every other layer.
Pour over tomato juice and water, cover with torn leaves and stew at 150 °C for three hours.
Cut the chicken into two-centimetre cubes and coat them in a mix of kecap manis, garlic, coriander and turmeric.
Marinate for at least two hours, ideally overnight in the fridge.
Grind the peanuts to a coarse crumb, keeping a few whole for serving.
Fry the shallot, garlic and chilli in oil until soft, add the ground peanuts and cook three minutes.
Add a cup of water, the tamarind, palm sugar and kecap manis and cook the sauce ten minutes to thicken.
Thread the pieces tight onto soaked skewers, five or six to each.
Grill over hot coals two minutes a side, basting with kecap manis. Serve with the sauce and rice.
Simmer the bird in salted water for an hour, lift it out and roast it at 200 °C for twenty minutes to colour.
Strain the broth, skim the fat and soften the finely chopped onion in it.
Grind the walnuts twice and press the released oil out by hand into a separate cup.
Crush the garlic with salt and the spices and work it into the walnut mass.
Let the walnut mass down with warm broth to the thickness of pouring cream and stir it into the onion.
Warm the sauce twenty minutes on the lowest heat without letting it boil, and stir in the vinegar.
Joint the bird, cover it with the sauce and chill it at least six hours. Drizzle the walnut oil over before serving.
Boil the vinegar with the wine, vegetables and spices, cool it completely and pour it over the beef. Keep it in the fridge three to five days, turning once a day.
Lift the meat out, dry it with kitchen paper and brown it hard on every side in a hot casserole. Strain the marinade, keeping the vegetables.
Fry the marinated vegetables in the same fat, add the sugar and let it catch a little colour. Pour in the marinade and bring it to the boil.
Return the meat, cover and braise over a low flame for two hours, turning it once halfway. A fork should meet no resistance.
Take the meat out and keep it warm. Stir the crumbled gingerbread and the raisins into the gravy and cook for fifteen minutes: the gingerbread dissolves and thickens it on its own.
Blend the gravy smooth and taste it for the balance of sour and sweet. Carve the meat across the grain and pour the gravy over.
Boil the potatoes in their skins until done, about twenty minutes from the boil. Test with a knife: it should go in without dropping through.
While they cook, warm the stock with the onion, vinegar, mustard, salt and pepper, without letting it boil.
Peel the potatoes while hot, holding them on a fork, and slice them three or four millimetres thick straight into the bowl.
Pour the hot dressing over and leave it twenty minutes, turning it once. The potato drinks almost all of the liquid.
Add the oil, turn it again and taste. It should be slightly sharper than feels right; the flavour settles as it stands.
Whisk the eggs and sugar over a water bath until warm, then beat them ten minutes to a thick pale foam.
Sift the flour with the cocoa and fold it in with a spatula in three additions, then the melted butter.
Bake the sponge at 175 °C for thirty-five minutes and cool it completely, ideally overnight.
Cut the sponge into three layers and soak each with cherry syrup mixed with kirsch.
Dissolve the gelatine, whip the cream with the icing sugar and add the gelatine in a thin stream.
Assemble: sponge, cream, cherries, cream again — three times over, finishing with cream.
Cover the sides and top with chocolate shavings, decorate with cherries and chill four hours.
Score the skin in diamonds every centimetre and a half, down to the fat but not into the meat.
Rub the knuckles with coarse salt, pepper, caraway and garlic, working it into the cuts.
Put them in a pot with the onion, carrot, celeriac and bay, and cover with beer and water.
Simmer for an hour, never letting it boil hard.
Move the knuckles to a tray, pat the skin dry and roast at 180 °C for an hour and twenty.
Every twenty minutes baste with beer from the pot and fat from the tray.
Raise the oven to 240 °C for the last ten minutes, until the crackling blisters.
Grate the onions finely and wring them dry in muslin, discarding the juice.
Toast the chickpea flour in a dry pan until it smells nutty and let it cool.
Mix the mince with the onion, ginger garlic paste, papaya, spices, coriander and chillies.
Work the mixture ten minutes, until it turns tacky and pulls back at your hand.
Fold in the chickpea flour and chill the mixture for at least an hour.
With wet hands mould the mince onto flat skewers in an even two-centimetre layer.
Grill over hot coals four minutes a side, basting with oil. Serve with naan.
Soak the rice in cold water overnight, drain it and pat it dry with a cloth.
Grind the wet rice in a blender with the milk to a smooth thick paste without grit.
Work in the sugar, melted ghee, mashed banana, cardamom, cloves and salt.
Beat the batter by hand for twenty minutes in circular movements, working air into it.
Let the batter stand an hour; it ferments slightly and turns bubbly.
Heat the oil to 165 °C and pour the batter into it in a ring, in one continuous movement.
Fry two minutes a side, turning with two chopsticks, to a golden colour.
Brown the diced pork in oil on all sides.
Add the onion and pepper and fry until soft, seven minutes.
Add the mushrooms and cook over a high heat for five minutes, until their water has gone.
Take it off the heat, stir in the paprika, garlic and tomato paste, add the wine and return it to the heat for three minutes.
Divide between clay pots, top up with water to the level of the meat, season and cover.
Bake at 180 °C for fifty minutes.
Take the lids off, cover with grated kashkaval and give it ten more minutes, to a browned cheese crust.
Rub the flour with a hundred grams of cold butter, a spoon of sugar, a yolk and the baking powder to a crumb and bring it into a dough.
Press the dough into a tin and bake it at 180 °C for fifteen minutes, to a pale gold.
Pass the curd through a sieve twice; the smoothness of the filling depends entirely on it.
Beat the remaining butter with the sugar until pale, add the yolks one by one, then the curd, soured cream, starch, vanilla and zest.
Whip the whites with a pinch of salt to firm peaks and fold them in with a spatula in three additions.
Fold in the raisins, pour the filling onto the base and level it.
Bake at 160 °C for fifty-five minutes, then switch the oven off and leave the cake inside with the door ajar for an hour.
Dissolve the yeast in the warm water, knead a soft dough with the flour, oil and salt, and work it ten minutes.
Leave the dough to rise somewhere warm for an hour, until doubled.
Grate the tomatoes and onion and drain them in a sieve, keeping a little of the juice.
Mix the mince with the grated vegetables, pomegranate molasses, tahini, baharat, salt and pepper.
Divide the dough into balls and roll them into ten-centimetre rounds.
Spread the topping in a thin layer, leaving half a centimetre at the rim, and scatter with pine nuts.
Bake at 220 °C for eight minutes, until the edges colour. Serve with lemon.
Soak the rice in salted water for an hour, then boil it seven minutes in plenty of water and drain.
Steep the saffron in three spoons of boiling water and leave it; it gives both colour and scent.
Brown the lamb, add the onion and cook until soft. Add the chestnuts, apricots, raisins and turmeric and stew for twenty minutes.
Butter a deep dish generously and line it with overlapping lavash, letting the edges hang outside.
Layer it: rice, filling, rice again. Pour over the saffron infusion and the rest of the butter.
Fold the lavash edges over the top, cover with foil and bake at 180 °C for forty minutes, then uncover and give it fifteen more to colour.
Rest ten minutes, cover with a platter and invert. Cut it at the table.
Fry the onion and peppers in the oil for ten minutes, until the pepper is soft and sweet.
Add the garlic, cumin, paprika and harissa and warm them for a minute — to the smell, not to burning.
Pour in the tomatoes, crush them and simmer for fifteen minutes. The sauce is ready when a spoon leaves a track on the bottom.
Make hollows with a spoon and break an egg into each. Cover and give it five to seven minutes: the whites set, the yolks stay loose.
Scatter over the feta and coriander and serve it in the pan with bread.
Char the peppers over a flame until the skin blackens, cover them with a bowl for ten minutes and peel them.
Cut the peeled peppers into strips, the tomatoes into dice and the onion into slices.
Fry the onion and garlic in olive oil until soft, eight minutes.
Stir in the harissa, tomato paste, caraway and coriander and cook them two minutes.
Add the peppers and tomatoes, season and stew twenty minutes to a thick paste.
Make wells in the sauce with a spoon and break an egg into each.
Cover and cook six minutes, until the whites set and the yolks stay liquid.
Boil the chickpeas in two litres of water with half the garlic for ninety minutes, until soft but whole.
Pound the remaining garlic with salt and cumin to a paste and stir it into the broth. Season.
Soft-boil the eggs, six minutes from the boil, and peel them.
Tear the bread into large pieces into deep bowls, filling them halfway.
Ladle the hot broth and chickpeas over the bread until it is thoroughly soaked.
Top with an egg, a spoon of harissa, olives, capers and tuna, then olive oil and lemon.
Fry the sliced shallot in oil until deep gold and set half aside for serving.
Add the garlic, paprika and turmeric and warm them a minute, until fragrant.
Add the minced chicken and fry it, breaking up lumps, until it whitens.
Add the chopped tomatoes and fish sauce and stew twenty-five minutes to a thick paste.
Grind the peanuts to a coarse crumb, keeping a few whole.
Boil the rice noodles, rinse them and divide them between bowls.
Spoon the sauce over the noodles and top with peanuts, fried shallot, pickled greens and coriander.
Mix the kefir with the bicarbonate and leave it five minutes; the mixture foams.
Add the egg, sugar, salt and melted butter and stir until even.
Work in the flour a little at a time and knead a soft dough that stays slightly tacky.
Cover it with a cloth and rest it half an hour at room temperature.
Divide it into seven balls and roll each into a thin twenty-centimetre round.
Prick each round in several places with a fork so it does not balloon in one bubble.
Fry them in hot oil a minute a side, to golden spots, and drain them on paper.
Fry the mince over a high flame, leaving it alone for the first minute so it takes dark colour. Lift it out, pouring off the excess fat.
In the same pan fry the onion and carrot for eight minutes, add the flour and tomato paste and cook two minutes.
Return the meat, pour in the stock and Worcestershire, add the thyme and cook uncovered for twenty minutes, until the gravy is thick.
Boil the potatoes and mash them with the butter and hot milk until smooth, seasoning generously. The mash should be firm rather than pourable.
Stir the peas into the meat, put it in a dish, cover with the mash and score the top with a fork.
Bake at 200 °C for twenty-five minutes until browned. Let it stand ten minutes before cutting.
Knead a stiff dough from the flour, water and salt and rest it forty minutes.
Fry the onion with the mince, baharat, salt and pepper, add the pine nuts and let it cool.
Roll the dough thin and cut four-centimetre rounds.
Shape half-moons around the filling and join the ends into a ring, like tortellini.
Bake the dumplings at 200 °C for twelve minutes, until golden.
Whisk the yoghurt with the starch, egg and salt and bring it to the boil, stirring without stopping in one direction.
Lower the dumplings into the sauce, cook ten minutes and pour over ghee with garlic and mint.
Char the peppers over a flame until the skin blackens, close them in a covered dish for ten minutes and peel them.
Cut the tomatoes and cucumbers into two-centimetre dice and the peppers into strips.
Mix the vegetables with the onion and parsley and dress with the oil, vinegar and salt.
Mound it on a dish and blanket it with the grated cheese without stirring. Finish with olives.
Soak the mustard seeds in warm water for twenty minutes.
Grind them with two chillies, a pinch of salt and a little water into a smooth paste.
Rub the fish steaks with turmeric and salt and leave them ten minutes.
Heat the mustard oil until it smokes, take it off and let it cool a minute; raw mustard oil is acrid.
Add the nigella, pour in the mustard paste let down with half a cup of water, and cook three minutes.
Lay the fish in a single layer, add the remaining chillies whole, cover and stew twelve minutes.
Finish with a spoon of raw mustard oil, take it off the heat and serve with rice.
Cover the carcasses with cold water, boil for ten minutes and pour it away. Rinse the bones and the pot: the clarity of the broth depends on it.
Cover again with fresh water, add the ginger and garlic and simmer for three hours. Put the kombu in twenty minutes before the end and lift it out before it boils — boiled kombu turns bitter.
For the tare, reduce the soy, mirin, sake and shiitake to a third. What is left is a thick dark liquid — two spoons per bowl.
Boil the eggs for six and a half minutes, cool them in iced water, peel and steep them in the leftover tare for two hours.
Boil the noodles separately, strictly to the time on the packet, drain and put them straight into bowls with the tare in the bottom.
Pour the hot broth over, stir once so the tare disperses, and lay on the pork, the egg and the spring onion. Finish with the sesame oil.
Cover the mutton with three litres of cold water and bring it slowly to the boil.
Skim for the first twenty minutes, never letting the broth bubble hard.
Add the chickpeas and simmer forty minutes.
Add the carrots halved lengthways and the onion in quarters and cook twenty minutes.
Add the potatoes whole, the tomatoes and the peppers and cook twenty-five minutes more.
Add the cumin, salt and the whole chilli and take it off the heat after five minutes.
Divide the meat and vegetables between bowls, ladle over the broth and pile chopped herbs on top.
Grind the garlic, all the spices, the crushed dried limes, vinegar, oil and salt into a thick paste.
Cut deep slashes to the bone and rub the paste inside them and all over the outside.
Refrigerate overnight, twelve hours at least.
Wrap the meat in banana leaves, then tightly in two layers of foil. No gap may remain.
Set the parcel on a tray, pour a cup of water into the tray and bake at 130 °C for eight hours.
Unwrap it, pour off the juices and cook the rice in them. Pull the meat into threads by hand.
Serve the meat over the rice, from a shared platter, eaten by hand.
Pound the meat under film to three or four millimetres. Work from the centre outwards or it tears.
Season and press into breadcrumbs with the flat of your hand. No egg wash is used here.
Dice the tomato, onion and beetroot small, mix with the parsley, salt and a spoon of oil.
Fry the boiled potato slices until golden and keep them warm.
Fry the steaks a minute and a half a side in hot oil; meat this thin cooks instantly.
Fry the eggs, leaving the yolks runny.
Build it: rice, potato, the steak across the whole plate, the egg, and the raw salsa over the top.
Cover the ribs with water, bring to the boil, skim and simmer for an hour with the onion and tomatoes.
Crush the softened tomatoes in the pot: they give the broth its body.
Add the tamarind paste and fish sauce, then taste. The sourness should be pronounced, not a hint.
Add the taro and daikon and cook ten minutes, then the aubergine and beans for five more.
Throw in the greens and chillies and take the pot off after thirty seconds. The greens should stay bright.
Rinse the barley and soak it in cold water for two hours.
Boil the barley in a litre and a half of water for an hour, until it collapses entirely.
Salt the porridge and cool it completely, stirring so no skin forms.
Work the curdled milk into the cold porridge gradually, to the consistency of a thick soup.
Leave it four hours somewhere cold so the sourness develops and evens out.
Boil the potatoes in their skins and serve them hot alongside.
Ladle it into bowls, add soured cream and scatter with spring onion and dill.
Knead a dough from the rye flour, warm water, melted butter and salt and rest it half an hour.
Boil the potatoes and carrots separately until completely soft.
Mash the potatoes with soured cream, an egg, caraway and salt into a smooth purée.
Mash the carrots with soured cream, an egg, sugar and cinnamon into a separate purée.
Roll the dough thin, cut rounds and shape rims with your fingers, folding the edges up.
Spread the potato purée as the first layer and the carrot over it, levelling with a spoon.
Bake at 200 °C for twenty-five minutes and dust them with cinnamon while still hot.
Dissolve the yeast in the warm milk with a spoon of sugar and leave it ten minutes.
Knead a dough from the flour, yeast mixture, sugar, cardamom, egg, salt and softened butter, working it fifteen minutes.
Let it rise somewhere warm for an hour, until doubled.
Cook a custard of milk, yolks, cornflour, sugar and vanilla and cool it completely under film.
Divide the dough into twelve balls, set them on a tray and prove them forty minutes.
Press a well into each bun with the base of a glass and spoon custard into it.
Bake at 200 °C for twelve minutes, cool them, pipe the icing in a ring and scatter the coconut.
Heat the milk to 85 °C, stirring, and hold it ten minutes without letting it boil.
Cool the milk to 40 °C by standing the pot in cold water.
Slacken the starter with a ladle of the warm milk and stir it back into the pot.
Add the rennet, stir for a few seconds and cover the pot.
Leave it somewhere warm for twelve hours, until the mass sets into a firm curd.
Turn the curd into a cloth and hang it over a bowl for six hours to drain the whey.
Whisk the skyr smooth and serve it with bilberries, cream and oats.
Dissolve the yeast with a spoon of sugar in the warm milk and leave it fifteen minutes, until it foams.
Knead a dough from the flour, sponge, yolks, remaining sugar, zest, salt and half the butter.
Let it rise somewhere warm for an hour, until doubled.
Divide it into twelve balls and flatten each into a disc on your palm.
Put a spoon of jam or curd in each, seal the seam and turn them seam down.
Dip each bun in melted butter and pack them touching in a tin.
Prove them forty minutes, bake at 180 °C for thirty-five minutes and dust them with icing sugar.
Butter every slice right to the edges. The layer should be visible to the eye rather than translucent.
For herring: a lettuce leaf, then pieces of herring, onion rings and capers. The lettuce keeps the brine off the bread.
For prawns: lay them in tight overlapping rows, then a spoon of mayonnaise, a slice of lemon and dill.
For egg: overlapping rounds of boiled egg, a line of mayonnaise, dill and a pinch of salt over the top.
Serve at once, with a knife and fork. Smørrebrød is not picked up by hand; it is not built for that.
Heat the oven to 220 °C in advance. The bread has to go in immediately after mixing; it cannot wait.
Mix both flours, the bicarbonate and the salt in a bowl and stir well so the soda spreads evenly.
Pour in the buttermilk and mix with a knife or your hand only until it comes together. The dough is sticky and uneven, which is correct.
Turn it onto a floured tray, shape it into a round loaf and cut a deep cross almost to the base.
Scatter the oats over and bake fifteen minutes at 220 °C, then thirty at 190 °C.
A finished loaf sounds hollow when its base is tapped. Cool it on a rack for at least an hour: hot soda bread will not slice.
Make a stock from the beef and the smoked ribs: an hour and a half at a bare simmer, skimming. Lift the meat out and pull it apart.
Fry the onion until soft, add the tomato paste and cook three minutes, until it darkens and stops smelling raw.
Add the cucumbers and cook them with the onion for five minutes, so they do not stay hard in the finished soup.
Put the fried mixture, the pulled meat, the sausage and the ham into the stock, pour in the brine and simmer for fifteen minutes.
Add the olives and capers, warm for five minutes and take it off. Check the salt only now: the brine and the smoked meat have already seasoned it.
In the bowl: a slice of lemon, soured cream and herbs. The lemon goes into the bowl rather than the pot, where boiling would turn it bitter.
Pound the conch with a mallet and cut it into small pieces. Squeeze lime over it.
Fry the onion, garlic and pepper in oil with the achiote until soft.
Add half the coconut milk let down with water and bring it up.
Add the conch and simmer forty minutes, until tender.
Add the cassava, plantain and carrot in large pieces and cook twenty minutes.
Add the remaining thick coconut milk and warm it five minutes without boiling.
Scatter with coriander and serve with lime and fried plantain.
Slice the onion thin and sweat it in the fat over a low heat for twenty minutes, until soft and sweet.
Pour the milk over the onion, take it off the heat and cool it to lukewarm.
Crumble the cheese and mix it with the corn flour and the sweetcorn kernels.
Stir in the onion and milk mixture and the yolks, salting cautiously; the cheese is salty already.
Whip the whites to firm peaks and fold them in with a spatula in three additions.
Spread the mixture into a greased tin in a four-centimetre layer.
Bake at 190 °C for fifty minutes, to a deep golden crust. Rest it twenty minutes before cutting.
Simmer the chicken in two litres of water for forty minutes, skimming for the first ten.
Slice half the shallots into thin rings, deep-fry them crisp and drain them on paper.
Pound the remaining shallot, garlic, turmeric, ginger and nuts into a bumbu paste.
Fry the paste in oil for five minutes with the bruised lemongrass and lime leaves.
Transfer the paste into the broth, season and simmer twenty minutes.
Lift out the chicken and shred it, soak the noodles and blanch the sprouts and cabbage.
Divide the noodles, chicken, vegetables and half an egg between bowls, ladle over the broth and top with fried shallot.
Cut the meat into large pieces of about two hundred grams, keeping the fat; it is needed.
Salt and pepper them generously all over and leave them half an hour at room temperature.
Light the coals and rake them to the sides, leaving the centre clear. Direct heat under the meat is not wanted.
Thread the pieces onto the spit, leaving a centimetre between them.
Turn the spit slowly and continuously for two hours. The meat should darken gradually rather than crust at once.
Dust with oregano ten minutes before the end and squeeze lemon over.
Take it off, cut it coarsely and serve in pita with onion, tomato and parsley.
Mix the oil, lemon juice and zest, oregano, crushed garlic, salt and pepper. Coat the meat and leave it two hours, and no more than four.
While it marinates, make the tzatziki: yoghurt with the squeezed cucumber, a clove of garlic, a spoon of oil and salt.
Thread the meat onto skewers loosely — the heat has to get between the pieces. A tightly packed skewer stays raw in the middle.
Cook on a hot grill or griddle, three minutes on each of the four sides. The meat should darken rather than pale.
Rest the meat for five minutes, warm the pitas thirty seconds a side, and serve with the tzatziki and lemon.
Bring a large pot of water to the boil and salt it properly — this is the only salt in the dish, since the cheese and the guanciale bring their own.
Put the guanciale into a cold pan and turn the heat to medium. The fat should render gradually and the pieces turn golden and crisp at the edges, about 6 to 8 minutes.
While the fat renders, beat the yolks, the whole egg, the grated pecorino and the pepper into a thick paste. Let it sit at room temperature so it does not seize when it meets hot pasta.
Cook the spaghetti a minute short of the packet time. Before draining, save a cup of the cooking water — the sauce will not come together without it.
Take the pan off the heat, add the pasta and toss it through the fat. Let the pan cool for twenty seconds — it should be warm, not hot.
Pour in the egg mixture and stir hard, adding pasta water a spoonful at a time until the sauce turns glossy and coats every strand. Serve immediately.
Chop the spinach, salt it and leave it twenty minutes. Squeeze it dry by the handful — more water comes out than seems possible.
Fry the spring onion in a spoon of oil until soft and let it cool.
Mix the spinach with the onion, feta, dill, eggs, nutmeg and pepper. Taste before salting: the feta is salty already.
Line the tin with seven sheets of filo, brushing each with olive oil and letting the edges overhang.
Spread the filling, fold the overhanging edges in and cover with six more sheets, brushing each one.
Score the top into portions without cutting through to the filling, flick water over it and bake at 180 °C for fifty minutes, to a deep gold.
Soak the dzavar overnight, then boil it in a litre of water until soft, about twenty-five minutes. Keep the water.
Whisk the matsun with the egg and flour until completely smooth. No lumps may remain; each one becomes a curd in the soup.
Pour the mixture into a cold pan and heat it over medium, stirring with a wooden spoon in one direction, until it comes to a boil.
At the first bubbles, stir in the wheat with its cooking water and hold it on a low heat for five more minutes.
Fry the onion in butter until golden and stir it into the soup with the dried mint. Salt to taste.
Ladle out and scatter with coriander. Spas must not be boiled twice; reheat it only until hot.
Soak the goraka in a cup of warm water for twenty minutes and keep the water.
Rub the fish with salt, turmeric and half the curry powder and leave it fifteen minutes.
Fry the onion, garlic, ginger, curry leaves, pandan, cinnamon and fenugreek until fragrant.
Add the remaining curry powder and chilli and warm them a minute without letting them scorch.
Add the thinned coconut milk with the goraka water and bring it to the boil.
Lay the fish steaks in a single layer, add the goraka and cook twelve minutes, rocking the pan.
Add the thick coconut milk and warm it five minutes without boiling. Serve with red rice.
Boil the potatoes in salted water for twenty minutes. Seven minutes before the end pile the kale on top to steam.
Meanwhile warm the sausage in water for twenty minutes without letting it boil: boiling splits the skin and the fat leaves.
Render the bacon until crisp and set it aside, keeping the fat.
Drain, crush the potato and kale together with a masher, working in the hot milk, butter, bacon fat and mustard.
Fold in the crackling, divide between plates, make a well and fill it with gravy. Slice the sausage and lay it over.
Pat the belly slices dry with paper and salt them on both sides.
Lay them in a single layer in a cold dry pan and turn the heat to medium.
Fry eight minutes a side, pouring the rendered fat off into a cup as it collects.
Boil the potatoes in their skins until tender and peel them hot.
Melt the butter, stir in the flour and cook it two minutes without letting it colour.
Pour in the milk in a thin stream, whisking until smooth, and cook the sauce five minutes.
Stir in the mountain of chopped parsley, the nutmeg, salt and pepper and serve with the pork, potatoes and beetroot.
Cover the chopped dates with a cup of boiling water and the bicarbonate and leave them fifteen minutes.
Mash the dates with a fork into a coarse paste, water and all.
Beat a hundred grams of the butter with a hundred and fifty of the sugar until pale, adding the eggs one by one.
Fold in the flour with the baking powder, then the date paste; the batter comes out loose, which is correct.
Pour it into a greased tin and bake at 180 °C for thirty-five minutes, to a skewer that comes out with moist crumbs.
Melt the remaining butter with the remaining sugar and the cream and cook the sauce five minutes to thicken.
Prick the warm sponge with a skewer, pour over half the sauce and serve the rest in a jug.
Knead a soft dough from the flour, warm water, oil and salt and work it fifteen minutes.
Cover it with a warmed bowl and rest it forty minutes; the dough has to turn pliable.
Work the curd with the eggs, soured cream, sugar and raisins until even.
Stretch the dough by hand on a cloth until translucent, as for strudel.
Spread the filling over the sheet, leaving the edges clear, and roll it up using the cloth.
Wrap the roll loosely in a clean cloth, tie the ends and lower it into boiling salted water.
Boil it forty minutes, unwrap it, cut it into rounds and fry them in butter with the breadcrumbs.
Strip the tough stems from the leaves, roll the leaves up and shred them fine.
Fry the onion in oil until soft, add the garlic and cumin and warm them a minute.
Add the chopped tomatoes and cook seven minutes, until they collapse into a paste.
Add the greens, salt them and stir. They collapse by half within a minute.
Add half a cup of water, cover and stew ten minutes; the greens should soften but stay green.
Finish with lemon juice and serve with ugali or rice.
Break up the brick tea and cover it with a litre of cold water in a pot.
Bring it to the boil and cook five minutes, until the liquor darkens.
Pour in the milk and bring it back to the boil, watching that it does not run over.
Salt it and cook five minutes more over a low heat.
Ladle the tea up and pour it back from a height a dozen times.
Add the butter and stir until it disappears.
Strain it into bowls and serve it hot, with toasted flour if you like.
Grind the peanuts to a fine crumb, wrap them in a cloth and press hard: the oil stays on the cloth and the powder comes out dry.
Mix the peanut powder with the ginger, garlic, cayenne, paprika, crumbled stock cube and salt: this is the yaji.
Oil the strips of beef and coat them in half the rub. Leave them half an hour.
Thread the meat onto skewers in waves so the heat gets between the folds, and grill it over a fierce fire two or three minutes a side.
Dust the hot meat with the other half of the rub and serve with onion rings, tomato and cabbage.
Lard the beef with strips of smoked fat laid along the grain. Bury it in the grated roots with the spices and vinegar and refrigerate for a day.
Dry the meat and brown it in butter on all sides. Lift it out.
In the same pan fry the roots from the marinade with the onion for twenty minutes: they should darken noticeably, which is where the colour comes from.
Return the meat, pour in the marinade and enough water to reach the vegetables, and braise covered for two hours over a low flame.
Take the meat out, remove the bay and blend the vegetables with the liquid until smooth. Pass it through a sieve: this is the step that separates a home svíčková from a restaurant one.
Stir in the cream, lemon juice and sugar, warm it without boiling and taste. Carve the meat across the grain and serve with the sauce, lingonberry and a slice of lemon.
Push the curd through a sieve or blitz it. Grainy curd makes grainy syrniki; this step is not optional.
Work in the egg, sugar, vanilla and salt, then the flour. The mixture stays sticky; that is correct.
With wet or lightly floured hands shape discs about a centimetre and a half thick. Thicker and the middle stays raw, thinner and they dry out.
Fry over medium heat with a lid on, three or four minutes a side. The lid matters more than the butter: it steams the middle through.
Rinse the bulgur and pour the juice of one lemon over it. Leave it to swell for fifteen minutes.
Wash the parsley well in advance and dry it thoroughly — an hour on a cloth is not too much. Strip the thick stems and chop it fine but without pulverising it.
Dice the tomatoes small and salt them separately: the juice they give up goes into the bulgur.
Mix everything with the juice of the second lemon, the oil and the allspice. Let it stand ten minutes before serving.
Seed the chillies and toast them in a dry pan until they smell — twenty seconds a side, no longer, or they turn bitter. Cover with boiling water for fifteen minutes.
Blend the softened chillies with half the pineapple, the achiote, vinegar, garlic, cumin and oregano to a smooth paste. Season it.
Coat the pork in the marinade and leave it at least two hours, ideally overnight. Do not go past a day: the pineapple will soften the meat to mush.
Get a pan searing hot and cook the meat in batches, two minutes a side. Do not stir until dark edges appear.
Sear the rest of the pineapple in the same pan and dice it. Chop the meat roughly, warm the tortillas twenty seconds a side and build: meat, pineapple, onion, coriander, lime.
Boil three litres of water with the root vegetables, bay and peppercorns and lower the beef into it.
Skim, and hold it just below a simmer for two and a half hours, never letting it bubble.
Halve the onions and char the cut faces black on a dry pan; they give the broth its colour.
Add the charred onion and the marrow bones to the pot for the last hour.
Grate the apples and mix them with the horseradish; that is Apfelkren, and it is made just before serving.
Boil the potatoes, slice them and fry them in butter until browned.
Slice the meat across the grain, serve the broth separately and the meat with the horseradish, potatoes and chives.
Grind the garlic, ginger, turmeric, saffron, chopped herbs, oil, salt and pepper into a paste. Rub it over the chicken and leave it an hour.
Spread the onion in an even layer over the base of the tagine or a heavy pan: it keeps the chicken off the bottom and becomes part of the sauce.
Set the chicken on top skin up, pour the water down the side, cover and cook over a low flame for forty minutes without lifting the lid.
Add the preserved lemon peel in strips and the olives, cover and give it twenty minutes more.
Take the lid off and reduce the sauce for five minutes if it is still loose. Check the salt only at the end: the lemon and olives have already provided it.
Rinse the rice until the water runs clear and soak it in salted water for an hour. That removes surplus starch and lets the grains grow longer.
Boil the rice in plenty of salted water for five to seven minutes: a grain should bend but snap under pressure. Drain and rinse with warm water.
Grind the saffron and steep it in two spoons of hot water. Mix a couple of spoons of the rice with the yoghurt and saffron: this becomes the crust.
Heat the fat in the pot, lay the potato rounds edge to edge, spread the rice and yoghurt mixture over them and pile the rest of the rice on top in a mound.
Make five holes down to the base with the handle of a spoon for the steam to travel. Pour melted butter over.
Cover with a lid wrapped in a cloth, five minutes on a high flame and forty-five on the lowest. Do not lift the lid.
Stand the base of the pot in cold water for a minute and the crust releases. Invert it onto a plate in one movement.
Peel the papaya and shred it into long fine strips with a knife or a som tam grater.
Pound the garlic and chillies in the mortar into a coarse paste.
Add the cut beans and bruise them lightly with the pestle.
Add the tomatoes and crush them until their juice runs.
Add the padaek, lime juice and palm sugar and mix with the pestle and a spoon.
Add the papaya and work the pestle, turning with the spoon, for two minutes, until the fibres soften.
Taste and adjust for sourness, salt and heat. Serve with sticky rice.
Simmer the pork with the onion and salt for an hour. Strain and keep the broth.
Toast the seeds, sesame, chillies and tomatoes in a dry pan and blend them with broth; that is the recado.
Cook the recado twenty minutes to thicken it and season.
Slake the masa harina with warm broth, add the melted lard and work it twenty minutes over a low heat.
Pass the banana leaves over a flame for ten seconds each so they turn pliable.
On a leaf spread the dough, then a piece of meat, a spoon of recado, a strip of pepper and an olive. Wrap in two leaves.
Stack the parcels seam down in a pot and steam them for an hour and a half.
Grate the cucumbers coarsely or dice them small and salt them.
Leave the cucumber ten minutes to give up its water, but do not pour that water away.
Crush the garlic with salt into a paste so it does not turn up in pieces.
Grind the walnuts to a fine crumb, keeping a few larger pieces back.
Whisk the yoghurt with the cold water until even and add the garlic and walnuts.
Stir in the cucumber with its juice, the chopped dill and the sunflower oil.
Chill it an hour and serve with an ice cube in each bowl.
Peel the apples, halve them, core them and squeeze lemon over them.
Melt the sugar in a cast-iron pan over medium heat to an amber caramel, without stirring it with a spoon.
Take it off the heat and beat in the butter piece by piece, with the vanilla and a pinch of salt.
Pack the apple halves cut side up, tight against each other, in a circle.
Cook on the hob for twenty minutes over medium heat, until the apples sink and take up the caramel.
Cover with a round of puff pastry, tucking the edges down inside the pan, and prick it in several places.
Bake at 200 °C for forty minutes, rest it five, and invert it onto a plate in one movement.
Drain the soaked beans, cover them with fresh water, bring it to the boil and drain again after ten minutes.
Cover them a third time, add one whole onion and boil an hour until soft, without salt.
Fry the sliced onion in oil until golden, take it off the heat and stir in the paprika and flour.
Pour off some of the bean water, leaving it level with the beans, salt them and stir in the onion mixture.
Transfer to a clay pan, arrange the dried peppers on top and scatter with mint.
Bake at 200 °C for forty minutes, until a browned crust forms on top.
Rest ten minutes and serve straight from the pan, scattered with parsley.
Rub the lamb with salt, pepper, garlic and oregano and roast it at 190 °C for forty minutes.
Parboil the rice for seven minutes and drain it.
Melt the butter, stir in the flour and cook it two minutes, to a nutty smell.
Whisk the yoghurt with the eggs and salt until completely smooth and add the flour mixture.
Spread the rice in an even layer in an earthenware dish and lay the meat and its juices on top.
Pour the yoghurt mixture over so it covers everything by a finger's depth.
Bake at 180 °C for fifty minutes, until the top browns and the middle still trembles slightly.
Rub the lamb with salt, pepper, garlic and oregano and roast it at 190 °C for forty minutes, dotted with butter.
Parboil the rice for seven minutes and drain it.
Melt the remaining butter, stir in the flour and cook two minutes to a nutty smell.
Whisk the yoghurt with the eggs and salt, add the flour mixture and beat until completely smooth.
Stir in the rice. It takes up some of the moisture and keeps the custard from splitting.
Arrange the meat and its juices in a dish and pour the yoghurt mixture over.
Bake at 180 °C for forty-five minutes, until the top colours and the centre still trembles slightly.
Score the prawns three times on the inner curve and straighten them slightly, so they do not curl into rings in the oil.
Combine the dashi, soy and mirin, bring them to the boil and take them off: this is tentsuyu. Serve it with grated daikon.
Heat the oil to 180 °C. Only when it is ready do you mix the batter — not before.
Beat the cold egg into the iced water, tip in the flour and cornflour and stir with chopsticks for five or six strokes. Leave the lumps.
Dust the pieces in dry flour, dip them in the batter and lower them in three or four at a time. Fry ninety seconds to two minutes.
Drain on a rack, never on paper. Between batches skim the floating scraps of batter out of the oil: they burn and taint the flavour.
Pound the parsley, garlic, chilli and salt into the rof paste and press it into slashes cut in the fish.
Fry the fish three minutes a side and set it aside.
In the same oil fry the onion until soft, add the tomato paste and cook five minutes, until it darkens.
Add two litres of water, the tamarind and the vegetables and cook twenty-five minutes.
Return the fish to the pot for ten minutes, then lift it and the vegetables out and keep them warm.
Add the rinsed rice to the remaining broth — twice as much liquid as rice — and cook covered for thirty minutes without stirring.
Turn the rice onto a large platter with the fish and vegetables on top. Share out the caught layer from the bottom separately.
Brown the meat in oil, add the onion and fry until soft.
Stir in the tomato paste and cook five minutes, until it darkens.
Add a litre and a half of water, season and cook forty minutes.
Slacken the peanut butter with two ladles of the broth until smooth and lump-free.
Pour the paste into the pot in a thin stream, stirring continuously.
Add the vegetables in large pieces and the whole chilli and stew thirty minutes, stirring.
Wait for the peanut oil to rise to the surface, remove the chilli and serve with rice.
Whisk the yolks with half the sugar over a pan of boiling water, without touching the water, until pale and thick — about seven minutes. Take it off and cool to room temperature.
Fold the cold mascarpone into the cooled yolks with a spoon rather than a mixer. A mixer breaks the fat and the cream turns grainy — the first place tiramisu usually fails.
Whip the whites with the rest of the sugar to firm peaks and fold them into the cream in three additions, lifting from underneath.
Mix the coffee with the marsala. Dip each savoiardo for one second a side and lay them in a tight layer in the dish.
Spread half the cream, level it, then repeat the biscuit and cream layers. Cover and refrigerate for at least six hours, better overnight.
Dust with cocoa through a sieve right before serving. Do it in advance and the cocoa takes on moisture and goes blotchy.
Drain the prawns in a sieve and let them sit for at least ten minutes.
Mix the mayonnaise with the crème fraîche, chopped dill, horseradish, lemon juice, salt and pepper.
Chop the red onion as fine as you can and stir it into the dressing.
Fold the prawns into the dressing gently, taking care not to crush them.
Trim the crusts from the bread and fry the slices in butter until browned on both sides.
Pile the prawns onto each toast, top with a spoon of roe and a sprig of dill. Serve at once.
Peel the prawns, leaving the tails on. Keep the shells and heads: the broth is built on them.
Fry the shells in the pot for a couple of minutes until bright orange, cover with the water and simmer fifteen minutes. Strain.
Return the broth to the heat, add the lemongrass, galangal and lime leaves and let them steep at a low simmer for five minutes.
Add the mushrooms and the crushed chillies, then after two minutes the prawns. They are done the moment they curl into a C — beyond that they turn rubbery.
Take the pot off the heat. Add the fish sauce, lime juice and sugar, stir and taste. Adjust a spoon at a time until sour, salty and hot sit where you want them.
Ladle into bowls and scatter over the coriander. Leave the lemongrass and galangal in the pot, or warn people not to eat them.
Mix the flour with the salt and baking powder in a large bowl.
Melt the lard and stir it into the hot water until even.
Pour the liquid into the flour and work it with a spoon until it cools enough to handle.
Knead by hand for ten minutes to a smooth elastic dough.
Cover it and rest it twenty minutes at room temperature.
Divide it into eight, roll each into a half-centimetre round and cut a slit in the centre.
Fry at 180 °C for a minute and a half a side and serve with sugar or dulce de leche.
Heat the oil in a deep pan until it is warm rather than hot — a slice of potato dropped in should sigh, not crackle. Add the potato and onion and salt them.
Poach for twenty minutes, turning gently now and then. It is ready when a slice breaks easily against the side of the pan. Drain through a colander, keeping the potato.
Beat the eggs with a pinch of salt and fold the warm potato through them. Let it sit for ten minutes: the potato gives up starch and the tortilla holds together for it.
In a 24 cm pan with a spoon of oil, pour the mixture in and cook over medium heat for four minutes, easing the edges towards the middle with a spatula.
Cover with a plate, flip in one movement and slide it back raw side down. Three minutes more leaves the centre slightly loose, which is how it should be.
Score the plantain skin lengthways and lever it off with a knife; a green one will not peel by hand.
Cut them across into three-centimetre pieces.
Crush half the garlic with salt and stir it into half a litre of warm water.
Fry the pieces at 160 °C for four minutes, until soft but not golden.
Flatten each piece with the base of a glass or a press to a centimetre thick.
Dip the discs in the garlic water for a second and pat them dry.
Fry them a second time at 190 °C for two minutes to a crisp shell, salt them and serve with a mojo of the remaining garlic, olive oil and lime.
Fry the onion and garlic until soft, add both minces and cook, breaking up lumps, for ten minutes.
Add all the spices, season, and pour in the stock.
Simmer gently for forty minutes, until the liquid has almost gone.
Stir in the mashed potato and cool the filling completely.
Line a tin with pastry, add the cold filling and level it.
Cover with a second sheet, crimp the edges, cut vents and glaze with egg.
Bake at 200 °C for fifteen minutes, then at 180 °C for forty more, to a deep golden crust.
Dissolve the yeast with a spoon of sugar in the warm milk and let it foam for ten minutes.
Knead a dough from the flour, the yeast liquid, eggs, sugar and salt for ten minutes, then work in the soft butter piece by piece. Prove for an hour.
Roll the dough out and cut two-centimetre ribbons. Butter the spits and roll them in sugar.
Wind a ribbon round each spit, overlapping by a third and pulling it slightly taut. Roll it on the table so the layers bond.
Brush with butter, roll in the sugar, nut and cinnamon mixture and bake at 190 °C for eighteen minutes, turning every five.
Let it cool three minutes and twist it off the spit. Hot, it tears; fully cooled, it sticks.
Knead a soft dough from the flour, baking powder, salt and warm water, working it ten minutes.
Cover it and rest it an hour; the dough should become pliable and stop springing back.
Marinate the chicken with the curry powder, garlic, thyme and salt and stew it with the potato for forty minutes.
Divide the dough into six balls, roll each one thin and brush it with oil.
Roll the round into a rope, coil it into a spiral and let it rest twenty minutes.
Roll the spirals out into rounds again and cook them on a dry pan a minute and a half a side, brushing with ghee.
Move the bread onto a board and beat it into soft rags with two spatulas. Serve with the curry.
Knead a stiff dough from the flour, water and salt and rest it thirty minutes.
Roll it thin, brush with fat, roll it up and cut across into half-centimetre strips.
Separate the strips by hand and spread them on a board so they do not stick.
Sear the mutton in the fat over a high heat, then add the onion, carrot, potato and cabbage.
Add a cup of water, season and bring it to the boil.
Lay the noodles in an even layer over the meat without stirring, cover and hold twenty minutes on a low heat.
Take the lid off, add the garlic and toss everything together. Serve at once.
Peel the apples and core them without going through, so each forms a cup.
Make a syrup of water, sugar, lemon juice and cinnamon, bringing it to the boil.
Lower the apples into the syrup and poach them twenty minutes on a low heat, turning them.
Lift the apples out with a slotted spoon and cool them completely, keeping the syrup.
Mix the ground walnuts with three spoons of the syrup into a pliable mass.
Fill the apples with the walnut mass, mounded, and set them in dishes.
Spoon over the remaining syrup and top with whipped cream and a walnut half.
Knead a stiff dough from the flour, egg, water and salt and work it fifteen minutes.
Cover the dough and rest it forty minutes; that is what makes it pliable.
Chop the lamb and tail fat by knife into a fine crumb.
Mix the meat with finely chopped onion, cumin, salt and pepper.
Roll the dough until translucent and cut five-centimetre rounds.
Fold the dumplings, sealing the edge and bringing two corners together into a ring.
Cook them in the boiling broth for eight minutes and serve them in a bowl with katyk and coriander.
Mix the kefir with the bicarbonate and leave it five minutes, until it bubbles. Add the egg, salt and flour and knead for eight minutes.
Cover the dough and rest it half an hour. Meanwhile let the cherries drain in a colander.
Mix the starch with the sugar and toss the cherries in it right before shaping.
Roll the dough to two millimetres, cut discs, put three or four cherries on each and seal the rim dry, pressing the air out.
Boil in batches in a wide pot of salted water. Two minutes after they float, lift them out and butter them at once.
Rub the pork with salt, pepper, caraway and garlic and leave it an hour at room temperature.
Brown the pork in lard on all sides, add the onion and pour in water to half the height of the meat.
Braise covered at 160 °C for an hour and a half, basting every twenty minutes.
Knead a dough from the flour, warm milk with yeast, the egg and salt and let it rise forty minutes.
Fold in the bread cubes, shape two logs and boil them ten minutes on each side.
Stew the sauerkraut with onion, caraway and sugar for twenty-five minutes.
Cut the dumplings with thread and the pork into slices, and serve with the cabbage under the pan juices.
Boil the barley in salted water for forty minutes, to half done, and drain it.
Render the pork fat to crackling, add the onion and fry it golden.
Cool both the barley and the fat with onion completely, or the blood sets when they meet.
Strain the blood through a sieve and mix it with the barley, fat, marjoram, allspice and salt.
Rinse the casings and fill them two-thirds full, leaving room for the barley to swell.
Tie the sausages every twenty centimetres and prick them in several places with a needle.
Bake at 180 °C for forty-five minutes, dotted with butter, and serve with lingonberry jam.
Shred the cabbage finely and mix it with the tomatoes, onion, vinegar, lime juice and salt.
Leave the curtido to pickle at least an hour, stirring it now and then.
Cut the pork skin into squares, salt it and leave it twenty minutes.
Render the skin in its own fat over a low heat for forty minutes.
Raise the heat and fry ten minutes more, until the crackling puffs and turns crisp.
Boil the cassava in salted water until tender, having cut out the woody core.
Lay the cassava on a banana leaf, the curtido over it and the crackling on top, with the chilli.
Drain the soaked rice and grind it with the coconut milk into a smooth, loose batter.
Stir in the yeast, sugar, cardamom, salt and grated coconut.
Leave the batter to ferment four hours in the warm, until it is covered in bubbles.
Stir the batter and check the body: it should pour in a ribbon rather than drop in a lump.
Heat the dimpled pan and brush each well with oil.
Fill the wells three-quarters full and cook three minutes, until the edges set.
Turn the cakes with a skewer and give them three minutes more, to a browned sphere.
Brown the chicken pieces with the annatto on every side.
Add the onion, pepper, tomatoes and carrot and stew until the vegetables soften.
Pour in two litres of water, salt it and simmer forty minutes over a low heat.
Mix the corn flour with the grated cheese, egg, oregano and a pinch of salt.
Add a couple of spoons of hot broth and work it into a firm dough that holds its shape.
Roll walnut-sized balls, compacting each between your palms.
Drop the balls into the boiling broth, leave them five minutes unstirred and cook twenty. Scatter with parsley.
Rinse the sorghum leaves and boil them in a litre and a half of water for ten minutes; the water turns deep red.
Take the leaves out, add a pinch of soda and the beans and cook forty-five minutes, until nearly done.
Rinse the rice until the water runs clear and add it to the pot. The liquid should stand a finger above the rice.
Salt it, cover and cook twenty minutes on a low heat without stirring.
Take it off the heat, leave it covered ten minutes, then fluff it with a fork.
Fry slices of ripe plantain until caramel-coloured.
Serve with egg, gari, shito and plantain, all on one plate.
Simmer the chicken with the onion, bay and thyme for forty minutes and strain the broth.
Cut the leek, carrot and celeriac into fine julienne of equal length.
Sweat the vegetables in butter for ten minutes, without letting them colour.
Add the broth and the potato in batons and cook fifteen minutes.
Joint the chicken, return it to the pot and take it off the heat.
Whisk the yolks with the cream and ladle in hot broth, stirring, until the bowl warms up.
Pour the mixture back into the pot off the heat, warm it through without boiling, and add lemon and parsley.
Rinse the whitebait in cold water and drain it in a sieve for ten minutes.
Pat the whitebait dry with a cloth; excess water stops the fritter setting.
Whisk the eggs with the flour, salt and pepper until smooth and lump-free.
Fold the whitebait into the egg mixture gently, taking care not to crush it.
Melt the butter in a pan over medium heat until it just sizzles.
Pour in a ladle of the mixture and spread it into a thin round a centimetre thick.
Fry a minute and a half a side and serve with lemon and buttered bread.
Beat the meat between two sheets of film to three millimetres. Use the flat side of the mallet, not the toothed one: teeth tear the fibres.
Beat the eggs to an even liquid without foam. Salt the meat and coat it in flour, then egg, then crumbs.
Do not press the crumbs on. The coating has to sit loosely; only then will it lift and puff.
Heat a centimetre of fat to 170 °C and lower the schnitzel in. Fry two minutes, swirling the pan the whole time so fat washes over the top.
Turn it and give it ninety seconds more, to gold. Drain on a rack and serve immediately with a wedge of lemon.
Separate two yolks and rub them through the cold rice with your hands until every grain is coated. Beat the remaining eggs separately.
Heat the wok with a spoon of oil until it smokes, pour in the beaten eggs, let them set and break them into pieces. Set them aside.
Fry the prawns for ninety seconds, add the ham, carrot and peas and cook a minute more. Add them to the eggs.
Add the rest of the oil, tip in the rice and fry three minutes at full heat, tossing constantly. The grains should be jumping in the wok, not sitting in it.
Return everything to the wok, pour the wine down the side and add the soy, season and toss for thirty seconds more. Scatter over the spring onion.
Mix the lemon juice, mustard, garlic, salt and pepper, pour it over the chicken and onions and chill for at least four hours.
Lift out the chicken, pat it dry and brown it in oil on all sides.
In the same pan cook the onion from the marinade over medium heat for twenty-five minutes, until golden and soft.
Pour in the remaining marinade and the stock and add the bay leaves and the whole chilli.
Return the chicken, cover and stew thirty minutes on a low heat.
Uncover and reduce the sauce ten minutes more until thick. Remove the chilli.
Serve with boiled rice, the onions piled over the chicken.
Knead a dough from the flour, warm water, oil, egg and salt for ten minutes to elasticity. Oil it and rest it half an hour.
Mash the curd with the eggs, soured cream and salt. The filling should be firm rather than pourable.
Stretch the dough on a cloth by hand until translucent, brush it with melted butter and spread the filling over a third of it.
Roll it up by lifting the cloth and cut it into eight-centimetre pieces, sealing the ends by pressing with the edge of your hand.
Boil them in salted water for five minutes after they float and lift them out with a slotted spoon.
Lay them in a dish, pour the cream over, trickle on melted butter and bake at 200 °C for twenty-five minutes, to a browned top.
Rinse the rice until the water runs clear and soak it twenty minutes.
Simmer the beef with half the spices for forty minutes, until tender. Keep the broth.
Fry the onion in oil over medium heat for twenty minutes, to a deep brown, almost black.
Add the garlic, ginger and the remaining spices and warm them two minutes.
Add the cooked meat and the diced potato, stir and warm through five minutes.
Add the rice, pour in broth at one and a half times the volume of the rice, and season.
Bring it up, cover and cook twenty minutes on a low heat without lifting the lid. Rest it ten minutes.
Cover the chicken with three litres of cold water, bring it up and skim.
Simmer forty minutes on a low heat with a whole onion.
Knead a stiff dough from the flour and eggs, roll it thin, let it dry and cut it into fine noodles.
Lift out the chicken and joint it, and add the carrot, pepper and potato to the broth.
After fifteen minutes add the noodles and cook five minutes.
Boil the borș separately, strain it and pour it into the soup. Cook five minutes.
Return the meat, season and stir in the lovage and parsley. Let it stand ten minutes.
Grate the potatoes finely and squeeze them lightly, leaving some moisture in.
Crush the garlic with salt into a paste and work it into the potato mass.
Add the egg, milk, marjoram, pepper and flour and stir to a loose batter.
Heat the oil over medium and pour in a ladle of batter, spreading it very thin.
Fry three minutes a side, to a deep golden crisp crust.
Drain them on a rack rather than paper and serve them at once.
Cut the veal into fine strips across the grain and pat them dry.
Heat a pan with butter and sear the meat in batches for thirty seconds, moving it onto a plate.
Fry the shallot and mushrooms in the same pan until their water has gone.
Stir in the flour, cook it a minute and add the wine, reducing it by half.
Add the stock and cream and reduce the sauce to a coating consistency, about eight minutes.
Return the meat with its collected juices, warm it a minute without boiling, and add lemon.
Scatter with parsley and serve with rösti set alongside rather than under the meat.
Marinate the lamb in yoghurt with the hawaij and salt for two hours.
Rinse the rice until the water runs clear and soak it thirty minutes.
Fry the onion in ghee to a deep gold and set half of it aside.
Brown the meat with the remaining onion, add the tomatoes and cardamom and stew an hour.
Fry the potato rounds to a golden crust in a separate pan.
Boil the rice in salted water for seven minutes, to half done, and drain it.
Layer the meat, rice, potato and raisins, streak the saffron over and bake it covered for thirty minutes.
Render the bacon in a pot, soften the onion in it, add the garlic and marjoram and warm them for half a minute.
Pour in the stock, lower the sausage in whole and simmer for thirty minutes. Do not pierce it, or its juices leave too early.
Lift the sausage out, slice it and return it to the pot. Shake the starter in its jar and pour it in, stirring.
Warm it for five minutes without letting it boil hard, stir in the cream and taste. If it is not sour enough, add more starter; salt at the end.
Ladle into bowls, add half a boiled egg each and serve with horseradish. In Poland żurek often comes in a hollowed loaf.
